Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 12, verse 1:

(p-176) Surat Yusuf [peace be upon him]

Section on its revelation

It is Meccan by consensus. Regarding the cause of its revelation there are two opinions. As for the first opinion, it is narrated from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, who said: "The Qur'an was revealed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he recited it to them for a time. They said: 'O Messenger of Allah, if only you would relate to us (qassa)!' So Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿Alif, Lam, Ra. These are the verses of the Clear Book﴾ up to His words: ﴿We relate to you the best of stories﴾. He recited it to them for a time, and they said: 'O Messenger of Allah, if only you would narrate to us (haddatha)!' So Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿Allah has sent down the best statement, a Book consistent and repeating﴾ [Az-Zumar: 23]. All of this they were commanded with regard to the Qur'an." (p-177) 'Awn ibn 'Abdullah said: "The Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) became weary for a time, and they said: 'O Messenger of Allah, narrate to us!' So Allah the Mighty and Majestic revealed: ﴿Allah has sent down the best statement, a Book consistent and repeating﴾ [Az-Zumar: 23]. Then they grew weary again and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, something above the narrative (hadith) and below the Qur'an,' meaning stories (qasas). So Allah revealed: ﴿We relate to you the best of stories﴾. They wanted narrative, so He guided them to the best narrative, and they wanted stories, so He guided them to the best stories." The second: Ad-Dahhak narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The Jews asked the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'Tell us about the affair of Ya'qub and his sons and the matter of Yusuf.' So Allah the Mighty and Majestic revealed: ﴿Alif, Lam, Ra. These are the verses of the Clear Book﴾ ﴿Indeed, We have sent it down as an Arabic Qur'an﴾." That is because the Torah is in Hebrew and the Gospel is in Syriac, while you are an Arab people; and had We sent it down in other than Arabic, you would not have understood it. We have already explained the tafsir of the opening of this surah at the beginning of (Surat) Yunus. However, Ibn al-Anbari has mentioned an additional aspect regarding this surah, saying: "When weariness and boredom afflicted the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), they said to him: 'Narrate to us something that will remove this weariness from us.' He said: 'Those narratives by which you can benefit and by which boredom is dispelled are the verses of the Clear Book.'"

Regarding the meaning of "al-Mubin" (the Clear) there are five opinions:

The first: its lawful and unlawful are clear; this is said by Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid. The second: it clarifies the letters that fall from the tongues of non-Arabs; narrated by Khalid ibn Ma'dan from Mu'adh ibn Jabal. The third: its guidance and right direction are clear; said by Qatadah. The fourth: it distinguishes truth from falsehood. The fifth: its inimitability is clear, so it cannot be opposed; both of these were mentioned by al-Mawardi.

(p-178) His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, We sent it down﴾. Regarding the pronoun (ha' al-kinaya) in it, there are two opinions:

One is that it refers to the Book. This is the view of the majority. The second is that it refers to the account of Yusuf. This was mentioned by al-Zajjaj and Ibn al-Qasim.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿an Arabic Qur'an﴾. We have already mentioned the meaning of "Qur'an" and its derivation in surah al-Nisa' (82). People have differed over whether there is anything in the Qur'an that is not Arabic. The position of our companions is that there is nothing in it that is not Arabic. Abu 'Ubayda said: "Whoever claims that the Qur'an contains a language other than Arabic has greatly exaggerated against God," and he argued with His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have made it an Arabic Qur'an﴾ (al-Zukhruf: 3). It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, and Ikrima that it contains words from other than the language of the Arabs, such as "sijjil," "al-mishkat," "al-yamm," "al-Tur," "abariq," and "istabraq," and others. I read to our shaykh Abu Mansur al-Lughawi, who said: Abu 'Ubayd said: "These men [Ibn 'Abbas and his circle] have more knowledge than Abu 'Ubayda, but they held one view while he held another, and both are correct, God willing. The matter is that these words were originally not of the Arabic language. Those (Ibn 'Abbas and his circle) spoke of the original, and then the Arabs pronounced them with their tongues and arabized them, so they became Arabic through their arabization of them. Thus they are Arabic in this state, though non-Arabic in origin." This view agrees with both groups together.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿that you may understand﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: "So that you may comprehend."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 12, verse 3:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We relate to you the best of stories﴾. We have already mentioned the occasion of its revelation at the beginning of the discussion (p-179). It has also been specified by another occasion: it is narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr who said: The companions of Muhammad (ﷺ) gathered around Salman and said: "Tell us about the Torah, for indeed it contains good things." So God, exalted is He, revealed: ﴿We relate to you the best of stories﴾, meaning: the stories of the Qur'an are better than what is in the Torah.

Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is: We explain to you the best of explanations. The qassas (narrator) is the one who presents the story according to its reality. He said: His saying, ﴿by what We have revealed to you﴾, means: by Our revelation to you of this Qur'an.

The scholars said: The story of Yusuf was called "the best of stories" because it combined the mention of prophets, righteous people, angels, devils, livestock, the conduct of kings, slaves, merchants, scholars, men and women, and their stratagems; the mention of tawhid (monotheism), jurisprudence (fiqh), secrets, the interpretation of dreams, politics, social dealing, the management of livelihood, patience over harm, forbearance, might, and rule, along with other wonders.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed you were﴾. Regarding "in" (inn) there are two opinions:
One of them: it means "qad" (indeed/already). The second: it means "ma" (not).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿before it﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: before the revelation of the Qur'an. ﴿Among the unaware﴾, meaning: without knowledge of the account of Yusuf and what his brothers did to him.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 12, verse 4–5:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿When Joseph said to his father﴾. Regarding "idh" (when) there are two opinions:

One: it is a complement (ṣilah) to the preceding verb, and the meaning is: "We relate to you [the account of] when Joseph said."

The second: it is a complement to a implied verb, its estimate being: "Remember when Joseph said." This is mentioned by al-Zajjaj and Ibn al-Anbari.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Father (yā abati)﴾. Abu Ja'far and Ibn 'Amir read it with a fatḥah on the tā', and they paused with the hā' (ah). Ibn Kathir agreed with them in pausing with the hā'. The rest read it with a kasrah on the tā'. As for the one who read it with a fatḥah, he intended "yā abatā," so he deleted the alif just as the yā is deleted, and the fatḥah remained indicating the alif, just as the kasrah remains indicating the yā. As for the one who paused on the hā', it is because the tā' of feminine marking is replaced by a hā' in pausing. Abu Ja'far read "aḥada 'ashara" (eleven) and "tisata 'ashara" (nineteen) with a sukun on the ʿayn in both.

Regarding what Joseph saw, there are two opinions:

One: he saw the sun, the moon and the stars, and this is the view of most. Al-Farra' said: He said "I saw them" using the plural form for those who reason, because prostration is an action of those who reason, as in His saying: ﴿O ants, enter your dwellings﴾ [al-Naml 18]. The exegetes said: the stars in interpretation were his brothers, the sun his mother, and the moon his father. When he related it to Ya'qub, he feared the envy of his brothers. Al-Suddi said: the sun was his father and the moon his maternal aunt, because his mother had died.

The second: he saw his parents and his brothers prostrating to him, and He referred to them by allusion. This is related from Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah. As for the repetition of the words "I saw them," al-Zajjaj said: He repeated it for emphasis when the speech had lengthened.

Regarding Joseph's age when he saw this dream, there are three opinions:

One: seven years. The second: twelve years. The third: seventeen years.

The exegetes said: Ya'qub knew that Joseph's brothers would understand the interpretation of his dream, so he said: "Do not ﴿relate your dream to your brothers, lest they devise a plot against you﴾." Ibn Qutaybah said: they will contrive a stratagem against you and seize you. Others said: the lam is a complement, and the meaning is: "they will plot against you." And "al-'aduww al-mubin" means the one whose enmity is evident.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 12, verse 6:

Allah's saying: ﴿And thus will your Lord choose you﴾. Al-Zajjaj and Ibn al-Anbari said: Just as you have seen of elevation and noble condition, your Lord will choose you and single you out from among your brothers. We have explained the meaning of al-ijtiba' (choosing, selecting) in (al-An'am: 87). Ibn 'Abbas said: He will single you out with prophethood.

Allah's saying: ﴿and teach you the interpretation of events (ta'wil al-ahadith)﴾. There are three opinions concerning this:

The first: it is the interpretation of dreams. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatadah. On this view it is called ta'wil (interpretation, lit. "that to which the matter of the dream will ultimately return") because it explains what the dream's matter will come to.

The second: it is knowledge and wisdom. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

The third: it is the interpretation of the stories of the prophets, the nations and the scriptures. Al-Zajjaj mentioned this. Muqatil said: "min" here is a connecting particle (silah).

Allah's saying: ﴿and complete His favour upon you﴾. There are three opinions concerning this:

The first: with prophethood. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: by raising the word (of truth) to prevail (i'la' al-kalimah).

The third: by making his brothers need him until he bestowed favour upon them. Al-Mawardi mentioned these two.

Concerning "the family of Ya'qub" there are three opinions:

The first: they are his sons. This was said by Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas. The second: Ya'qub, his wife and his eleven sons; He completed His favour upon them by the prostration to Yusuf. This was said by Muqatil. The third: his household (ahl). This was said by Abu 'Ubaydah, who argued that when you diminutive al-al (the family), you say: uhayl.

Allah's saying: ﴿as He completed it upon your two forefathers before, Ibrahim and Ishaq﴾. 'Ikrimah said: His favour upon Ibrahim was that He saved him from the fire, and His favour upon Ishaq was that He saved him from the slaughter.

Allah's saying: ﴿Indeed your Lord is All-Knowing﴾, i.e., Knowing where He places prophethood, ﴿All-Wise﴾ in the management of His creation.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 12, verse 7:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, in Joseph and his brothers are signs﴾, meaning: in the account of Joseph and the story of his brothers are "signs" (āyāt), that is, lessons for those who ask about them; every state of theirs is a sign. Ibn Kathir read "āyah" (in the singular). The exegetes (mufassirūn) said: the Jews had asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about the story of Joseph, so he informed them of it as it is in the Torah, and they marveled at that.

Regarding the aspect of these signs, there are five opinions:

The first: the proof of the truthfulness of Muhammad ﷺ, when he related the reports of a people he had not witnessed and had not consulted the books about. The second: what Allah manifested in the story of Joseph of the consequences of transgression against him. The third: the truth of his dream and the soundness of its interpretation. The fourth: his restraint of himself and his subduing of his desire until he fulfilled the duty of trust (amānah). The fifth: the occurrence of joy after despair.

If it is said: Why did He specify the questioners, when there are also signs in it for others? In answer to this there are two responses:

One of them: the meaning is "for the questioners and others," and so the mention of the questioners sufficed in place of others, just as the mention of heat sufficed in place of cold in His saying: ﴿That protects you from the heat﴾ [al-Nahl: 81].

The second: that if there is a sign in it for the questioners about the report of Joseph, there is also a sign in it for others; but He specified the questioners because their asking brought about the wonder and uncovered the report.

(p-183) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿When they said﴾, meaning the brothers of Yusuf. ﴿Yusuf and his brother are dearer to our father than we are﴾, meaning Ibn Yamin (Benjamin). It was said of him "Ibn Yamin" because his mother died in childbirth (nufasa'). Yamin means "pain" (waja'), and he was the full brother of Yusuf, from the same mother and father. The rest were his half-brothers from the father, not from his mother.

As for ʿusba (the group), al-Zajjaj said: in the language, it is the group whose affair is one, whose members follow one another in action, and who show partisanship (yata'assab) toward one another.

The exegetes gave six opinions concerning ʿusba:

The first: it is more than ten. This was narrated by al-Dahhak from Ibn ʿAbbas. The second: it is between ten and forty; this too was reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Qatada said the same. The third: it is six or seven; this was said by Saʿid ibn Jubayr. The fourth: it is from ten to fifteen; this was said by Mujahid. The fifth: it is the group; this was said by Ibn Zayd, Ibn Qutayba, and al-Zajjaj. The sixth: it is ten; this was said by Muqatil. al-Farra' said: the ʿusba is ten or more.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed our father is in manifest error﴾. Concerning this there are three opinions:

The first: he is in error in his judgment; this was said by Ibn Zayd. The second: he is in hardship; this was said by Muqatil, meaning the toil of this world. The third: he is in error away from the path of rightness, which requires equal love between us, since our benefit to him is greater. Al-Zajjaj said: Had they attributed to him error in religion, they would have been disbelievers; they only meant: he has preferred two young sons over us in love, while we are a group whose benefit is greater.

(p-184) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Kill Joseph﴾. Abu 'Ali said: Ibn Kathir, Nafi', and al-Kisa'i read "mubinun uqtulu" with a damma on the tanwin, because its vowelling would otherwise necessitate the meeting of two unvocalised letters (al-iltiqa' al-sakinayn). So they vocalised it with a damma, in order that the damma follow the damma, as they said "mudd" and "zulumat". Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, and Hamzah read it with a kasra on the tanwin, and they did not make the damma follow the damma, as they said "mudd" and "zulumat". The exegetes said: this is their saying among themselves, "or cast him onto some land" (ardan). Al-Zajjaj said: the accusative of "ardan" is by the dropping of "fi" (in), and the verb reached it directly; the meaning is: or cast him onto a land whereby he will be far from his father. Others said: a land where wild beasts will devour him.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Your father's face will be free for you﴾, i.e., it will be free for you from the preoccupation with Joseph. "And you will be after him" i.e., after Joseph, ﴿a righteous people﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions:

One: righteous through repentance after killing him; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: your condition will be made right in the sight of your father; this was said by Muqatil. In their story there is a remarkable subtle point, namely that they resolved to repent before the sin, and likewise the believer does not forget repentance even if he is committing transgressions.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 12, verse 10–14:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿A speaker among them said﴾. Concerning this there are three opinions.

The first: he was Yahudha (Judah). This was said by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas, and Wahb ibn Munabbih, (p-185) al-Suddi, and Muqatil also said it. The second: he was Shim'un (Simeon), as said by Mujahid. The third: he was Ruwabil (Reuben), as said by Qatadah and Ibn Ishaq.

As for ghayabat al-jubb (the depths of the well), Abu 'Ubaida said: "Everything that conceals something from you is a ghayaba (a hiding place), and al-jubb is the well that has not been lined with stone." Al-Zajjaj said: "al-Ghayaba is everything that is absent from you, or that hides something from you." Al-Munakhkhal said:

"If one day my hiding place conceals me, then travel by my course among the tribe and the family."

And al-jubb is the well that has not been lined; it was called jubb because it was cut out (hewn) by cutting alone, and nothing had been done to it other than cutting, such as lining with stone or the like. Ibn 'Abbas said: "fi ghayabat al-jubb" means "in its darknesses." al-Hasan said: "in its bottom." Nafi' recited "ghayabat al-jubb" (in the plural), so that each part of it is a ghayaba. Kharija related from Nafi': "ghayyabat" with a doubled ya. al-Hasan, Qatadah, and Mujahid recited "ghaybat al-jubb" without an alif, with the ya sukun. As for where this well was, there are two opinions:

One: in the land of Jordan, said by Wahb. Muqatil said: it is in the land of Jordan, three farsakh (leagues) from the dwelling of Ya'qub. The second: in Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), said by Qatadah.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Some caravan travelers will pick him up﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: "some of those who travel will take him." ﴿If you are going to act﴾ means: if you are resolved to carry out what you intend for him.

Most reciters read yaltaqithu (with ya) (ﷺ-free). al-Hasan, Qatadah, and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read taltaqithu (with ta). al-Zajjaj said: "All the grammarians permit this, because 'some of the caravan' is itself a caravan, so it is as if he said: 'a caravan of some of the caravan will pick him up.'" Ibn al-Anbari said: "Whoever reads with ta has made the verb feminine though 'ba'd' is masculine, and he did this by taking the meaning into account, since the implication is: 'the caravan will pick him up.'" The poet said:

"She saw the passage of years take from me, as the crescent is diminished by the lunar phases."

He meant: she saw the years. Another said:

"The length of nights hastened to wear me down; they wore out my length and my breadth."

He meant: the nights hastened. Jarir said:

"When the news of al-Zubayr came, the walls of Madina humbled themselves, and the lofty mountains."

He meant: Madina humbled itself. Another said:

"And it chokes on the word I have spread, as the spear-shaft chokes with blood."

He meant: as the spear chokes.

The exegetes said: When the people resolved upon the plot against Yusuf, they said to their father: ﴿What is wrong with you that you do not trust us﴾. The majority read ta'manna with a fatha on the mim and idgham of the first nun into the second, with an indication of the i'rab of the idgham nun by a damma. Makki said: "Because the original form is ta'mannu-na, then the first nun was assimilated, and the ishmam remains indicating the damma of the first nun." Ishmam is closing your lips without an audible sound, so it is after the idgham and before he pronounces the second nun with fatha. Ibn Kaysan calls ishmam "al-ishara" (indication), and calls rawm "ishmam"; rawm is a weak sound heard faintly. Abu Ja'far read ta'manna with a fatha on the nun without ishmam, indicating the assimilated form. al-Hasan read "ma laka la ta'munna" with a damma on the mim. Ibn Miqsam read ta'mannunna with two nuns, (p-187) according to the original form. The meaning: "What is wrong with you that you do not trust us regarding Yusuf, so that you send him with us? He has grown old and knows nothing of the matters of livelihood. ﴿And indeed we are sincere advisers to him﴾ in what we have pointed out to you. ﴿Send him with us tomorrow﴾ to the open country." Muqatil said: there is inversion (taqdim and ta'khir) in the speech, because they said to him: "Send him with us," and he said: "Indeed it grieves me that you should take him," so they said: "What is wrong with you that you do not trust us."

His saying, Exalted is He: "Naratha' wa nal'ab" (we will frolic and play). Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, and Abu 'Amr read "narta' wa nal'ab" with nun in both, the 'ayn sakin; Zayd, from Ya'qub, agreed with them only in "narta'."

Concerning the meaning of "narta'" there are three opinions:

One: "nalhu" (we will amuse ourselves), said by al-Dahhak. The second: "nas'a" (we will run/graze freely), said by Qatadah. The third: "na'kul" (we will eat). It is said: "ratafat al-ibil" when the camels grazed, and "artaftuha" when you let them graze. The poet said:

"And a beloved of mine: when I meet him, and when he is alone, my flesh is his pasture."

That is: he ate it. This is the view of Ibn al-Anbari and Ibn Qutayba. 'Asim, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i read ﴿yarta' wa yal'ab﴾ with ya in both and the 'ayn and ba' jazm, meaning Yusuf. Nafi' read "narta'i" with a kasra on the 'ayn from "narta'," without reaching the ya. Ibn Qutayba said: its meaning is "we will guard one another, and each of us will watch over the other," that is, protect; from this one says "ra'aka Allah," meaning "may God keep you." It is also related from Ibn Kathir "narta'i" with a ya after the 'ayn in both pause and connection. Anas and Abu Raja' read "nurti'" with a raised nun, a kasra on the ta', and sukun on the 'ayn, and "nal'ab" with nun. Abu 'Ubayda said: that is, "nurti' ibilana" (we will let our camels graze).

As for his saying "wa nal'ab," Ibn 'Abbas said: "nalhu" (we will amuse ourselves).

(p-188) If it is said: How did Ya'qub not object to them about mentioning play?

The answer is from two aspects: One: they were not prophets at that time, said by Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala'. The second: they meant permissible play, said by al-Mawardi.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed it grieves me that you should take him away﴾, meaning: your going away with him grieves me, because he will part from me and I will not see him. ﴿And I fear that the wolf will devour him﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, and Hamza read "al-dhi'b" (the wolf) with hamza in all three places. al-Kisa'i, Abu Ja'far, and Shayba read it without hamza. Abu 'Ali said: "al-dhi'b" is originally hamzated. It is said: "tadha'abat al-rih" (the wind blew from every direction), as the wolf comes.

Concerning the reason for singling out the wolf for mention there are three opinions: One: he saw in his dream that a wolf attacked Yusuf, said by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas. The second: their land had many wolves, said by Muqatil. The third: he feared for him from them, so he alluded to the wolf by mentioning it, said by al-Mawardi.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿While you are heedless of him﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions: One: heedless of him in play. The second: occupied with your flock.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿If the wolf devours him while we are a band﴾, meaning: a group who see the wolf has targeted him and we do not repel it from him. ﴿Indeed we would then be losers﴾, meaning: incapable. Ibn al-Anbari said: whoever reads "'usbatan" in the accusative, its estimate is: "wa nahnu najtami'u 'usbatan" (and we gather as a band).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 12, verse 10–14:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿A speaker among them said﴾. Concerning this there are three opinions.

As for ghayabat al-jubb (the depths of the well), Abu 'Ubaida said: "Everything that conceals something from you is a ghayaba (a hiding place), and al-jubb is the well that has not been lined with stone." Al-Zajjaj said: "al-Ghayaba is everything that is absent from you, or that hides something from you." Al-Munakhkhal said:

"If one day my hiding place conceals me, then travel by my course among the tribe and the family."

And al-jubb is the well that has not been lined; it was called jubb because it was cut out (hewn) by cutting alone, and nothing had been done to it other than cutting, such as lining with stone or the like. Ibn 'Abbas said: "fi ghayabat al-jubb" means "in its darknesses." al-Hasan said: "in its bottom." Nafi' recited "ghayabat al-jubb" (in the plural), so that each part of it is a ghayaba. Kharija related from Nafi': "ghayyabat" with a doubled ya. al-Hasan, Qatadah, and Mujahid recited "ghaybat al-jubb" without an alif, with the ya sukun. As for where this well was, there are two opinions:

One: in the land of Jordan, said by Wahb. Muqatil said: it is in the land of Jordan, three farsakh (leagues) from the dwelling of Ya'qub. The second: in Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), said by Qatadah.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Some caravan travelers will pick him up﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: "some of those who travel will take him." ﴿If you are going to act﴾ means: if you are resolved to carry out what you intend for him.

Most reciters read yaltaqithu (with ya) (ﷺ-free). al-Hasan, Qatadah, and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read taltaqithu (with ta). al-Zajjaj said: "All the grammarians permit this, because 'some of the caravan' is itself a caravan, so it is as if he said: 'a caravan of some of the caravan will pick him up.'" Ibn al-Anbari said: "Whoever reads with ta has made the verb feminine though 'ba'd' is masculine, and he did this by taking the meaning into account, since the implication is: 'the caravan will pick him up.'" The poet said:

"She saw the passage of years take from me, as the crescent is diminished by the lunar phases."

He meant: she saw the years. Another said:

"The length of nights hastened to wear me down; they wore out my length and my breadth."

He meant: the nights hastened. Jarir said:

"When the news of al-Zubayr came, the walls of Madina humbled themselves, and the lofty mountains."

He meant: Madina humbled itself. Another said:

"And it chokes on the word I have spread, as the spear-shaft chokes with blood."

He meant: as the spear chokes.

The exegetes said: When the people resolved upon the plot against Yusuf, they said to their father: ﴿What is wrong with you that you do not trust us﴾. The majority read ta'manna with a fatha on the mim and idgham of the first nun into the second, with an indication of the i'rab of the idgham nun by a damma. Makki said: "Because the original form is ta'mannu-na, then the first nun was assimilated, and the ishmam remains indicating the damma of the first nun." Ishmam is closing your lips without an audible sound, so it is after the idgham and before he pronounces the second nun with fatha. Ibn Kaysan calls ishmam "al-ishara" (indication), and calls rawm "ishmam"; rawm is a weak sound heard faintly. Abu Ja'far read ta'manna with a fatha on the nun without ishmam, indicating the assimilated form. al-Hasan read "ma laka la ta'munna" with a damma on the mim. Ibn Miqsam read ta'mannunna with two nuns, (p-187) according to the original form. The meaning: "What is wrong with you that you do not trust us regarding Yusuf, so that you send him with us? He has grown old and knows nothing of the matters of livelihood. ﴿And indeed we are sincere advisers to him﴾ in what we have pointed out to you. ﴿Send him with us tomorrow﴾ to the open country." Muqatil said: there is inversion (taqdim and ta'khir) in the speech, because they said to him: "Send him with us," and he said: "Indeed it grieves me that you should take him," so they said: "What is wrong with you that you do not trust us."

His saying, Exalted is He: "Naratha' wa nal'ab" (we will frolic and play). Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, and Abu 'Amr read "narta' wa nal'ab" with nun in both, the 'ayn sakin; Zayd, from Ya'qub, agreed with them only in "narta'."

Concerning the meaning of "narta'" there are three opinions:

One: "nalhu" (we will amuse ourselves), said by al-Dahhak. The second: "nas'a" (we will run/graze freely), said by Qatadah. The third: "na'kul" (we will eat). It is said: "ratafat al-ibil" when the camels grazed, and "artaftuha" when you let them graze. The poet said:

"And a beloved of mine: when I meet him, and when he is alone, my flesh is his pasture."

That is: he ate it. This is the view of Ibn al-Anbari and Ibn Qutayba. 'Asim, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i read ﴿yarta' wa yal'ab﴾ with ya in both and the 'ayn and ba' jazm, meaning Yusuf. Nafi' read "narta'i" with a kasra on the 'ayn from "narta'," without reaching the ya. Ibn Qutayba said: its meaning is "we will guard one another, and each of us will watch over the other," that is, protect; from this one says "ra'aka Allah," meaning "may God keep you." It is also related from Ibn Kathir "narta'i" with a ya after the 'ayn in both pause and connection. Anas and Abu Raja' read "nurti'" with a raised nun, a kasra on the ta', and sukun on the 'ayn, and "nal'ab" with nun. Abu 'Ubayda said: that is, "nurti' ibilana" (we will let our camels graze).

As for his saying "wa nal'ab," Ibn 'Abbas said: "nalhu" (we will amuse ourselves).

(p-188) If it is said: How did Ya'qub not object to them about mentioning play?

The answer is from two aspects: One: they were not prophets at that time, said by Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala'. The second: they meant permissible play, said by al-Mawardi.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed it grieves me that you should take him away﴾, meaning: your going away with him grieves me, because he will part from me and I will not see him. ﴿And I fear that the wolf will devour him﴾. Abu 'Ali said: "al-dhi'b" is originally hamzated. It is said: "tadha'abat al-rih" (the wind blew from every direction), as the wolf comes.

Concerning the reason for singling out the wolf for mention there are three opinions: One: he saw in his dream that a wolf attacked Yusuf, said by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas. The second: their land had many wolves, said by Muqatil. The third: he feared for him from them, so he alluded to the wolf by mentioning it, said by al-Mawardi.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿While you are heedless of him﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions: One: heedless of him in play. The second: occupied with your flock.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿If the wolf devours him while we are a band﴾, meaning: a group who see the wolf has targeted him and we do not repel it from him. ﴿Indeed we would then be losers﴾, meaning: incapable. Ibn al-Anbari said: whoever reads "'usbatan" in the accusative, its estimate is: "wa nahnu najtami'u 'usbatan" (and we gather as a band).
