He meant: she saw the years. Another said:

"The length of nights hastened to wear me down; they wore out my length and my breadth."

He meant: the nights hastened. Jarir said:

"When the news of al-Zubayr came, the walls of Madina humbled themselves, and the lofty mountains."

He meant: Madina humbled itself. Another said:

"And it chokes on the word I have spread, as the spear-shaft chokes with blood."

He meant: as the spear chokes.

The exegetes said: When the people resolved upon the plot against Yusuf, they said to their father: ﴿What is wrong with you that you do not trust us﴾. The majority read ta'manna with a fatha on the mim and idgham of the first nun into the second, with an indication of the i'rab of the idgham nun by a damma. Makki said: "Because the original form is ta'mannu-na, then the first nun was assimilated, and the ishmam remains indicating the damma of the first nun." Ishmam is closing your lips without an audible sound, so it is after the idgham and before he pronounces the second nun with fatha. Ibn Kaysan calls ishmam "al-ishara" (indication), and calls rawm "ishmam"; rawm is a weak sound heard faintly. Abu Ja'far read ta'manna with a fatha on the nun without ishmam, indicating the assimilated form. al-Hasan read "ma laka la ta'munna" with a damma on the mim. Ibn Miqsam read ta'mannunna with two nuns, (p-187) according to the original form. The meaning: "What is wrong with you that you do not trust us regarding Yusuf, so that you send him with us? He has grown old and knows nothing of the matters of livelihood. ﴿And indeed we are sincere advisers to him﴾ in what we have pointed out to you. ﴿Send him with us tomorrow﴾ to the open country." Muqatil said: there is inversion (taqdim and ta'khir) in the speech, because they said to him: "Send him with us," and he said: "Indeed it grieves me that you should take him," so they said: "What is wrong with you that you do not trust us."

His saying, Exalted is He: "Naratha' wa nal'ab" (we will frolic and play). Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, and Abu 'Amr read "narta' wa nal'ab" with nun in both, the 'ayn sakin; Zayd, from Ya'qub, agreed with them only in "narta'."

Concerning the meaning of "narta'" there are three opinions:

One: "nalhu" (we will amuse ourselves), said by al-Dahhak. The second: "nas'a" (we will run/graze freely), said by Qatadah. The third: "na'kul" (we will eat). It is said: "ratafat al-ibil" when the camels grazed, and "artaftuha" when you let them graze. The poet said:

"And a beloved of mine: when I meet him, and when he is alone, my flesh is his pasture."

That is: he ate it. This is the view of Ibn al-Anbari and Ibn Qutayba. 'Asim, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i read ﴿yarta' wa yal'ab﴾ with ya in both and the 'ayn and ba' jazm, meaning Yusuf. Nafi' read "narta'i" with a kasra on the 'ayn from "narta'," without reaching the ya. Ibn Qutayba said: its meaning is "we will guard one another, and each of us will watch over the other," that is, protect; from this one says "ra'aka Allah," meaning "may God keep you." It is also related from Ibn Kathir "narta'i" with a ya after the 'ayn in both pause and connection. Anas and Abu Raja' read "nurti'" with a raised nun, a kasra on the ta', and sukun on the 'ayn, and "nal'ab" with nun. Abu 'Ubayda said: that is, "nurti' ibilana" (we will let our camels graze).

As for his saying "wa nal'ab," Ibn 'Abbas said: "nalhu" (we will amuse ourselves).

(p-188) If it is said: How did Ya'qub not object to them about mentioning play?

The answer is from two aspects: One: they were not prophets at that time, said by Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala'. The second: they meant permissible play, said by al-Mawardi.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed it grieves me that you should take him away﴾, meaning: your going away with him grieves me, because he will part from me and I will not see him. ﴿And I fear that the wolf will devour him﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, and Hamza read "al-dhi'b" (the wolf) with hamza in all three places. al-Kisa'i, Abu Ja'far, and Shayba read it without hamza. Abu 'Ali said: "al-dhi'b" is originally hamzated. It is said: "tadha'abat al-rih" (the wind blew from every direction), as the wolf comes.

Concerning the reason for singling out the wolf for mention there are three opinions: One: he saw in his dream that a wolf attacked Yusuf, said by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas. The second: their land had many wolves, said by Muqatil. The third: he feared for him from them, so he alluded to the wolf by mentioning it, said by al-Mawardi.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿While you are heedless of him﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions: One: heedless of him in play. The second: occupied with your flock.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿If the wolf devours him while we are a band﴾, meaning: a group who see the wolf has targeted him and we do not repel it from him. ﴿Indeed we would then be losers﴾, meaning: incapable. Ibn al-Anbari said: whoever reads "'usbatan" in the accusative, its estimate is: "wa nahnu najtami'u 'usbatan" (and we gather as a band).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 12, verse 15:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So when they took him away﴾: there is abridgment and implication in the speech; its sense is: he sent him with them, so when they went off. ﴿And they agreed﴾: that is, they resolved to put him into the depths of the well.

(p-189) The reference to the story of their going off

The exegetes said: They said to Joseph, "Do you not long to go out with us, to play and to hunt?" He said, "Yes." They said, "Ask your father to send you with us." He said, "I will do so." So they entered upon Jacob all together and said, "O our father, Joseph has wished to go out with us." He said, "What do you say, my son?" He said, "Yes, father, I see from my brothers gentleness and kindness, so I love that you permit me." So he sent him with them. When they got out into the open, they showed him what was in their hearts of enmity and spoke harshly to him. He began to flee to one of them, and that one would strike him, and to another, who would hurt him. When he perceived what they had resolved upon, he began to call out, "O my father! O Jacob! If you saw Joseph and what his brothers are doing to him, it would grieve you and make you weep. O my father! How quickly they have forgotten your covenant and neglected your charge!" And he began to weep intensely.

Al-Dahhak said, from Ibn ʿAbbās: Ruwbil seized him and threw him to the ground, then sat on his chest and wanted to kill him. Joseph said to him, "Gently, my brother, do not kill me." He said, "O son of Rahil, the possessor of dreams! Tell your dream to save you from our hands!" And he twisted his neck to break it. Then Joseph called out, "O Yahudha! Fear God regarding me, and leave between me and the one who wants to kill me." Then compassion seized him, and Yahudha said, "O my brothers! Shall I not show you a matter that is better for you and easier on him?" They said, "And what is that?" He said, "Throw him into this well; some passing caravan will pick him up." They said, "We will do it." So they set off with him to the well, stripped off his shirt, and he said, "O my brothers! Why have you taken off my shirt? Return it to me, that I may cover my nakedness with it and that it may serve as my shroud when I die." So God brought up for him a rock in the well, raised above the water, and his feet settled upon it.

As-Suddi said: They began lowering him into the well, and he would catch hold of the well's edge. So they tied his hands and took off his shirt. He said, "O my brothers, return my shirt to me, that I may cover myself with it." They said, "Call upon the sun, the moon, and the eleven stars." Then they lowered him into the well until, when he had reached halfway down, they dropped him, intending that he should die. There was water in the well, so he fell into it, then took refuge on a rock in it and stood upon it. When they threw him into the well he began to weep, and they called to him. He thought that it was a mercy that had reached them, so he answered them. They wanted to crush him with a stone, but Yahudha prevented them. Yahudha used to bring him food.

Ka'b said: They gathered his hands to his neck and took off his shirt. God sent to him an angel who loosed him and brought up for him a rock from the water, and he sat upon it. Jacob had folded the shirt of Abraham, which God had clothed him in on the day he was thrown into the fire, into a reed, and had placed it around Joseph's neck. The angel then clothed him in it, and the well was lit up for him.

Al-Hasan said: He was thrown into the well, and its water became sweet, so that it sufficed him instead of food and drink. Gabriel came to him, and he was comforted by him. When evening came, Gabriel rose to leave, and Joseph said to him, "If you leave me, I will feel lonely." He said, "When you fear something, say: O helper of those who seek help, O rescuer of those who call out for aid, O reliever of the distress of the afflicted, You see my place and know my state, and nothing of my affair is hidden from You." When he said it, the angels surrounded him, and he became at ease in the well and remained in it for three days, while his brothers were grazing around the well.

Muhammad ibn Muslim al-Ta'ifi said: When Joseph was thrown into the well, he said, "O Witness not absent, O Near not distant, O Victorious not defeated, make for me a way out of what I am in." He said: So he did not spend the night in it.

Regarding his age when he was thrown into the well, there are four sayings:

One: twelve years old, said by al-Hasan. Second: six years old, said by al-Dahhak. Third: seventeen, said by Ibn al-Sa'ib, and it is also related from al-Hasan. Fourth: eighteen.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We revealed to him﴾. Regarding this there are two sayings:

(p-191) One: that it was inspiration (ilhām), said by Abu Salih from Ibn ʿAbbās. Second: that it was revelation in the true sense.

The exegetes said: It was revealed to him: "You will surely inform them of their affair," that is, of what they did to you while you will be high above them.

Regarding His saying: ﴿while they do not perceive﴾ there are two sayings:

One: they do not perceive that you are Joseph at the time you inform them; this was said by Abu Salih from Ibn ʿAbbās, and Muqatil also said so. Second: they do not perceive the revelation; this was said by Mujahid, Qatada, and Ibn Zayd. According to the first, the phrase belongs with "you will surely inform them"; according to the second, it belongs with ﴿And We revealed to him﴾.

Humayd said: I said to al-Hasan, "Does a believer envy a believer?" He said, "No, may you have no father! Did the sons of Jacob not make you forget?"

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 12, verse 16–17:

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And they came to their father in the evening, weeping﴾. Abu Hurayrah, al-Hasan, Ibn al-Sumayfa' and al-A'mash recited "ʿushaʾan" with a ḍammah on the ʿayn.

The exegetes (mufassirun) said: They came at the time of ʿatamah (the late part of the night, after the evening prayer), so that they would be bolder in the darkness in offering a lie as an excuse. When he heard their voice, he was alarmed and said: "What is the matter with you, my sons? Has something befallen your sheep?" They said: "No." He said: "Then what has befallen you? And where is Joseph?" They said: "O our father, we went off racing (nastabiq)." On this word there are three opinions:

The first: we shoot at targets (nantadil). This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Qutaybah, who said: the meaning is that some of us compete with others in shooting. The second: we run (nashtadd), reported from al-Suddi. The third: we hunt (natasayyad), reported from Muqatil. So the meaning on the first view is: we compete in archery to see which of us has the swifter arrow; on the second: we race on foot; on the third: for the purpose of hunting.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And we left Joseph by our belongings﴾, i.e., our clothes. "But you will not believe us" means: you will not accept us as truthful.

Regarding His words: ﴿Even though we were truthful﴾, there are two views:

The first: the meaning is "even though we had been truthful," reported by Ibn Ishaq. The second: "If we were among the people of truthfulness in your sight, you would have accused us concerning Joseph because of your love for him, and you would have thought that we were lying to you," reported by al-Zajjaj.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 12, verse 16–17:

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And they came to their father in the evening, weeping﴾. Abu Hurayrah, al-Hasan, Ibn al-Sumayfa' and al-A'mash recited "ʿushaʾan" with a ḍammah on the ʿayn.

The exegetes (mufassirun) said: They came at the time of ʿatamah (the late part of the night, after the evening prayer), so that they would be bolder in the darkness in offering a lie as an excuse. When he heard their voice, he was alarmed and said: "What is the matter with you, my sons? Has something befallen your sheep?" They said: "No." He said: "Then what has befallen you? And where is Joseph?" They said: "O our father, we went off racing (nastabiq)." On this word there are three opinions:

The first: we shoot at targets (nantadil). This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Qutaybah, who said: the meaning is that some of us compete with others in shooting. The second: we run (nashtadd), reported from al-Suddi. The third: we hunt (natasayyad), reported from Muqatil. So the meaning on the first view is: we compete in archery to see which of us has the swifter arrow; on the second: we race on foot; on the third: for the purpose of hunting.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And we left Joseph by our belongings﴾, i.e., our clothes. "But you will not believe us" means: you will not accept us as truthful.

Regarding His words: ﴿Even though we were truthful﴾, there are two views:

The first: the meaning is "even though we had been truthful," reported by Ibn Ishaq. The second: "If we were among the people of truthfulness in your sight, you would have accused us concerning Joseph because of your love for him, and you would have thought that we were lying to you," reported by al-Zajjaj.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 12, verse 18:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they came upon his shirt with false blood﴾. The philologists said: its meaning is "with blood that is falsely claimed (maktub) in it." The Arabs often make the verbal noun (masdar) take the form of a passive participle (maf'ul) in much speech, so they say for "falsehood" *maktub* (lit. "written/claimed"), for "intellect" *ma'qul* (lit. "understood"), and for "flogging" *majlud* (lit. "flogged"). The poet said:

﻿"Until, when they left nothing of his bones with flesh, nor of his heart with intellect (ma'qul)."

He meant: "with intellect" ('aqlan). Another said:

"By Him who raised the sky by power, consolation has been reached and the flogging (majlud) has been attained."

He means: the flogging (jald) has been attained. They also say: "So-and-so has no firm opinion (ʿaqd ra'y), nor a bound opinion (ma'qud ra'y)." They say: "This is spilled water (sakb)," meaning spilled (maskub); "this is poured drink (sabb)," meaning poured (masbub); "water that has sunk (ghawr)," meaning sunk (ghair); "a man who fasts (sawm)," meaning fasting (sa'im); and "a woman who wails (nawh)," meaning wailing (na'iha). This whole discussion is the combined statement of al-Farra', al-Akhfash, al-Zajjaj, Ibn Qutayba, and others.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: "They took a young goat, slaughtered it, dipped Joseph's shirt in its blood, and brought it to him, but there was no tear in it. So he said: 'You have lied. Had the wolf eaten him, it would have torn the shirt.'" Qatada said: "It was the blood of a gazelle." Ibn Abi ʿAbla read *bi-damin kadhiban* with the accusative (naṣb). Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan, and Abu al-ʿAliya read *bi-damin kadibin* with a *dal* that is unpointed (ghayr mu'jama), meaning: fresh blood (tari).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Rather, your souls have beautified for you a matter﴾, that is, adorned it, ﴿other than what you describe﴾. ﴿So patience is beautiful﴾. Al-Khalil said: the meaning is: "so my affair is beautiful patience, and what I hold to be true is beautiful patience." Al-Farra' said: "Ṣabr" is in the nominative (marfu'), because he consoled himself and said: "It is nothing but patience." Had he commanded them to be patient, it would have been in the accusative (nasb). Qutrub said: the meaning is: "so my patience is beautiful patience." Ibn Mas'ud, Ubayy, and Abu al-Mutawakkil read *fa-sabran jamilan* with the accusative. Al-Zajjaj said: beautiful patience is that in which there is no lamentation and no complaint to people.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And Allah is the One sought for help against what you describe﴾. In this there are two views:

One: against what you describe of falsehood. The second: against the endurance of what you describe.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 12, verse 19:

His saying, Most High: ﴿And there came a caravan﴾, meaning: a company traveling (sayyarah, "caravan"). ﴿Then they sent their water-drawer﴾. Al-Akhfash said: he made the caravan feminine and the water-drawer masculine, because the caravan in meaning refers to men. Al-Zajjaj said: the warid (water-drawer) is the one who comes to the water to draw it for the people.

(p-194) Regarding the name of this warid there are two views:

The first: Malik ibn Dhu'r ibn Yu'ib ibn 'Ifa ibn Madyan ibn Ibrahim. This was said by Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas. The second: Mijlath ibn Ra'wil, said by Wahb ibn Munabbih.

His saying, Most High: ﴿So he let down his bucket﴾, meaning: he sent it down. Al-Zajjaj said: it is said adlaytu al-dalw (I let down the bucket) when you send it down to fill it, and dalawtuha (I drew it up) when you bring it out. "He said: O good news!" (qala ya bushra). Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir recited: "Ya bushraya" with a fatha on the ya and the alif affirmed. Warsh related from Nafi': "bushrayi" and "mahyaya" [al-An'am: 162] and ﴿mathwaya﴾ [Yusuf: 23] with the ya sukun. 'Asim, Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited "ya bushra" with an alif and without a ya. 'Asim with a fatha on the ra', while Hamza and al-Kisa'i imala it (incline the vowel). Al-Zajjaj said: whoever recites "ya bushraya", this call is an alert to those addressed, because good news does not answer or understand; so the meaning is: rejoice, and "O good news, this is your time," just as when you say "ya 'ajabaha" (how wonderful!), it is as if you said: be amazed, and "O wonder, this is from your time." We have already explained this meaning (Hud: 69 and 74).

As for the reading of the one who recites "ya bushra", it is permissible that the meaning be: O you who are present, this is good news. It is also permissible that the meaning be: O good news, this is your time, according to the explanation already given regarding alerting those present. Al-Suddi mentioned that he called out with that to one of them whose name was Bushra. Ibn al-Anbari said: these views are all permissible, and it is also permissible that it be the name of a woman. Abu Raja' and Ibn Abi 'Abla recited: "ya bushraya" with a shadda on the ya and a fatha, without an alif. Ibn 'Abbas said: when he let down his bucket, Yusuf grasped the rope, and he looked at him and saw a boy of the finest appearance among boys. He said to his companions: "Good news!" They said: "What is behind you?" He said: "This is a boy in the well." They came to him asking to share in him, and they drew him out of the pit. (p-195) Some of them said to others: "Conceal him from your companions, lest they ask you to share in him. If they say, 'What is this?' say: 'The people of the water entrusted him to us so we could sell him for them in Egypt.'" Then Yusuf's brothers came and searched for him, but they did not find him in the well. They looked and saw the company with Yusuf, and they said to them: "This is a runaway slave of ours." Malik ibn Dhu'r said: "I will buy him from you." So they sold him for twenty dirhams, a garment, and two sandals. Malik ibn Dhu'r concealed him from his companions and said: "The people of the water entrusted him to us to sell for them in Egypt."

His saying, Most High: ﴿And they concealed him as merchandise﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: "bidda'atan" (as merchandise) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state, as if he said: they concealed him, making him merchandise. Ibn Qutaybah said: they concealed among themselves that he was merchandise and goods. Regarding the doers of that there are two views:

The first: that they are the ones who came to the well; they concealed their purchase of him from the rest of their companions, and agreed that he was merchandise which the people of the water had entrusted to them. This meaning is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, and Mujahid said likewise.

The second: that they are his brothers; they concealed his matter, sold him, and said: "He is our merchandise." This meaning is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas.

His saying, Most High: ﴿And Allah is All-Knowing of what they do﴾, which encompasses both the sellers and the buyers.

(p-١٩٦) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they sold him﴾. This is one of the words of the *adhdad* (words that carry two opposite meanings). One says *sharaytu al-shay'*, meaning *I sold the thing*, and also *sharaytuhu*, meaning *I bought it*. If it means *they sold him*, then there are two opinions about who "they" are.

The first: they were his brothers, which is the view of most scholars.

The second: they were the *sayyarah* (a passing caravan), and his brothers did not sell him. This was said by al-Hasan and Qatadah. If it means *they bought him*, then they are the *sayyarah*.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿for a paltry price﴾. There are three opinions about this:

The first: it means *haram* (unlawfully gained). This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak, and Qatadah, among others.

The second: it means *few*. This was said by Ikrimah and al-Sha'bi. Ibn Qutaybah said: *al-bakhs* is the base thing by which the seller was cheated.

The third: it means *deficient*. The dirhams were twenty in number, but they fell short of twenty by weight. This was said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿a few counted dirhams﴾. Al-Farra' said: it was only said "counted" so that it would be taken as an indication of smallness. Ibn Qutaybah said: that is, few, easy to count because of their small number; if they had been many, counting them would have been burdensome. Ibn 'Abbas said: in that era they did not weigh anything less than forty dirhams. It was also said that they did not weigh them out because of their indifference to them.

Regarding the number of those dirhams, there are five opinions:

The first: twenty dirhams. This was said by Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas in one narration, Ikrimah in one narration, Nawf al-Shami, Wahb ibn Munabbih, al-Sha'bi, Atiyyah, al-Suddi, and Muqatil, among others.

The second: twenty dirhams and a garment, and two sandals. This is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas.

(p-١٩٧) The third: twenty-two dirhams. This was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas, and Mujahid said likewise.

The fourth: forty dirhams. This was said by Ikrimah in one narration, and by Ibn Ishaq.

The fifth: thirty dirhams, two sandals, and a garment. They had said to him in Hebrew: either you acknowledge to us that you are a slave, or we will take you from them and kill you. He said: rather, I acknowledge to you that I am a slave. This was related by Ishaq ibn Bishr from some of his shaykhs.

The exegetes said: they divided his price among themselves, and with it they bought sandals and shoes.

Some of the righteous used to say: By God, Yusuf, even though his enemies sold him, is no more astonishing than you in selling your soul for the lust of an hour of your sins.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and they were among those indifferent to it﴾. *Zuhd* is little desire for a thing.

Regarding the referent of "they" (al-mushar ilayhim), there are two opinions:

The first: they are his brothers. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. On this view, there are two opinions about the pronoun in *fihi* (in it, or him):

The first: it refers to Yusuf, because they did not know his station with God, Exalted is He. This was said by al-Dahhak and Ibn Jurayj.

The second: it refers to the price. Regarding the reason for their indifference, there are two opinions: the first is its badness (its poor quality); the second is that they intended Yusuf's distance (his removal from them), not the price.

The second: they are the *sayyarah* who bought him. Regarding the reason for their indifference, there are three opinions: the first is that they doubted it because of the smallness of its price. The second is that his brothers had described him to them as treacherous and a runaway slave. The third is that they knew he was free.

(p-198) The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And the one who bought him from Egypt said﴾. Wahb said: When the caravan took him to Egypt, they stood him in its marketplace to offer him for sale. People bid against one another for his price until his price reached his weight in musk, his weight in silver, and his weight in silk. He was bought for that price by a man called Qitfir, who was the trusted official and treasurer of Pharaoh, and who was a believer. Ibn Abbas said: Qitfir bought him from Malik ibn Dhu'r for twenty dinars, a pair of sandals, and two white garments. When he returned to his home, he said to his wife: "Make his lodging honorable." Some people said: his name was Itfir.

There are two opinions about the name of the woman. One: Ra'il, daughter of Ra'a'il, reported by Ibn Ishaq. The second: Azlikha, daughter of Tamlikha, reported by Muqatil. Ibn Qutaybah said: "Make his lodging honorable" means: make his dwelling and his stay with you honorable, from your saying "I dwelt (thawaytu) in the place" when you remained in it. Al-Zajjaj said: Treat him well during his long stay with us. Ibn Mas'ud said: There are three people who have the keenest insight: the Aziz, when he perceived (in Joseph), so he said to his wife: ﴿Make his lodging honorable; perhaps he will benefit us﴾; the daughter of Shu'ayb, when she said: ﴿O my father, hire him﴾ [al-Qasas 28:26]; and Abu Bakr, when he appointed Umar as his successor.

Regarding His words ﴿perhaps he will benefit us﴾ there are two opinions:
One: that he will suffice us when he reaches our affairs. The second: that he will bring profit through his price.

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿or we may adopt him as a son﴾. Ibn Abbas said: we may adopt him. Others said: they had no child, and the Aziz did not approach women.

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And thus We established Joseph﴾, that is: just as We delivered him from his brothers and brought him out of the darkness of the well, We established him in the land, that is: We gave him sovereignty in the land of Egypt, and We placed him over its treasuries. ﴿And that We might teach him﴾. Ibn al-Anbari said: the waw in "and that We might teach him" was introduced for an implied verb which is the thing the lam requires, and the meaning is: We established Joseph in the land, and We singled him out for that (p-199) in order that We might teach him the interpretation of events. The explanation of "the interpretation of events" has already been given [Yusuf 12:6].

﴿And Allah is predominant over His affair﴾. Regarding the pronoun there are two opinions:
One: it refers to Allah, so the meaning is: He is predominant over what He has decreed of His decree, and this is the meaning of Ibn Abbas's statement.
The second: it refers to Joseph, so the meaning is: He is predominant over Joseph's affair until He delivers to him what He willed for him, and this is the meaning of Muqatil's statement. Some of them said: Allah is predominant over His affair in that when Jacob commanded Joseph not to relate his dream to his brothers, they came to know of it. Then Jacob wished that they would not plot against him, but they plotted against him. Then Joseph's brothers wished to kill him, but He did not decree it for them. Then they wished that some of the caravan would pick him up so that his affair would be erased, but his affair prevailed. Then they sold him so that he would be a slave, but his affair prevailed until he became a ruler. They wished to turn their father's heart away from him, but he refused them. Then they wished to deceive Jacob with weeping and with the blood they had smeared on the shirt, but it was not hidden from him. Then they wished to become a righteous people after him, but they forgot their sin until, years later, they confessed it, saying: ﴿Indeed we were sinners﴾ [Yusuf 12:97]. Then they wished to erase his love from their father's heart, but it increased. Then Azlikha wished to place the accusation upon him by her saying: ﴿What is the penalty for one who intended harm to your wife?﴾ [Yusuf 12:25], but his affair prevailed, until a witness from her own family testified. And Joseph wished to free himself from prison by mentioning the cupbearer, but the cupbearer forgot, so that he remained in prison for several years.

[p-200] The words of the Most High: ﴿When he reached his maturity (ashudd)﴾. We have already explained the meaning of al-ashudd (the age of full physical and mental maturity) in (al-An'am: 152). The scholars differed about what is meant by it here, giving eight opinions:

The first: it is thirty-three years. This was narrated by Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas, and Mujahid and Qatadah also held this view. The second: it is eighteen years. Abu Salih said this from Ibn 'Abbas, and Ikrimah also held this view. The third: it is forty years. This was said by al-Hasan. The fourth: it is reaching puberty (bulugh al-hulum). This was said by al-Sha'bi, Rabi'ah, Zayd ibn Aslam, and his son. The fifth: it is twenty years. This was said by al-Dahhak. The sixth: it is from about seventeen years up to about forty. This was said by al-Zajjaj. The seventh: it is reaching thirty-eight years. Ibn Qutaybah related this. The eighth: it is thirty years. Some of the exegetes mentioned this.

The words of the Most High: ﴿We gave him wisdom (hukm)﴾. Concerning this there are four opinions:

The first: it is understanding (fiqh) and reason ('aql). Mujahid said this. The second: it is prophethood. Ibn al-Sa'ib said this. The third: it means that he was made wise (hakim). al-Zajjaj said this, and he added: "Not every learned person is wise. The wise person is the one who knows and acts on his knowledge, and who restrains himself thereby from doing what is ignorant." The fourth: it is correctness in speech. al-Tha'labi mentioned this. The linguists said: among the Arabs, hukm is that which turns a person away from ignorance and error and prevents them, and restrains the self from what disgraces it and would harm it. From this comes the term hikmat al-dabba (the bridle of the beast). The original meaning of ahkamtu in the language is "I prevented," and the judge is called hakim because he prevents injustice and deviation.

[p-201] Concerning what is meant by "knowledge" ('ilm) here there are two opinions: the first is fiqh; the second is the knowledge of dreams (ilm al-ru'ya).

The words of the Most High: ﴿Thus do We reward the good-doers﴾. That is: just as We described the teaching and guardianship of Yusuf, We reward whoever does good deeds and avoids sins. So We save him from ruin, rescue him from misguidance, and make him one of the people of knowledge and wisdom, just as We did with Yusuf.

Concerning what is meant by "the good-doers" (al-muhsinin) here there are three opinions:

The first: those who are patient through calamities. The second: those who are guided; this is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas. The third: the believers. Muhammad ibn Jarir (al-Tabari) said: "Although the outward wording is general for every good-doer, what is meant by it is Muhammad (ﷺ). The meaning is: just as I did with Yusuf after he met with trials, so I established him in the land and gave him knowledge, so I will do with you and save you from the polytheists of your people."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 12, verse 23:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And she, in whose house he was, sought to seduce him from himself﴾. That is, she asked him to have intercourse with her, and her name has already been mentioned. Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is: she sought to seduce him toward what she wanted, which is what women want from men. ﴿And she said, "Come, you," ﴾ Ibn Kathir recited: "Hayta lak" (هَيْتُ لَكَ) with a fatha on the ha', sukun on the ya', and a damma on the ta'. Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir recited: "Hayta lak" (هِيْتَ لَكَ) with a kasra on the ha', sukun on the ya', and a fatha on the ta'. This is also narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib. Al-Halwani related from Hisham, from Ibn 'Amir, the same, except that he pronounced it with a hamza. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: This is an error. It is also narrated from Ibn 'Amir: "Hi'ta lak" (هِئْتُ لَكَ) with a kasra on the ha', a hamza on the ya', and a damma on the ta'; this is the recitation of Ibn 'Abbas, Abu al-Darda', and Qatadah. Al-Zajjaj said: It is from the (word) hay'ah (form, appearance), as if she said: "I have prepared myself for you." From Ibn Muhaysin and Talhah ibn Musarrif, it is like the recitation of Ibn 'Abbas, except without a hamza. From Ibn Muhaysin, with a fatha on the ha' and a kasra on the ta'; this is the recitation of Abu Razin and Humayd. From al-Walid ibn 'Utbah, with a kasra on the ha' and the ta' along with the hamza; this is the recitation of Abu al-'Aliyah. Ibn Khuthaym recited the same, except that he did not use a hamza. From al-Walid ibn Muslim, from Nafi', with a kasra on the ha' and a fatha on the ta', along with the hamza. Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn al-Sumayfa', Ibn Ya'mar, and al-Jahdari recited: "Huyyi'tu lak" (هُيِّئْتُ لَكَ) with a damma on the ha' and the ta', and a shaddah-ed kasra ya' followed by a silent hamza. Ubayy ibn Ka'b recited: "Ha ana lak" (ها أنا لَكَ). The rest recited with a fatha on the ha' and the ta', without a hamza. Al-Zajjaj said: This is the best of the dialects and the most common in the speech of the Arabs, and its meaning is: "Halumma lak" (come, i.e., turn towards what I call you to). The poet said:

Tell the Commander of the Faithful, brother of Iraq, when you both arrive, that Iraq and its people are a neck extended towards you, so hayta hayta (come, come).

That is: so come forward and approach. Ibn Qutaybah said: It is said "hayyata fulan li-fulan" (so-and-so called out to so-and-so and shouted at him). The poet said:

Indeed, the silence of the ... has troubled me; had he been addressed by it, he would have called out.

That is: he became one who keeps silent. The scholars differed concerning His saying "Hayta lak," in which language it is, according to four opinions:

The first: that it is Arabic; this was said by Mujahid. Ibn al-Anbari said: It has also been said that it is from the speech of Quraysh, but it had become obsolete and rare on their lips in later times, so God brought it back, since its origin is from their speech. This word has no verbal noun, no inflection, no dual, no plural, and no feminine form. It is said to two people: "hayta lakuma," to a group: "hayta lakum," and to women: "hayta lakunna."

The second: that it is Syriac; this was said by al-Hasan.

The third: that it is Hauranian; this was said by 'Ikrimah and al-Kisa'i. Al-Farra' said: It is said that it is a dialect of the people of Hawran, which spread to the people of Makkah, and they spoke it.

The fourth: that it is Coptic; this was said by al-Suddi.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said, "God forbid!"﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: It is a verbal noun, and the meaning is: I seek refuge in God from doing this. One says "‘adtu ‘iyadan, wa ma'adan, wa ma'adhah" (I sought refuge). ﴿Indeed, he is my lord﴾ That is: indeed the Aziz, my master, ﴿has made my residence excellent﴾. He said: It is also permissible that "indeed, He is my lord" refers to God, mighty and majestic, ﴿has made my residence excellent﴾, that is: He took care of me during the length of my stay.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, the wrongdoers will not succeed﴾. That is: if I did this, I would betray him regarding his family after he had honored me, and then I would be a wrongdoer. It was also said: the wrongdoers here are the fornicators.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 12, verse 24:**

(p-204) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And she certainly desired him﴾. *Al-hamm bi-al-shay'* (intention or impulse toward a thing) in the speech of the Arabs means a person's inner conversation with himself about committing it when he has not yet committed it. As for the desire of Zulaykha (al-Aziz's wife), the exegetes (*mufassirun*) said: she invited him to herself and lay down for him. They differed about his desire for her, in five opinions:

The first: it was of the same kind as hers, and had Allah Exalted not protected him, he would have done it. This meaning was held by al-Hasan, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Dahhak and al-Suddi, and it is the view of the majority of the early exegetes. A group of later scholars, including Ibn Jarir (al-Tabari) and Ibn al-Anbari, chose it. Ibn Qutayba said: "It is not permissible in the language to say *hamamtu bi-fulan* (I desired so-and-so) or *hamma bi* (he desired me) while you mean a mutual desire." Those who supported this view argued that it is the position of most of the Salaf and the great scholars, and what we will mention about the proof (*burhan*) he saw supports it. They said: his turning back from what he intended, out of fear of Allah Exalted, erases the evil of the intention and raises him to high ranks. This is shown by the authentic hadith from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Three men went out and took refuge in a cave, and a rock sealed the entrance upon them. They said: Let each one of you mention the best of his deeds. One of them said: O Allah, You know that I had a cousin whom I sought to seduce, but she refused unless I paid one hundred dinars. When I brought them to her and sat with her as a man sits with a woman, she trembled and said: This is a thing I have never done before. So I got up from her and gave her the hundred dinars. If You know that I did that seeking Your face, then relieve us of this." Thereupon a third of the rock moved away. The hadith is well known, and I have mentioned it in *al-Hada'iq*. On this basis we say: she desired, and her desire rose to resolve, so she persisted in committing adultery. As for him, what afflicts human beings of passing thoughts of the heart and inner conversation, without resolve, confronted him. This desire did not bind him to any sin, for a righteous man may have a passing thought, while fasting, of drinking cold water; if he does not drink, he is not held accountable for what crossed his mind. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "My community is pardoned for what its souls whisper, so long as they do not speak it or act upon it." He (ﷺ) also said: "The persisters are destroyed," and persistence (*al-israr*) is nothing but the resolve of the heart. Thus he distinguished between the inner conversation of the soul and the resolve of the heart. Sufyan al-Thawri was asked: "Is a servant held accountable for an intention?" He said: "If it is a resolve." This is supported by the authentic hadith from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he said: "Allah Exalted says: When My servant intends an evil deed and does not do it, I do not record it against him; but if he does it, I record it as one evil deed."

Al-Qadi Abu Ya'la argued that his desire was not from the side of resolve, but from the promptings of desire, by His saying: ﴿He said: I seek refuge in Allah; indeed, he is my lord﴾ and His saying: ﴿Thus, that We might turn away from him evil and immorality﴾. All of this is a statement of the innocence of his person from resolve to disobey.

If it is said: the Qur'an has equated the two desires, so why do you distinguish between them?

The answer: the equality occurred at the beginning of the desire, then her desire rose to resolve, as is shown by her seeking him and lying down before him. His desire did not exceed its station; rather it descended from its rank, and its knot was undone, as is shown by his fleeing from her and his saying: ﴿I seek refuge in Allah﴾. On this basis his desire was merely a passing thought that did not proceed to resolve. What is narrated from some exegetes, that he untied his trousers and sat from her as a man sits, is not sound; for if this were so, it would indicate resolve, and the prophets are protected from resolve to commit adultery.

The second opinion: she desired that he would lie with her, and he desired her, meaning he wished that she would be his wife. This was narrated by al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third opinion: in the speech there is an inversion (*taqdim wa-ta'khir*), its meaning being: ﴿And she certainly desired him, and he would have desired her had he not seen the proof of his Lord﴾. When he saw the proof, the desire did not occur from him. The answer of *law-la* (had it not been for) is thus placed before it, as one says: "You were certainly among the doomed, had it not been that so-and-so rescued you; you would have been among the doomed." From this is the saying of the poet:

*So my people do not leave me to a free woman's pure marriage proposal (?)—if I am slain, may 'Amir be safe.*

He meant: "If I am slain and 'Amir is safe, then my people will not leave me," so he placed the answer first. This view was held by Qutrub, but a group denied it, among them Ibn al-Anbari, and they said: placing the answer of *law-la* before it is anomalous, reprehensible, and not found in the eloquent speech of the Arabs. As for the verse cited as evidence, it is due to the compulsion of poets, for the poet's speech becomes constrained when he is concerned with making the parts of his poem correct; so he places a word in other than its place, puts first what should be later, puts later what should be first, and departs from preference to what is disliked out of necessity. The poet said:

*May his Lord reward on my behalf 'Adi ibn Hatim, for my abandonment and forsaking of him, with a full reward.*

Its intended order is: "May his Lord reward 'Adi ibn Hatim on my behalf," so he was compelled to place "his Lord" first. Another said:

*When his brothers turned away from Mus'ab, he paid for that sale, a sa' for a sa'.*

He meant: "When his brothers turned away from Mus'ab." Al-Farra' recited:

*Seeking your favour, O son of Yahya, after the means have been cut off between me and you.*

He added a *ta'* to "taqatta'at" (were cut off), which has no root, to correct the meter of his poem. Tha'lab recited:

*Indeed my form and your form are different, so keep to lowering and be soft and fair-complexioned.*

He added a *dad* that has no root so that the parts of the line would be complete. Al-Farazdaq said:

*They two spat into my mouth from their two mouths, upon the barking, growling dog, my bridle is tighter.*

He added a *waw* after the *mim* to correct his poem. Such things should not be applied to the Book of Allah, which was revealed in eloquence, for they are the necessities of poets.

The fourth opinion: he intended to strike her and push her away from himself. The proof he saw from his Lord was that Allah placed in his soul that if he struck her, his striking her would be an argument against him, for she would say: "He solicited me, and I refused him, so he struck me." This was mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari.

The fifth opinion: he intended to flee from her. This was related by al-Tha'labi, but it is a rejected view. Do you suppose he intended to flee from her, and then when he saw the proof he stayed with her? Some scholars said: the desire of Yusuf was a minor sin of the permissible kind for prophets; Allah tested them with it so that they would be in fear of it, and so that He would make them aware of the places of His blessing in pardoning them, and make them leaders for the people of sins in hope of mercy. Al-Hasan said: Allah Exalted did not relate the sins of the prophets to you to shame them, but so that you would not despair of His mercy. Al-Hasan means: the proof against the prophets is more binding, so when He accepts their repentance, He is quicker to accept it from you. It was narrated from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he said: "No one meets Allah Exalted without having intended a sin or committed it, except Yahya ibn Zakariyya, for he neither intended it nor committed it."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Had he not seen the proof of his Lord﴾. The answer of *law-la* is omitted. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: "Had he not seen the proof of his Lord, he would have carried out what he intended." Ibn al-Anbari said: "He would have committed fornication; but when he saw the proof, it was the cause of the fornication being turned away from him."

Regarding the proof, there are six opinions:

The first: Ya'qub was depicted to him. Ibn Abi Mulaykah related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: a call came: "O Yusuf! Will you commit fornication and be like the bird whose feathers were plucked, so that it tries to fly but cannot?" He did not respond to the call, so the call came a second time, and he did not respond to it. Then Ya'qub appeared to him, struck his chest, and he stood up, and his desire came out through his fingertips. Al-Dahhak related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: he saw the image of his father Ya'qub in the middle of the house, biting his fingers, so he turned and fled, saying: "By your right, my father, I will never return again." Abu Salih related from Ibn 'Abbas: he saw the likeness of Ya'qub on the wall, biting his lips. Al-Hasan said: Jibril was depicted to him in the form of Ya'qub on the ceiling of the house, biting his thumb or some of his fingers. This view was held by Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ikrimah, Qatadah, Ibn Sirin, al-Dahhak and others. Ikrimah said: every son of Ya'qub was born with twelve sons, except Yusuf, who had eleven sons, so one son was lost because of that desire.

The second: it was Jibril, peace be upon him. Ibn Abi Mulaykah related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Ya'qub was depicted to him, but he did not refrain. He was called: "Will you commit fornication and be like the bird whose feathers were plucked?" But he did not refrain until Jibril struck him on his back, and he leapt.

The third: she stood up to an idol in a corner of the house and covered it with a garment. Yusuf said to her: "What are you doing?" She said: "I am ashamed before this god of mine that it should see me in this state of shame." He said: "Are you ashamed before an idol that does not understand and does not hear, and I am not ashamed before my God, who watches over every soul for what it has earned?" This is the proof he saw. This was said by 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, 'Ali ibn al-Husayn, and al-Dahhak.

The fourth: Allah sent an angel to him, who wrote on the woman's face in blood: ﴿And do not approach adultery; indeed, it is an abomination and an evil way﴾. This was said by al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas. It was also narrated from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi that he saw this verse written between his eyes; and in another narration from him, he saw it written on the wall. Mujahid related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: between them appeared a palm with no upper arm and no wrist, and on it was written: ﴿And do not approach adultery; indeed, it is an abomination and an evil way﴾ [al-Isra: 32]. So he stood up fleeing, and she stood up. When the terror left her, she returned and he returned. When he sat down, behold, a palm appeared between them, on which was written: ﴿And fear a Day when you will be returned to Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 281], so he stood up fleeing. When he returned, Allah Exalted said to Jibril: "Overtake My servant before he commits the sin." So Jibril descended, biting his palm or his finger, saying: "O Yusuf! Will you do the deeds of the foolish, while you are recorded with Allah among the prophets?" Wahb ibn Munabbih said: that palm appeared, and on it was written in Hebrew: ﴿Then is He who is standing over every soul in what it has earned [like those who associate others with Him]?﴾ [al-Ra'd: 33]. So they departed, and when they returned, she returned and on it was written: ﴿And indeed, over you are guardians, noble and writing﴾ [al-Infitar: 10–11]. So they departed, and when they returned, she returned and on it was written: ﴿And do not approach adultery...﴾ and the verse continued, so he returned, and the fourth time she returned and on it was written: ﴿And fear a Day when you will be returned to Allah﴾, and Yusuf fled.

The fifth: his master, al-Aziz, drew near to the door. This was related by Ibn Ishaq from some people of knowledge. Ibn Ishaq said: it is said that the proof was the apparition of his master, whom he saw at the door, so he fled.

The sixth: the proof was that he knew what Allah had made lawful and what He had made unlawful, so he saw the prohibition of fornication. This was related from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi. Ibn Qutayba said: he saw the argument of Allah against him, which is the proof. This is the sound view, and what came before it is nothing; those are only tales from the storytellers, and I have already pointed out their corruption in my book *al-Mughni fi al-Tafsir*.

(p-210) How can one suppose of a noble prophet of Allah that he was frightened, terrified, and compelled to abandon this disobedience while he persisted in it? This is the utmost ugliness.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Thus﴾, meaning: thus did We show him the proof, ﴿that We might turn away from him evil﴾, which is betrayal by its companion, ﴿and immorality﴾, which is committing indecency. ﴿Indeed, he was of Our chosen servants﴾. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir recited it with a *kasra* on the *lam* (*mukhlisin*, those who make sincere), and the meaning is: "He is among Our servants who made their religion sincere." 'Asim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited it with a *fatha* on the *lam* (*mukhlasin*, those whom Allah purified), meaning: "those whom Allah purified from evils and indecencies." Some exegetes say: *al-su'* (evil) is fornication, and *al-fahsha'* (immorality) is sins.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 12, verses 25–27:

(p. 211) His saying, Most High: ﴿And they both raced to the door﴾. He means Yusuf and the woman. Each of them hurried toward the door, striving to get ahead of the other. Yusuf wanted to get ahead in order to open the door and leave, while she wanted, if she got ahead, to hold the door shut so that he could not leave. She caught up with him and seized his shirt from behind, pulling him toward her, and she tore his shirt from the back, meaning she cut it from behind, because he was the one fleeing and she was the one pursuing him. The exegetes (mufassirun) said: she tore his shirt in two. When they both came out, they found her master (sayyid), that is, they encountered her husband at the door. At that moment, deceit (kayd) came over her, so she spoke first with words, clearing herself of the matter: ﴿What is the penalty for one who intended evil against your wife, except that he be imprisoned or suffer a painful punishment?﴾. Ibn Abbas said: she meant adultery. ﴿Except that he be imprisoned﴾, meaning the penalty for him is nothing but prison. ﴿Or a painful punishment﴾, she meant being beaten with whips. Then Yusuf became angry and said: ﴿It was she who sought to seduce me﴾. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: the Aziz (al-Aziz) then said to him: "Have you betrayed me, O Yusuf, regarding my household, and deceived me? Did you deceive me with what I used to see of your righteousness?" Then he said: ﴿It was she who sought to seduce me from myself﴾.

His saying, Most High: ﴿And a witness from her household testified﴾. This was because, when their two statements conflicted, they needed a witness by whom the truthful speaker would be known.

Regarding that witness there are three opinions:

The first: he was an infant in the cradle. This was narrated by Ikrimah from Ibn Abbas, and by Shahr ibn Hawshab from Abu Hurayrah. Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Dahhak, Hilal ibn Yasaf, and others also said this.

The second: he was one of the king's close associates. This was narrated by Ibn Abi Mulaykah from Ibn Abbas. Abu Salih said, from Ibn Abbas: he was her paternal cousin, and he was a wise man. He said: "We have heard the rushing and the commotion from behind the door. If the tear in the shirt is from the front, then you are truthful and he is lying; but if it is from behind, then he is truthful and you are lying." Some said he was her maternal cousin.

The third: the witness was the tear in the shirt. This was narrated by Ibn Abi Najih from Mujahid, and it is weak, because of His saying: ﴿from her household﴾.

If it is said: how did the testimony of this witness come to be stated conditionally, when the one who states the condition does not know what he is conditioning?

On this there are two answers, mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari:

The first: the witness testified concerning a matter he knew. It is as if he heard some of the speech between Yusuf and Zulaykha and so came to know. However, he placed a condition in his testimony so that the addressees would be bound to accept his testimony by reason and discernment. It is as if he said: "He is truthful in my view; if you reflect on the condition I stipulate for you, you will understand my statement." Similar to this is the saying of the wise: "If destiny is true, then greed is vain; and if death is certain, then trust in this world is foolishness."

The second answer: the witness did not speak with certainty, and did not know the reality of what had occurred. He only said what he said by way of expressing an opinion that occurred to him. So the meaning of His saying: ﴿and a witness testified﴾ is: he indicated and made clear. He said: "My opinion is that we should measure the shirt, so that the traitor may be identified." These two answers indicate that the speaker was a man. But if we say he was an infant in the cradle, then the entry of the condition serves to vindicate Yusuf, because the speech of such a one is a marvel and a miracle, with which no doubt remains.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 12, verses 25–27:

(p. 211) His saying, Most High: ﴿And they both raced to the door﴾. He means Yusuf and the woman. Each of them hurried toward the door, striving to get ahead of the other. Yusuf wanted to get ahead in order to open the door and leave, while she wanted, if she got ahead, to hold the door shut so that he could not leave. She caught up with him and seized his shirt from behind, pulling him toward her, and she tore his shirt from the back, meaning she cut it from behind, because he was the one fleeing and she was the one pursuing him. The exegetes (mufassirun) said: she tore his shirt in two. When they both came out, they found her master (sayyid), that is, they encountered her husband at the door. At that moment, deceit (kayd) came over her, so she spoke first with words, clearing herself of the matter: ﴿What is the penalty for one who intended evil against your wife, except that he be imprisoned or suffer a painful punishment?﴾. Ibn Abbas said: she meant adultery. ﴿Except that he be imprisoned﴾, meaning the penalty for him is nothing but prison. ﴿Or a painful punishment﴾, she meant being beaten with whips. Then Yusuf became angry and said: ﴿It was she who sought to seduce me﴾. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: the Aziz (al-Aziz) then said to him: "Have you betrayed me, O Yusuf, regarding my household, and deceived me? Did you deceive me with what I used to see of your righteousness?" Then he said: ﴿It was she who sought to seduce me from myself﴾.

His saying, Most High: ﴿And a witness from her household testified﴾. This was because, when their two statements conflicted, they needed a witness by whom the truthful speaker would be known.

Regarding that witness there are three opinions:

The first: he was an infant in the cradle. This was narrated by Ikrimah from Ibn Abbas, and by Shahr ibn Hawshab from Abu Hurayrah. Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Dahhak, Hilal ibn Yasaf, and others also said this.

The second: he was one of the king's close associates. This was narrated by Ibn Abi Mulaykah from Ibn Abbas. Abu Salih said, from Ibn Abbas: he was her paternal cousin, and he was a wise man. He said: "We have heard the rushing and the commotion from behind the door. If the tear in the shirt is from the front, then you are truthful and he is lying; but if it is from behind, then he is truthful and you are lying." Some said he was her maternal cousin.

The third: the witness was the tear in the shirt. This was narrated by Ibn Abi Najih from Mujahid, and it is weak, because of His saying: ﴿from her household﴾.

If it is said: how did the testimony of this witness come to be stated conditionally, when the one who states the condition does not know what he is conditioning?

On this there are two answers, mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari:

The first: the witness testified concerning a matter he knew. It is as if he heard some of the speech between Yusuf and Zulaykha and so came to know. However, he placed a condition in his testimony so that the addressees would be bound to accept his testimony by reason and discernment. It is as if he said: "He is truthful in my view; if you reflect on the condition I stipulate for you, you will understand my statement." Similar to this is the saying of the wise: "If destiny is true, then greed is vain; and if death is certain, then trust in this world is foolishness."

The second answer: the witness did not speak with certainty, and did not know the reality of what had occurred. He only said what he said by way of expressing an opinion that occurred to him. So the meaning of His saying: ﴿and a witness testified﴾ is: he indicated and made clear. He said: "My opinion is that we should measure the shirt, so that the traitor may be identified." These two answers indicate that the speaker was a man. But if we say he was an infant in the cradle, then the entry of the condition serves to vindicate Yusuf, because the speech of such a one is a marvel and a miracle, with which no doubt remains.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 12, verse 28:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿When he saw his shirt torn from behind﴾. Concerning who this seer and speaker is, in ﴿Indeed, it is of your guile, surely your guile is mighty﴾, there are two opinions:

One of them: that he is the husband. The second: that he is the witness.

Concerning the pronoun (ha' al-kinayah, the pronoun of reference) in his saying ﴿Indeed, it is of your guile﴾, there are three opinions:

(p-213) One of them: that it refers to the tearing of the shirt. This was said by Muqatil.

The second: that it refers to her saying ﴿What is the recompense for one who intended evil to your wife, except imprisonment or a painful punishment?﴾ So the meaning is: your saying this is of your guile. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

The third: that it refers to the evil to which she invited him. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi. Ibn Abbas said: ﴿Indeed, your guile is mighty﴾, meaning your deeds are great, as you mix the innocent with the sick (i.e., the guilty).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 12, verse 29–30:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Yusuf, turn away from this﴾. The meaning: O Yusuf, turn away.

Regarding the one who said this to him there are two opinions:

One: that he was her cousin (ibn ʿammihā), who was the witness. This is related from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: that he was the husband. This was mentioned by a group of the exegetes (mufassirun). Ibn ʿAbbas said: "Turn away from this matter, do not mention it to anyone, and keep it hidden for her sake." Al-Halabi related from ʿAbd al-Warith: ﴿Yusuf, turn away from this﴾ with the letter rāʾ vocalized with a fatḥa, as a statement (khabar).

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And seek forgiveness for your sin﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions:

One: ask your husband for pardon so that he does not punish you. This is related from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: repent from your sin, for you have indeed committed wrong.

Regarding the one who said this there are two opinions: one is her cousin; the second is the husband.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, you were among those who erred﴾, meaning: among the sinners. The exegetes said: Then this story spread in Egypt until the women spoke of it, and this is His saying: ﴿And women in the city said﴾. Regarding their number there are two opinions:

(p-214) One: they were four women: the wife of the king's cupbearer, the wife of the king's chief of records, the wife of his baker, and the wife of the keeper of his prison. This is related from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: they were five: the wife of the baker, the wife of the cupbearer, the wife of the jailer, the wife of the keeper of the inkwell, and the wife of the doorkeeper. This is related by Muqatil.

As for al-ʿAziz, in their language it means the king, and fata (youth) carries the meaning of servant (ʿabd). Al-Zajjaj said: "They used to call a slave a fata." The women only spoke concerning her right, disparaging her and establishing the innocence of Yusuf.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿She has been overcome by love﴾, meaning: his love reached the innermost covering of her heart.

Regarding the shaghaf (innermost covering) there are four opinions:

One: it is a membrane between the heart and the fu'ad (inner heart), related by ʿIkrimah from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: that it is the sheath of the heart, said by Abu ʿUbayda. Ibn Qutayba said: "He did not mean the sheath; he meant the heart itself. It is said: shaghaftu fulanan (I pierced his shaghaf) when you reach his shaghaf, just as it is said: kabidtuhu (I struck his liver) when you reach his liver, and battantuhu (I struck his belly) when you reach his belly."

The third: that it is the core of the heart and its black clot.

The fourth: that it is an ailment in the interior, beneath the sharasif (lower ribs). They recited:

"A concern has come between that, entering as the shaghaf enters, which the fingers seek."

Al-Zajjaj mentioned both opinions. Al-Asmaʿi said: "The shaghaf, among the Arabs, is an ailment that occurs beneath the sharasif on the right side of the belly. The sharasif are the ends of the rib heads (maqatt ruʾus al-adlaʿ), whose singular is sharsuf."

ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr, ʿAli ibn al-Husayn, al-Hasan al-Basri, Mujahid, Ibn Muhaysin, and Ibn Abi ʿAbla read ﴿qad shaʿafaha﴾ with the letter ʿayn. Al-Farraʾ said: "It is as if he took her every way, and al-shaʿaf are the mountain peaks."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, we see her in clear error﴾, meaning: away from the path of right guidance, because of her love for him. And al-mubin means: the evident.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 12, verse 31–32:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When she heard of their scheming﴾, meaning: the wife of the Aziz (al-'Aziz). Regarding "their scheming" there are two opinions:

The first: it is their speech and their criticism of her. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, al-Suddi, and Ibn Qutaybah. Al-Zajjaj said: This speech was called scheming because she had revealed her matter to them and asked them to keep it secret, so they schemed and spread her secret.

The second: it was actual scheming, and they said this as a scheme against her in order to make them see Yusuf. This is the view of Ibn Ishaq.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and she prepared for them﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: it is "a'taddat," from al-'ata (preparation). Everything you take as a preparation for something is 'ata', and al-'ata' is a firm, binding thing. Ibn Qutaybah said: "a'taddat" has the meaning of "a'addat" (she prepared). As for al-muttaka' (a reclining place), there are three opinions:

(p-216) The first: it is the assembly (majlis). The meaning is: she prepared for them a gathering place. This is the view of al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: it is the cushions upon which they lean. This is the view of Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Zajjaj said: al-muttaka' is that upon which one leans for food, drink, or conversation.

The third: it is food. This is the view of al-Hasan, Mujahid, and Qatadah. Ibn Qutaybah said: It is said, "We reclined (ittaka'na) at so-and-so's place," meaning when we ate. Jamil ibn Ma'mar said:

﻿"So we remained in bounty and reclined, and drank the lawful from its jars"

The origin of this is that whoever you invite to eat, you prepare for him a cushion for comfort and tranquility, so food was called "muttaka'" by way of metaphor. Al-Azhari said: Food was called "muttaka'" because when people sat down to eat they reclined, and this community was forbidden from that. Mujahid read "mutkan" with a light, unvowelled ta', and regarding it there are four opinions:

The first: it is the citron (utrujj), the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, and Yahya ibn Ya'mar, among others. From this is the poet's saying:

"We drink sin openly from the cup, and we see the mutk lent among us"

He means the citron.

The second: it is also food, the view of Ikrimah. The third: it is anything that is cut with knives, the view of al-Dahhak. The fourth: it is the zumawward (a fragrant flower), also related from al-Dahhak. (p-217) It has been related from a group that they explained al-muttaka' with what they explained al-mutk. It is related from Ibn Jurayj that he said: al-muttaka' is the citron and everything that is cut with knives. From al-Dahhak he said: al-muttaka' is everything that is cut with knives. Others distinguished between the two readings. Mujahid said: whoever reads "muttaka'" with the emphatic ta' means food, and whoever reads with the light ta' means the citron. Ibn Qutaybah said: whoever reads "mutkan" intends the citron, and it is said to be the zumawward. Whatever the case, I do not think it was called mutk except by cutting, as if it is derived from al-batk (cutting), and the mim was replaced by a ba', as is said: "sammada ra'sahu" and "sabadahu" when he uprooted it, and "sharrun lazimun" and "lazibun," and mim is often substituted for ba' because their points of articulation are close.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and she gave each one of them a knife﴾. She only did this because the food she had served them required knives. It was also said: her intent was to expose them by having them cut their hands, just as they had exposed her. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: she gave each one of them a citron and a knife, and said to them: "Do not cut or eat until I tell you." Then she said to Yusuf: "Go out to them." Al-Zajjaj said: if you wish, you may vowel the ta' in His saying "waqalat" (she said), and if you wish, you may kasra it; the kasra is the original, given the sukun of the ta' and the kha'. Whoever vowels the ta', does so because of the heaviness of the damma after a kasra. He could not refuse to go out, because he was like a slave to her. Some scholars of knowledge mentioned that she only said "go out," while concealing within herself "to them," so the Truth reported what was in the self as if the tongue had spoken it. Similar to this is His saying: ﴿We feed you only for the sake of Allah...﴾ [al-Insan 76:9]; they did not say that, rather they concealed it. What confirms the soundness of this is that if she had said to him, while he was a handsome young man, "Go out to women whose nature is temptation," he would not have done so.

Regarding His saying "akbarnahu" there are two opinions:

(p-218) The first: they exalted him (a'zamnahu). This is related by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas, and Ibn Abi Najih from Mujahid, and this is the view of Qatadah and Ibn Zayd.

The second: they menstruated (hadan). This is related by al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas. 'Ali ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas related from his father who said: "hadna" means from joy. He said: and in this the poet says:

"We come to women during their purity, and we do not come to women when they menstruate with great menstruation"

This meaning was also related by Layth from Mujahid, and Ibn al-Anbari preferred it, but some philologists rejected it. It is related from Abu 'Ubaydah that he said: there is no usage in the speech of the Arabs of "akbarna" meaning "hadna," but perhaps they menstruated from the intensity of what they exalted. Likewise it is related from al-Zajjaj that he denied it.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and they cut their hands﴾. There are three opinions:

The first: they cut their hands, thinking they were cutting food. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Zayd.

The second: they cut their hands until they threw them away. This is the view of Mujahid and Qatadah.

The third: they wounded the palms and peeled the fingertips. This is the view of Wahb ibn Munabbih.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and they said: Allah forbid!﴾ Abu 'Amr read "hasha" with an alif in pause in both places, and they agreed on omitting the alif in stopping. Abu 'Amr came with it in full and original form, while the others omitted it. This word is used in two places: first, as an exception; second, as clearing oneself of evil. The original is "hasha," and it is derived from your saying: "I was in the hasha of so-and-so," meaning in his side. Al-hasha is the side, and they recited:

"By which side has the departing companion gone?"

meaning: by which sides. The meaning is that Yusuf is far removed from being a human, because of the excess of his beauty. It was also said: he is far removed from what she accused him of. Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid said: "Hasha lillah" means "ma'adh Allah" (God forbid). Al-Farra' said: "bashaamong" is in the accusative, because the preposition (ba') has been used with it, and the people of the Hijaz almost always speak with the ba'; when they omit it, they want it to have an effect on what it has left, so they put it in the accusative on that basis. Similarly His saying: ﴿mā hunna ummahātihim﴾ [al-Mujadila 58:2]. As for the people of Najd, they speak both with and without the ba'; when they drop it, they use the nominative, which is the stronger of the two options in Arabic. Al-Zajjaj said: his saying that the nominative is the stronger of the two options is an error, because the Book of Allah is the strongest of languages, and no one read in the nominative. Al-Khalil, Sibawayh, and all the early grammarians claimed that "basharan" is in the accusative, because it is the predicate of "ma," and "ma" functions as "laysa." I say: Abu al-Mutawakkil, Abu Nuhayk, Ikrimah, and Mu'adh al-Qari among others read "ma hadha basharun" in the nominative. Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Abu al-Jawza', and Abu al-Sawwar read "ma hadha bi-shira" with a kasra on the ba' and shin, defective and nunated. Al-Farra' said: meaning, this is not something purchased. Ibn Mas'ud read "bi-shira'" with the long vowel and hamza, genitive and nunated.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿This is none but an honourable angel﴾. Ubayy, Abu Razin, Ikrimah, Abu Haywa, and al-Jahdari read "malik" with a kasra on the lam.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That is the one about whom you blamed me﴾. The exegetes said: when their minds departed upon cutting their hands, she said this to them.

If it is asked: "How could she point to him while he was present with her saying 'dhalikunna'?" Ibn al-Anbari mentioned two answers regarding this:

The first: she pointed with "dhalikunna" to Yusuf after he had departed from the assembly.

The second: in the speech there is an implied "hadha," its meaning being: "fa-hadha dhalikunna." The meaning of (p-220) ﴿you blamed me regarding him﴾ is: regarding his love. Then she confessed before them, saying: ﴿And I did seek to seduce him, but he refused﴾, meaning: he abstained.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and he will surely be among the debased﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: the good recitation is the light "wa-la-yakunan" and stopping on it with an alif, because the light nun is replaced by an alif in pause; you say "idribanna Zaydan," and when you stop you say "idriba." It has also been read "wa-la-yakunanna" with a shadda on the nun, but I dislike it, because it contradicts the Mushaf, since the heavy nun is not replaced by anything. The "saghirun" are the humiliated.
