﻿"So we remained in bounty and reclined, and drank the lawful from its jars"

The origin of this is that whoever you invite to eat, you prepare for him a cushion for comfort and tranquility, so food was called "muttaka'" by way of metaphor. Al-Azhari said: Food was called "muttaka'" because when people sat down to eat they reclined, and this community was forbidden from that. Mujahid read "mutkan" with a light, unvowelled ta', and regarding it there are four opinions:

The first: it is the citron (utrujj), the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, and Yahya ibn Ya'mar, among others. From this is the poet's saying:

"We drink sin openly from the cup, and we see the mutk lent among us"

He means the citron.

The second: it is also food, the view of Ikrimah. The third: it is anything that is cut with knives, the view of al-Dahhak. The fourth: it is the zumawward (a fragrant flower), also related from al-Dahhak. (p-217) It has been related from a group that they explained al-muttaka' with what they explained al-mutk. It is related from Ibn Jurayj that he said: al-muttaka' is the citron and everything that is cut with knives. From al-Dahhak he said: al-muttaka' is everything that is cut with knives. Others distinguished between the two readings. Mujahid said: whoever reads "muttaka'" with the emphatic ta' means food, and whoever reads with the light ta' means the citron. Ibn Qutaybah said: whoever reads "mutkan" intends the citron, and it is said to be the zumawward. Whatever the case, I do not think it was called mutk except by cutting, as if it is derived from al-batk (cutting), and the mim was replaced by a ba', as is said: "sammada ra'sahu" and "sabadahu" when he uprooted it, and "sharrun lazimun" and "lazibun," and mim is often substituted for ba' because their points of articulation are close.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and she gave each one of them a knife﴾. She only did this because the food she had served them required knives. It was also said: her intent was to expose them by having them cut their hands, just as they had exposed her. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: she gave each one of them a citron and a knife, and said to them: "Do not cut or eat until I tell you." Then she said to Yusuf: "Go out to them." Al-Zajjaj said: if you wish, you may vowel the ta' in His saying "waqalat" (she said), and if you wish, you may kasra it; the kasra is the original, given the sukun of the ta' and the kha'. Whoever vowels the ta', does so because of the heaviness of the damma after a kasra. He could not refuse to go out, because he was like a slave to her. Some scholars of knowledge mentioned that she only said "go out," while concealing within herself "to them," so the Truth reported what was in the self as if the tongue had spoken it. Similar to this is His saying: ﴿We feed you only for the sake of Allah...﴾ [al-Insan 76:9]; they did not say that, rather they concealed it. What confirms the soundness of this is that if she had said to him, while he was a handsome young man, "Go out to women whose nature is temptation," he would not have done so.

Regarding His saying "akbarnahu" there are two opinions:

(p-218) The first: they exalted him (a'zamnahu). This is related by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas, and Ibn Abi Najih from Mujahid, and this is the view of Qatadah and Ibn Zayd.

The second: they menstruated (hadan). This is related by al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas. 'Ali ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas related from his father who said: "hadna" means from joy. He said: and in this the poet says:

"We come to women during their purity, and we do not come to women when they menstruate with great menstruation"

This meaning was also related by Layth from Mujahid, and Ibn al-Anbari preferred it, but some philologists rejected it. It is related from Abu 'Ubaydah that he said: there is no usage in the speech of the Arabs of "akbarna" meaning "hadna," but perhaps they menstruated from the intensity of what they exalted. Likewise it is related from al-Zajjaj that he denied it.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and they cut their hands﴾. There are three opinions:

The first: they cut their hands, thinking they were cutting food. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Zayd.

The second: they cut their hands until they threw them away. This is the view of Mujahid and Qatadah.

The third: they wounded the palms and peeled the fingertips. This is the view of Wahb ibn Munabbih.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and they said: Allah forbid!﴾ Abu 'Amr read "hasha" with an alif in pause in both places, and they agreed on omitting the alif in stopping. Abu 'Amr came with it in full and original form, while the others omitted it. This word is used in two places: first, as an exception; second, as clearing oneself of evil. The original is "hasha," and it is derived from your saying: "I was in the hasha of so-and-so," meaning in his side. Al-hasha is the side, and they recited:

"By which side has the departing companion gone?"

meaning: by which sides. The meaning is that Yusuf is far removed from being a human, because of the excess of his beauty. It was also said: he is far removed from what she accused him of. Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid said: "Hasha lillah" means "ma'adh Allah" (God forbid). Al-Farra' said: "bashaamong" is in the accusative, because the preposition (ba') has been used with it, and the people of the Hijaz almost always speak with the ba'; when they omit it, they want it to have an effect on what it has left, so they put it in the accusative on that basis. Similarly His saying: ﴿mā hunna ummahātihim﴾ [al-Mujadila 58:2]. As for the people of Najd, they speak both with and without the ba'; when they drop it, they use the nominative, which is the stronger of the two options in Arabic. Al-Zajjaj said: his saying that the nominative is the stronger of the two options is an error, because the Book of Allah is the strongest of languages, and no one read in the nominative. Al-Khalil, Sibawayh, and all the early grammarians claimed that "basharan" is in the accusative, because it is the predicate of "ma," and "ma" functions as "laysa." I say: Abu al-Mutawakkil, Abu Nuhayk, Ikrimah, and Mu'adh al-Qari among others read "ma hadha basharun" in the nominative. Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Abu al-Jawza', and Abu al-Sawwar read "ma hadha bi-shira" with a kasra on the ba' and shin, defective and nunated. Al-Farra' said: meaning, this is not something purchased. Ibn Mas'ud read "bi-shira'" with the long vowel and hamza, genitive and nunated.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿This is none but an honourable angel﴾. Ubayy, Abu Razin, Ikrimah, Abu Haywa, and al-Jahdari read "malik" with a kasra on the lam.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That is the one about whom you blamed me﴾. The exegetes said: when their minds departed upon cutting their hands, she said this to them.

If it is asked: "How could she point to him while he was present with her saying 'dhalikunna'?" Ibn al-Anbari mentioned two answers regarding this:

The first: she pointed with "dhalikunna" to Yusuf after he had departed from the assembly.

The second: in the speech there is an implied "hadha," its meaning being: "fa-hadha dhalikunna." The meaning of (p-220) ﴿you blamed me regarding him﴾ is: regarding his love. Then she confessed before them, saying: ﴿And I did seek to seduce him, but he refused﴾, meaning: he abstained.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and he will surely be among the debased﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: the good recitation is the light "wa-la-yakunan" and stopping on it with an alif, because the light nun is replaced by an alif in pause; you say "idribanna Zaydan," and when you stop you say "idriba." It has also been read "wa-la-yakunanna" with a shadda on the nun, but I dislike it, because it contradicts the Mushaf, since the heavy nun is not replaced by anything. The "saghirun" are the humiliated.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 12, verse 33–34:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said: "My Lord, prison is dearer to me"﴾. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: When she said, ﴿"That is the one about whom you blamed me"﴾, they said: "There is no blame upon you." She said: "Then ask Yusuf to grant me my need." So they said: "O Yusuf, do it." She said: "If he does not do it, I will certainly keep him in prison." At that point he said: ﴿"My Lord, prison is dearer to me"﴾.

And Ya'qub (Ya'qub ibn Ishaq al-Hadrami, one of the readers of the Qur'an) read "al-Sijn" (السَّجْنُ) with a fatha on the sin here alone. Al-Zajjaj (Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj, grammarian) said: Whoever reads the sin of "al-Sijni" (السِّجْنِ) with a kasra, it is in the sense of a noun of place, so the meaning is: the descent into prison is dearer to me than committing disobedience. And whoever reads it with a fatha, it is in the sense of a verbal noun, so the meaning is: that I be imprisoned is dearer to me.

﴿And unless You turn away from me their plot﴾, i.e., unless You protect me, ﴿I would incline toward them﴾, i.e., I would lean toward them. It is said: "Saba ila al-lahw yasbu sabwan wa subuwwan wa saba'an," meaning he inclined. Ibn al-Anbari said: The meaning of this statement is: O Allah, turn away from me their plot, and for this reason He said: ﴿So his Lord responded to him﴾.

He said: If it is said: It was the wife of the ruler alone who plotted against him, so how did He say "their plot"?

To this there are three answers:

One of them: The Arabs use the plural for the singular, so one of them says: "I went out to Basra in the ships," while he only went out in one ship.

The second: The one referred to is the wife of the ruler and the women who supported her in her matter.

The third: He meant the wife of the ruler and others of the women of the worlds who have a similar plot to hers.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 12, verse 35:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then it occurred to them, after they had seen the signs﴾. Regarding what is meant by "the signs" there are three opinions:

The first: they are the tearing of the shirt and the judgment of his cousin (ibn ʿammihā) against her. This was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: they are the tearing of the shirt, the testimony of the witness, the cutting of the hands, and the women's great esteem for him. This was narrated by Mujahid from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The third: his beauty and his chastity. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: The women then advised her to imprison him, hoping that they might seduce him when he was alone with them in the prison, and they said: "As soon as you imprison him, that will cut off from you the talk of the people that has spread, and they will see that you hate him, and the prison will humble him for you." When they departed, she returned to soliciting him, but he only grew further from her. When she despaired, she said to her master: "This servant has disgraced me, and I have come to hate the sight of him, so permit me to imprison him." He permitted her, and she imprisoned him and harmed him. Al-Suddi said: She said, "Either you permit me to go out and make my excuse with my own excuse, or you imprison him as you imprisoned me." Then the decision to imprison Yusuf appeared to the Aziz and his companions. Al-Zajjaj said: The Aziz had ordered only that he be turned away, then his opinion changed from that. Ibn al-Anbari said: In the meaning of the verse there are two sayings:

One of them: ﴿Then it occurred to them﴾, meaning: the imprisoning of him became apparent to them through speech, opinion and thought.

The second: then a change of mind (badaʾ) came upon them concerning Yusuf, and they said: "By God, we shall imprison him," so the lam is the answer to a suppressed oath. As for "ḥīn" (a period of time), it applies to a short time and a long time.

Regarding what is meant by it here, the exegetes have five opinions:

The first: five years, narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn ʿAbbas. The second: one year, also narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas. The third: seven years, said by ʿIkrimah. The fourth: until the talk ceased, said by ʿAtaʾ. The fifth: that it is an unspecified period of time, mentioned by al-Mawardi, and this is the correct view, because they did not resolve to imprison him for a known period; rather, the exegetes mentioned only the duration he remained.

Ibn al-Jawzi's commentary on Surah Yusuf, verse 36

Allah's words: ﴿And there entered the prison with him two young men﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: This indicates that he (Yusuf) was imprisoned, even though this is not mentioned. As for "fataan" (two young men), it is possible that they were two youths or two elders, because they used to call a slave "fata" (young man). Ibn al-Anbari said: He only said "fataan" because they were both slaves, and the Arabs call a slave "fata," whether he is young or old. The exegetes said: The king of Egypt grew angry with them and dismissed them, so they secretly approached his baker and his cupbearer, asking them to poison him. The king learned of this and imprisoned them both. Yusuf had said to the people of the prison: "Indeed, I interpret dreams." One of the two young men said: "Come, let us test this Hebrew slave."

They differed as to whether their dreams were true or not, with three opinions:

The first: that they were false, and that they only asked him as a test. This was said by Ibn Mas'ud and al-Suddi.

The second: that they were true. This was said by Mujahid and Ibn Ishaq.

The third: that the one of them who was crucified was lying, and the other was truthful. This was said by Abu Mijlaz.

Allah's words: ﴿One of them said﴾, meaning the cupbearer: "Indeed, I see myself" (in sleep) "pressing wine," meaning grapes. Concerning the naming of grapes as wine, there are three opinions:

The first: he named it by the name of what it becomes, since the meaning is not ambiguous, as one says: "So-and-so bakes bricks and makes date-syrup," while in fact he bakes clay and makes dates. This is the view of most exegetes. Ibn al-Anbari said: It was like this because the Arabs apply to the branch what applies to the root, as when they say: "So-and-so bakes bricks."

The second: that in the dialect of the people of Oman, "khamr" is the name for grapes. This was said by al-Dahhak and al-Zajjaj. Ibn al-Qasim said: The Quraysh also spoke this dialect and knew it.

The third: that the meaning is: "I press the grapes of wine," and the origin of wine, and the cause of wine, so the qualifying word was omitted and the qualified word was put in its place, as in His words: ﴿And ask the town﴾ [Yusuf 82]. Abu Salih reported from Ibn Abbas: One day Yusuf saw the baker and the cupbearer looking distressed, and he said: "What is your matter?" They said: "We have seen a dream." He said: "Relate it to me." The cupbearer said: "I saw that I had entered a vineyard and picked three bunches of grapes, and I pressed them into the cup, then I brought it to the king and he drank it." The baker said: "I saw that I came out of the king's kitchen carrying three baskets of bread upon my head, and a bird landed on the uppermost of them and ate from it." ﴿Inform us of its interpretation﴾, meaning: tell us its explanation.

Concerning His words: ﴿Indeed, we see you to be of the good-doers﴾, there are five opinions:

The first: that he used to visit the sick, treat them, and console the grieving. This was narrated by Mujahid from Ibn Abbas.

The second: "Indeed, we see you as a good-doer if you inform us of its interpretation." This was said by Ibn Ishaq.

(p-224) The third: "Indeed, we see you among the knowledgeable, having excelled in knowledge." This was said by al-Farra'. Ibn al-Anbari said: According to this, the object of "ihsan" (excelling) is omitted, as it is omitted in His words: ﴿and in it they press﴾ [Yusuf 49], meaning grapes and sesame. They knew he was knowledgeable because he spread knowledge among them.

The fourth: "Indeed, we see you among those who excel in interpretation." This was mentioned by al-Zajjaj.

The fifth: "Indeed, we see you as one who does good to himself by adhering to the obedience of Allah." This was mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 12, verses 37–39:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said: "No food will come to you that you are given as provision, but I will inform you of its interpretation before it reaches you."﴾ There are two views regarding the meaning of the statement:

The first: "No food will come to you that you are given as provision while awake, but I will tell you about it before it reaches you, because he would inform people of what was hidden, like Jesus, peace be upon him." This is the view of al-Hasan.

The second: "No food will come to you that you are given as provision in a dream, but I will tell you its interpretation (ta'wil, the explanation of a dream's meaning) before it comes to you while awake." This is the view of al-Suddi. Ibn Abbas said: They said to him, "How do you know that, when you are neither a sorcerer, nor a soothsayer, nor an astrologer?" He said: ﴿That is of what my Lord has taught me.﴾

If it is said: All of this is not an answer to their question. Where is the answer to their question? There are four answers regarding this:

The first: When he knew that one of them would be killed, he invited them to their share of the Hereafter. This was said by Qatadah.

The second: He turned away from answering because of the displeasing news it contained for one of them. This was said by Ibn Jurayj.

The third: He began by calling them to faith before answering the question. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

The fourth: He thought they were lying about their dreams, so he turned away from their request so that they would stop demanding an answer. When they insisted, he answered them. This was mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari.

As for the millah (religion, creed), it means the religion. The repetition of his saying "they" (hum) is for emphasis.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿It is not for us to associate anything with Allah.﴾ Ibn Abbas said: He means that Allah protected us from shirk (associating partners with Allah). ﴿That is from the bounty of Allah upon us﴾ meaning our following of faith by Allah's guidance. ﴿And upon mankind﴾ meaning the believers, by Him guiding them to His religion. Ibn Abbas also said: ﴿That is from the bounty of Allah upon us﴾ that He made us prophets, ﴿and upon mankind﴾ that He sent us to them, ﴿but most of mankind﴾ from the people of Egypt ﴿do not give thanks﴾ for the favours of Allah, so that they would affirm His oneness.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Are separate lords better, or Allah, the One, the Subduer?﴾ This means the idols, small and large. "Better" means greater in attribute of praise. ﴿Or Allah, the One, the Subduer﴾ meaning: is He not more worthy of divinity than the idols?

As for al-Wahid (the One), al-Khattabi said: He is the Single who has always been alone. It was also said: He is the one who has no equal, no partner, and no like, and He is unlike the other singular things of composite bodies, for everything other than Him is called one from one aspect but not one from other aspects. And "one" (wahid) is not dualized from its own word; one does not say "two ones" (wahidan). As for al-Qahhar (the Subduer), it is the One who subdued the tyrants among His haughty creatures through punishment, and who subdued all creation through death. Others said: al-Qahhar is the One who subdued everything and made it submissive, so that it yielded and became humbled before Him.

And "one" (wahid) is not dualized from its own word; one does not say "two ones" (wahidan). As for al-Qahhar (the Subduer), it is the One who subdued the tyrants among His haughty creatures through punishment, and who subdued all creation through death. Others said: al-Qahhar is the One who subdued everything and made it submissive, so that it yielded and became humbled before Him.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 12, verses 40–41:

Allah's words: ﴿What you worship besides Him are but names﴾. He used the plural in address to the two of them because he meant all who shared their polytheism. His words "besides Him" mean besides Allah. "Only names" means: lords and gods. The meanings of those names do not apply to the idols, so they are like empty names; it is as if they worship names, since their meanings do not hold true of them. ﴿Allah has sent down no authority for them﴾, meaning: no proof for worshipping them. ﴿Judgment belongs to none but Allah﴾, meaning: decision, command and prohibition belong to Him alone. ﴿That is the upright religion﴾, meaning: the straight one, pointing to monotheism (tawhid).

﴿But most people do not know﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions:

One: they do not know that it is impermissible to worship other than Him. The second: they do not know the reward for the obedient and the punishment for the disobedient.

Allah's words: ﴿As for one of you, he will give his lord wine to drink﴾. "Lord" here means master (sayyid). Ibn al-Sa'ib said: when the cupbearer related his dream to Joseph, he said to him: "How good is what you saw! As for the three branches, they are three days; the king will send for you at their end, and will restore you to your position, and you will return as you were in your best state." And he said to the baker: "How bad is what you saw! The three baskets are three days; then the king will send for you at the end of them, and he will kill you, crucify you, and birds will eat from your head." They both said: "We saw nothing." He said: "The matter about which you inquire has been decided," meaning: it has been finished, and it will befall you both, whether you spoke truthfully or lied.

If it is asked: why did he make the fulfilment of the interpretation certain, when a dream's interpretation may sometimes be true and sometimes false? In answer there are two replies:

(p-227) One: he made it certain because of a revelation that came to him from Allah. The way of a false dream is that its interpretation does not come to pass; so when he said ﴿The matter has been decided﴾, this indicated that it was by revelation.

The second: he did not make it certain, as evidenced by his words: ﴿And he said to the one he thought would be saved of the two﴾. Those who hold this answer say: the meaning of ﴿The matter has been decided﴾ is: the answer you sought from me has been cut off; it did not mean that the matter will certainly befall you both. Those who hold the first answer say: "thought" (ẓann) here means knowledge ('ilm).

﴿He said to the one he thought would be saved from the two﴾: meaning the cupbearer.

﴿Mention me before your lord﴾: that is, before your master, who is the king. Say to him: "There is in the prison a young man who was imprisoned unjustly." The name of the king was al-Walid ibn al-Rayyan.

﴿So Satan caused him to forget the mention of his lord﴾. On this there are two opinions:

First: Satan caused the cupbearer to forget to mention Yusuf to his lord. This was said by Abu Salih, on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas, and Ibn Ishaq also said it.

Second: Satan caused Yusuf to forget the mention of his Lord, and he commanded him to mention the king, seeking relief from him. This was said by Mujahid, Muqatil and al-Zajjaj. This is forgetting by deliberate intent, not forgetting by inadvertence, and the opposite of the opinion before it.

(p-228) ﴿So he remained in the prison for several years﴾: that is, beyond what he had remained before that, as a punishment for him for relying on a created being.

Regarding the word bid' (several), there are nine opinions:

First: it is between seven and nine. Ibn 'Abbas related that when Abu Bakr wagered with the Quraysh at the revelation of ﴿Alif, Lam, Meem. The Romans have been defeated﴾ [al-Rum 1-2], the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: "Why did you not take precaution? Indeed, bid' is between seven and nine." Second: twelve years. This was said by al-Dahhak, on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas. Third: seven years. This was said by 'Ikrimah. Fourth: between five and seven. This was said by al-Hasan. Fifth: between four and nine. This was said by Mujahid. Sixth: between three and nine. This was said by al-Asma'i and al-Zajjaj. Seventh: that bid' lies between three, nine and ten. This was said by Qatadah. Eighth: that it is less than ten. This was said by al-Farra'. Al-Akhfash said: bid' is from one to ten. Ninth: that it is what does not reach a full decade nor half of it. This was said by Abu 'Ubaydah. Ibn Qutaybah said: meaning between one and four. Al-Athram related from Abu 'Ubaydah: bid' is between three and five.

Regarding the total period he remained in the prison, there are three opinions:

First: twelve years. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. Second: fourteen. This was said by al-Dahhak. Third: seven years. This was said by Qatadah.

Malik ibn Dinar said: When Yusuf said to the cupbearer, ﴿Mention me before your lord﴾, it was said to him: "O Yusuf, did you take other than Me as a guardian? I will surely prolong your imprisonment." So he wept and said: "O my Lord, the abundance of trials has made my heart forget. I said one word, so woe to my brothers."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 12, verse 43:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And the king said﴾, meaning the greatest king of Egypt, ﴿"Indeed, I see﴾, meaning in a dream, and he did not say "I saw." This is permissible in the language, that a speaker says "I see" meaning "I saw." Wahb ibn Munabbih said: When the period that Allah the Exalted had set for Yusuf in his imprisonment ended, Jibril entered upon him in the prison, and gave him good news of his release, of the kingship of Egypt, and of meeting his father. When the king had entered the evening of that night, he saw seven fat cows coming out of the river, and behind them were seven lean ones. The lean ones came upon the fat ones and took hold of their tails and devoured them up to the horns, and nothing was added to the lean ones. And he saw seven green ears of grain, and seven dry ones had come upon them, and devoured them until they reached them, and nothing was added to the dry ones. So he summoned the nobles of his people and recounted it to them, and they said: ﴿"A confusion of dreams"﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: "The lean" are those that have reached the utmost in emaciation. "Al-mala'" are those to whom matters are referred and whose opinion is followed. The lam in His saying ﴿"for dreams"﴾ entered upon the object for clarification; the meaning is: "if you are interpreters." Then he clarified with the lam, saying "for dreams." The meaning of "I interpreted the dream" (ʿabartu al-ru'ya) and "ʿabbartuha" is: I informed of the final outcome to which its matter would return. Its derivation is from ʿabr al-nahr, which is the bank of the river; so the sense of "ʿabartu al-nahr" is: I reached its ʿabr, that is, its bank, which is its far end.

(p-230) Ibn al-Anbari mentioned two opinions regarding the lam:

One of them: that it is for emphasis. The second: that it conveyed the meaning of "ila" (to), and the meaning is: "if you direct the interpretation to the dream."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 12, verse 44:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They said: "They are confused dreams."﴾ Abu Ubayda said: Its singular is ḍighth (ضِغْث), with the ḍad kasra-vowelled, and it refers to a dream without interpretation that one sees as bundles, gathered from dreams the way grass is gathered, so it is said ḍighth, meaning a handful of it. Al-Kisa'i said: al-adghath (الأضغاث) are mixed dreams. Ibn Qutayba said: "Confused dreams" means mixtures, like bundles of plants that a man gathers, so that in them there are various kinds mixed together. Al-Zajjaj said: the ḍighth in the language is a bundle or sheaf of something, such as herbs and the like, so they said to him: your dream is confused bundles, that is, mixed bundles, which are not a clear dream. ﴿"And we are not those who know the interpretation of dreams."﴾ That is, there is no interpretation for the mixed dream in our view. Others said: ﴿And we are not those who know the interpretation of dreams of this kind which he has described.﴾ The word al-aḥlam (الأحلام) is the plural of ḥulm (حُلُم), which is what a person sees in his sleep, of which some is true and some is false.

(p-231) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the one of the two who had been delivered said﴾ — meaning the one of the two young men who was saved from execution, namely the cupbearer. ﴿And remembered﴾ — i.e., he recalled the matter of Yusuf and what he had enjoined upon him. Al-Zajjaj said: The original form of "idhkara" (remembered) was "idhtakara," but the taa' was replaced by a daal, and the dhaal was assimilated into the daal. Al-Hasan recited "wa-adhkara" with a doubled dhaal. His saying: ﴿after a period﴾ — i.e., after a time, which is the length of time Yusuf remained in prison after that. Its explanation has already preceded. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan recited "ba'da ummatin" and intended: after forgetfulness (nisyan).

If it is said: This indicates that the one who forgot in His saying ﴿But Satan made him forget the remembrance of his Lord﴾ was the cupbearer, and there is no doubt that whoever says the one who forgot was Yusuf says: the cupbearer did not forget.

The answer is that whoever says Yusuf forgot says: the meaning of His saying ﴿and remembered﴾ is "he remembered," just as the Arabs say "ihtalaba" meaning "halaba" and "ightada" meaning "ghada." Therefore it does not indicate a forgetfulness that preceded it. Abu Salih related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: The cupbearer only did not mention Yusuf's news to the king until the king needed the interpretation of his dream, out of fear that mentioning him to Yusuf would be a cause for recalling the sin for which he had been imprisoned. Ibn al-Anbari mentioned this answer.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿I will inform you of its interpretation﴾ — i.e., from the side of Yusuf. ﴿So send me forth﴾. Ya'qub (Yaʻqūb) kept the yaʼ in this and in ﴿And do not approach me﴾ [Yusuf: 60] and ﴿That you think me senile﴾ [Yusuf: 94] in both cases. He addressed the king alone with the plural form, as a mark of honor. It was also said that he addressed him and his companions. There is an ellipsis in the speech; the meaning is: they sent him, so he came to Yusuf and said: "O Yusuf, O man of truth (al-Siddiq)." Al-Siddiq: one who is very truthful, just as it is said fissiq and sikkir (intensive forms), and its explanation has already preceded [al-Nisa': 69].

(p-232) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿That I may return to the people﴾ — meaning the king and his companions and the scholars whom he gathered to interpret his dream. Regarding His saying ﴿That they may know﴾ there are two opinions:

One: they may know the interpretation of the king's dream. The second: they may know your whereabouts, so that it becomes the cause of your release.

Ibn al-Anbari mentioned two views regarding the repetition of "la'alli" (perhaps I): One: the first "la'alla" relates to giving the interpretation, and the second is based on returning. Both carry the meaning of "kay" (so that). The second view: the first carries the meaning of "'asa" (perhaps), and the second carries the meaning of "kay," and it was repeated because the two meanings differ. This is also the answer to His saying: ﴿That they may recognize it when they return to their family; that they may return﴾ [Yusuf: 63]. The commentators said: His master, al-Aziz, had died, and his wife had been occupied away from him. Others said: al-Aziz had not died, so Yusuf said to the cupbearer: "Tell the king: these are seven fruitful years, and after them seven years of hardship, unless provision is made for them." The messenger went to the king and informed him. The king said to him: "Return to him and say: how should he act?" He said: ﴿You will sow for seven years in succession﴾. "Al-shidad" means the barren years that bear hard upon people. ﴿They will eat﴾ — i.e., they will consume what you had stored for them during the fruitful years. He described the years with eating, though it is eaten in them, just as it is said "a sleeping night."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿except a little of what you store﴾ — i.e., what you keep safe and save.

(p-231) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the one of the two who had been delivered said﴾ — meaning the one of the two young men who was saved from execution, namely the cupbearer. ﴿And remembered﴾ — i.e., he recalled the matter of Yusuf and what he had enjoined upon him. Al-Zajjaj said: The original form of "idhkara" (remembered) was "idhtakara," but the taa' was replaced by a daal, and the dhaal was assimilated into the daal. Al-Hasan recited "wa-adhkara" with a doubled dhaal. His saying: ﴿after a period﴾ — i.e., after a time, which is the length of time Yusuf remained in prison after that. Its explanation has already preceded. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan recited "ba'da ummatin" and intended: after forgetfulness (nisyan).

If it is said: This indicates that the one who forgot in His saying ﴿But Satan made him forget the remembrance of his Lord﴾ was the cupbearer, and there is no doubt that whoever says the one who forgot was Yusuf says: the cupbearer did not forget.

The answer is that whoever says Yusuf forgot says: the meaning of His saying ﴿and remembered﴾ is "he remembered," just as the Arabs say "ihtalaba" meaning "halaba" and "ightada" meaning "ghada." Therefore it does not indicate a forgetfulness that preceded it. Abu Salih related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: The cupbearer only did not mention Yusuf's news to the king until the king needed the interpretation of his dream, out of fear that mentioning him to Yusuf would be a cause for recalling the sin for which he had been imprisoned. Ibn al-Anbari mentioned this answer.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿I will inform you of its interpretation﴾ — i.e., from the side of Yusuf. ﴿So send me forth﴾. Ya'qub (Yaʻqūb) kept the yaʼ in this and in ﴿And do not approach me﴾ [Yusuf: 60] and ﴿That you think me senile﴾ [Yusuf: 94] in both cases. He addressed the king alone with the plural form, as a mark of honor. It was also said that he addressed him and his companions. There is an ellipsis in the speech; the meaning is: they sent him, so he came to Yusuf and said: "O Yusuf, O man of truth (al-Siddiq)." Al-Siddiq: one who is very truthful, just as it is said fissiq and sikkir (intensive forms), and its explanation has already preceded [al-Nisa': 69].

(p-232) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿That I may return to the people﴾ — meaning the king and his companions and the scholars whom he gathered to interpret his dream. Regarding His saying ﴿That they may know﴾ there are two opinions:

One: they may know the interpretation of the king's dream. The second: they may know your whereabouts, so that it becomes the cause of your release.

Ibn al-Anbari mentioned two views regarding the repetition of "la'alli" (perhaps I): One: the first "la'alla" relates to giving the interpretation, and the second is based on returning. Both carry the meaning of "kay" (so that). The second view: the first carries the meaning of "'asa" (perhaps), and the second carries the meaning of "kay," and it was repeated because the two meanings differ. This is also the answer to His saying: ﴿That they may recognize it when they return to their family; that they may return﴾ [Yusuf: 63]. The commentators said: His master, al-Aziz, had died, and his wife had been occupied away from him. Others said: al-Aziz had not died, so Yusuf said to the cupbearer: "Tell the king: these are seven fruitful years, and after them seven years of hardship, unless provision is made for them." The messenger went to the king and informed him. The king said to him: "Return to him and say: how should he act?" He said: ﴿You will sow for seven years in succession﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Abu Bakr from 'Asim recited "da'aban" with a sukun on the hamzah, except that Abu 'Amr, when he recited continuously, did not pronounce the hamzah. Hafs related from 'Asim "da'aban" with a fatha on the hamzah. Abu 'Ali said: The more common form of "da'ab" is with sukun, and perhaps the fatha is a dialect form. The meaning of "da'aban" is: continuous sowing according to your custom; the meaning is: you will sow persistently. Thus "da'aban" stands in place of "da'ibin." Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is: you will persist in the manner of persistence, and "tazra'un" indicates "tad'abun." Al-Da'b means constant adherence to a thing and habit.

If it is said: How did he judge by knowledge of the unseen, saying ﴿you will sow﴾, and not say "if God wills"? There are four answers regarding this:

(p-233) One: it was by revelation from God, Mighty and Majestic. The second: he based it on knowledge that God had taught him of the true interpretation, so he did not doubt. The third: he implicitly intended "if God wills," just as his brothers implicitly intended it in their saying: ﴿And we will bring provision for our family and guard our brother﴾ [Yusuf: 65], so they implicitly intended the exception in their intentions, because they were not confident of what they had promised. Ibn al-Anbari mentioned this. The fourth: he spoke as one giving a command to them, as if he had said: "Sow."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then leave it in its ear﴾ — for that keeps it better and further from spoiling. "Al-shidad" means the barren years that bear hard upon people. ﴿They will eat﴾ — i.e., they will consume what you had stored for them during the fruitful years. He described the years with eating, though it is eaten in them, just as it is said "a sleeping night."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿except a little of what you store﴾ — i.e., what you keep safe and save.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 12, verse 49:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then after that will come a year﴾. If it is said: why did He refer to the years with "that" (ذَلِكَ) when they are feminine?

On this there are two answers, which Ibn al-Qasim mentioned:

One of them: the seven (years) are feminine, and there is no sign of feminine gender in their wording, so they resembled the masculine, as in His saying: ﴿the sky splitting asunder thereby﴾ [al-Muzzammil 18], where He used the masculine (munfatir) for the sky because the sky has no mark of the feminine. The poet said:

"Neither a cloud that poured its rain, nor a land that brought forth its herbage (abqala)"

Here he used the masculine "abqala" for the reason we have described.

The second: "that" (dhalika) refers to the drought (al-jadb). This is the view of Muqatil, while the first is the view of al-Kalbi. Qatadah said: "God increased him in knowledge of a year they had not asked him about."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿In it the people will be given rain﴾. On this there are two views:

One: they will be rained upon, said by Ibn Abbas. The second: they will be granted relief through abundance, mentioned by al-Mawardi.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And in it they will press (yaʿsirun)﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir and 'Asim read "yaʿsirun" with the letter ya (yaʿsirūna). Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it with the letter ta, thereby directing the address to those who sought the interpretation.

On His saying "yaʿsirun" there are five views:

One: they will press grapes, olives and fruits. This was narrated by al-'Awfi from Ibn Abbas, and Qatadah and the majority said likewise.

The second: "yaʿsirun" means "yahtalibun" (they will milk), narrated by Ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn Abbas. Ibn al-Anbari related from his father, from Ahmad ibn 'Ubayd, who said: the interpretation of "yaʿsirun" is that they will milk the milk, because of the abundance of their good and the breadth of their fertility, and he cited the poet's verse:

"What protects the Arabs if there is no food for them, nor any milk from their wealth that is pressed (yuʿsar)?"

That is: milked (yuhlab).

The third: they will be saved (yanjun), and it is from al-'asar, and al-'asar means salvation, and al-'usrah means a refuge. It is said: "So-and-so is in 'usrah" if he is in a fortress that cannot be overcome. The poet said:

"Thirsty, seeking help, not given help, and indeed he was the refuge of the one who was saved (al-manjud)"

That is: a helper for the defeated, subdued one. And 'Adi said:

"If my throat were choked with something other than water, I would be like one who is choking on water, (i'tisari)."

The fourth: they will attain what they love. It was also narrated from Abu 'Ubaydah that he said: al-mu'tasir is the one who attains a thing and takes it, and from this is this verse. From it is the saying of Ibn Ahmar:

"For life is only in its freshness, and you are among its branches, one who is pressed (mu'tasar)."

The fifth: they will give and have surplus because of the breadth of their living, narrated by Ibn al-Anbari from some people of lexicography. Sa'id ibn Jubayr read "yuʿsarun" with a damma on the ya and a fatha on the sad. Al-Zajjaj said: he meant "yumtarun" (they will be rained upon), from His saying: ﴿And We sent down from the pressing clouds (al-mu'sirat) water pouring forth﴾ [al-Naba' 14].

(p-236) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The king said, "Bring him to me."﴾ The exegetes (mufassirun) said: When the cupbearer returned to the king and informed him of the interpretation of his dream, the truth of what he had said settled in the king's heart, so he said, "Bring me the one who interpreted my dream." The messenger came to Yusuf and said, "Answer the king." But he refused to leave until his innocence of what he had been accused of was made clear. So he said: ﴿Return to your lord﴾, meaning the king, ﴿and ask him: what was the matter with the women who cut their hands?﴾ Ibn Abi Abla recited "al-nuswati" (النُّسْوَةِ) with a dammah on the nun. The meaning is: ask the king to inquire into the affair and condition of those women, so that he may know the truth of my innocence. He only feared that the king would look at him with the eye of one whose affair is doubted or who is accused of indecency, and he wished that the king would see him after his innocence had been firmly established in his sight. The apparent meaning of his saying, ﴿Indeed my lord is well aware of their guile﴾, is that he meant God, exalted is He. Ibn Jarir al-Tabari reported that he meant his master, al-Aziz, and the meaning would be that he knows my innocence. It has been narrated from our Prophet (ﷺ) that he praised Yusuf's firmness and his patience in not rushing to leave prison, and he (ﷺ) said: "The noble son of a noble son of a noble son [the son of the noble], Yusuf son of Ya'qub son of Ishaq son of Ibrahim, if I had remained in prison as long as Yusuf remained, and then the caller had come to me, I would have answered."

On his mention of "the women" rather than the wife of al-Aziz, there are four opinions:
First: he mixed her in with the women because of the good conduct and courtesy he had shown her, as said by al-Zajjaj.
Second: because she was the wife of a king, so he protected her.
Third: because the women were witnesses against her for him.
Fourth: because mentioning her specifically would carry a kind of accusation. al-Mawardi mentioned the first three opinions.

The exegetes said: The messenger returned to the king with Yusuf's message, so the king summoned the women, among them the wife of al-Aziz, (p-237) and said: ﴿What was your affair when you sought to seduce Yusuf?﴾ That is, what was your matter and your story?

If it is said: only one of them sought to seduce him, so why did he gather them together? There are three answers to this:
First: he gathered them in the question so that he might know the precise act of seduction.
Second: Zulaykha sought to seduce him for herself, and the rest of the women urged him to accept her.
Third: he addressed them collectively, though the meaning applied to one of them, because a collective term may be applied to a category when there is no risk of confusion. This is supported by the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying to the women: "Indeed you are the majority of the people of the Fire." He addressed them collectively, though the meaning applied to some of them. This was mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They said, "Hashasha lillah (Far be God from it)!"﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: al-Hasan read "hash" (حَاشَ) with the shin pronounced with sukun. There is no disagreement among the grammarians that sukun is not permissible here, because joining two sakin letters is not allowed, and it is not from the speech of the Arabs. The women informed the king of Yusuf's innocence of any wrongdoing. Then the wife of al-Aziz said: ﴿Now the truth has come to light (haṣḥaṣa al-ḥaqq)﴾. That is: it became manifest and clear. Its etymology in the language is from ḥiṣṣa (portion): the portion of truth and its direction became distinct from the portion of falsehood's direction. Ibn al-Qasim said: (p-238) "ḥaṣḥaṣa" (حَصْحَصَ) means became clear and was uncovered. The Arabs say: "ḥaṣḥaṣa al-ba'ir fi burukihi" when the camel settled firmly in its kneeling and made an impression on the ground and scattered the pebbles.

Regarding the beginning of Zulaykha's confession, the exegetes have two opinions:
One: when she saw that the women had cleared him, she said: nothing remains except that they will turn to me for an account, so she confessed. This was said by al-Farra'.
The second: she showed repentance and affirmed the truthfulness of Yusuf. This was said by al-Mawardi.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 12, verse 52:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿That is so that he may know that I did not betray him in secret﴾. Muqatil said: "That" (dhalika) means "this" (hadha). Ibn al-Anbari said: The linguists said that "hadha" and "dhalika" are both suitable in this place and similar places, because the news is close to its people, so it becomes like something witnessed that is pointed to with "hadha"; and when it has passed, it is possible to point to it with "dhalika," because what has passed is like what is absent.

They differed concerning the speaker of this, in three views:

The first: that it is Yusuf. This is one of the most obscure forms of speech, where you relate something of one person and then connect it to the report of another. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿He wants to drive you out of your land﴾ [al-A'raf: 110], which is the saying of the council (al-mala'), and ﴿So what do you advise?﴾, which is the saying of Pharaoh. Similar to it is ﴿And thus they do﴾ [al-Naml: 34], which is the saying of Allah, the Exalted, and ﴿They make the mighty of its people abased﴾ [al-Naml: 34], which is the saying of Bilqis. Likewise ﴿Who has raised us from our sleeping place?﴾ [Ya-Sin: 52], which is the saying of the disbelievers, then the angels said: ﴿This is what the Most Merciful promised﴾. Such a thing is only permissible in speech when the indication of the meaning is clear.

They differed about where Yusuf said this, in two views:

One of them: when the cupbearer returned to Yusuf and informed him, while he was in prison, of the reply of the wife of the Aziz and the women to the king, he then said: ﴿That is so that he may know﴾. This was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas, and Ibn Jurayj said likewise.

The second: that he said it after his attendance at the king's assembly. This was narrated by Ata' from Ibn Abbas:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿That is so that he may know﴾, meaning: that which I did in returning the king's messenger is so that he may know.

They differed concerning what is referred to by His saying ﴿so that he may know﴾ and His saying ﴿I did not betray him﴾, in four views:

The first: that it is the Aziz, and the meaning is: so that the Aziz may know that I did not betray him regarding his wife ﴿in secret﴾, meaning when he was absent from me. This was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas, and al-Hasan, Mujahid, Qatadah and the majority said likewise.

The second: that what is referred to by His saying ﴿so that he may know﴾ is the king, and what is referred to by His saying ﴿I did not betray him﴾ is the Aziz, and the meaning is: so that the king may know that I did not betray the Aziz in his family ﴿in secret﴾. This was narrated by al-Dahhak from Ibn Abbas.

The third: that what is referred to by both is the king, so the meaning is: so that the king may know that I did not betray him, meaning also the king, ﴿in secret﴾.

Concerning the aspect of betraying the king in this matter there are two views:

One: because the Aziz was his minister, so the meaning is: I did not betray him regarding his minister's wife. This was said by Ibn al-Anbari.

The second: I did not betray him regarding his sister's daughter, and Zulaykha was the daughter of the king's sister. This was said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi.

The fourth: that what is referred to by His saying ﴿so that he may know﴾ is Allah, so the meaning is: so that Allah may know that I did not betray him. This was narrated from Mujahid. Ibn al-Anbari said: He attributed the knowing to Allah in outward form, while in meaning it is for the created beings, as in His saying: ﴿until We know those of you who strive﴾ [Muhammad: 31].

If it is said: If Yusuf said this in the king's assembly, how did he say "li-ya'lama" (he may know) and not "li-ta'lama" (you may know), when he was addressing him?

The answer: If we say that he was present before the king, then he preferred the third-person form out of respect for the king, as a man says to the minister: "If the minister sees fit to endorse my petition." And if we say that he was absent, there is no reason for the feminine form, and likewise if we say that he meant the Aziz, since the Aziz was absent from the king's assembly at that time.

The second view: that it is the saying of the wife of the Aziz. On this view it connects to what precedes it, and the meaning is: so that Yusuf may know that I did not betray him in his absence just now by lying about him.

The third: that it is the saying of the Aziz, and the meaning is: so that Yusuf may know that I did not betray him in secret, so I did not neglect to reward him for his trustworthiness. al-Mawardi related both views.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And that Allah does not guide the plot of the betrayers﴾. Ibn Abbas said: He does not make right the deed of the adulterers. Others said: He does not guide one who betrays his trust, and He exposes him in his outcome.

[p. 241] **His saying, Most High: ﴿Nor do I absolve myself﴾.** Concerning the speaker of this, there are three opinions, which were mentioned in the verse before it.

Those who said it was Joseph disagreed about the reason he said this, giving five opinions:

First: when he said, ﴿So that he may know that I did not betray him in his absence﴾, Gabriel nudged him and said, "Nor when you desired her?" So he said, ﴿Nor do I absolve myself﴾. This was narrated by ʿIkrimah from Ibn ʿAbbas, and most scholars held this view.

Second: when Joseph said, ﴿I did not betray him﴾, he mentioned that he had desired her, and so he said, ﴿Nor do I absolve myself﴾. This was narrated by al-ʿAwfi from Ibn ʿAbbas.

Third: when he said that, he feared he had praised himself, so he said, ﴿Nor do I absolve myself﴾. This was said by al-Hasan.

Fourth: when he said it, the angel with him said to him, "Remember what you desired," so he said, ﴿Nor do I absolve myself﴾. This was said by Qatadah.

Fifth: when he said it, the wife of the ʿAziz said, "Nor on the day you untied your trousers," so he said, ﴿Nor do I absolve myself﴾. This was said by al-Suddi.

Those who said this is the statement of the wife of the ʿAziz understood the meaning as: "I do not absolve myself, that I had sought to seduce him."

Those who said it is the statement of the ʿAziz understood the meaning as: "I do not absolve myself from entertaining an evil opinion of Joseph, because it has occurred to me."

His saying, Most High: ﴿Indeed, the soul is a persistent enjoiner of evil﴾. Ibn ʿAmir, the people of Kufa, and Yaʿqub, except Ruways, recited ﴿bi-l-suʾ illa﴾ with both hamzahs made clear (*tahqiq*). Abu ʿAmr and Ibn Shanbudh, on the authority of Qunbul, recited with the second hamzah made clear and the first omitted. Nazif, on the authority of Qunbul, narrated with the first hamzah made clear and the second changed into a *yaʾ*. Abu Jaʿfar, Warsh, and Ruways recited with the first hamzah made clear and the second softened to an intermediate sound (*bayna bayna*), like "al-suʾ ʿillā". Ibn Fulayh narrated with the second hamzah made clear and the first changed into a *waw*, which he then assimilated into the *waw* preceding it, so that it became a *waw* with a kasra and a shadda before the hamzah of *illā*.

His saying, Most High: ﴿Except what my Lord has mercy upon﴾. Ibn al-Anbari said: The linguists say this is a disjunctive exception (*istithnāʾ munqaṭiʿ*), and the meaning is: "But the mercy of my Lord is what is relied upon." Abu Salih narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas: the meaning is "except those whom my Lord protects." It was also said that *mā* here means *man* ("whoever"). Al-Mawardi said: whoever holds that this is the statement of the wife of the ʿAziz, the meaning is "except whom my Lord has mercy upon in restraining him from his desire, or in removing it from him." Whoever holds that it is the statement of the ʿAziz, the meaning is "except whom my Lord has mercy upon by sparing him evil suspicion, or by keeping him steady so that he does not hastily judge."

Ibn al-Anbari said: The view that this is the statement of Joseph is more correct, for two reasons:

One: because the scholars hold it.

Two: because the woman was a worshipper of idols, and what the verse contains is more fitting to be the statement of Joseph than of one who does not know God, Mighty and Majestic.

The exegetes said: When the king became convinced of Joseph's innocence and knew his trustworthiness, he said: ﴿Bring him to me; I will take him exclusively for myself﴾, that is, I will make him devoted to me, with no one sharing him with me.

If it is objected: You have narrated earlier that Joseph said in the king's assembly, ﴿That is so that he may know that I did not betray him in his absence﴾, so how could the king say, "Bring him to me," when he was present with him?

The answer: The proponents of this view say that the king ordered him to be brought so that he might appoint him over affairs outside the assembly in which he had been summoned to interpret the dream. Wahb said: When Joseph entered upon the king, and the king spoke in seventy languages, whenever the king addressed him in one language, Joseph answered him in that same language, and the king was amazed. Joseph was then thirty years old. The king said, "I love to hear my dream from you directly," and he related it to him. He said, "What do you think, O truthful one?" [p. 243] He said, "I think you should sow a great deal of crops during these fertile years and gather the grain, so that people will come to you to buy, and you will accumulate in your possession treasures such as no one has ever gathered."
