Second: when Joseph said, ﴿I did not betray him﴾, he mentioned that he had desired her, and so he said, ﴿Nor do I absolve myself﴾. This was narrated by al-ʿAwfi from Ibn ʿAbbas.

Third: when he said that, he feared he had praised himself, so he said, ﴿Nor do I absolve myself﴾. This was said by al-Hasan.

Fourth: when he said it, the angel with him said to him, "Remember what you desired," so he said, ﴿Nor do I absolve myself﴾. This was said by Qatadah.

Fifth: when he said it, the wife of the ʿAziz said, "Nor on the day you untied your trousers," so he said, ﴿Nor do I absolve myself﴾. This was said by al-Suddi.

Those who said this is the statement of the wife of the ʿAziz understood the meaning as: "I do not absolve myself, that I had sought to seduce him."

Those who said it is the statement of the ʿAziz understood the meaning as: "I do not absolve myself from entertaining an evil opinion of Joseph, because it has occurred to me."

His saying, Most High: ﴿Indeed, the soul is a persistent enjoiner of evil﴾. Ibn ʿAmir, the people of Kufa, and Yaʿqub, except Ruways, recited ﴿bi-l-suʾ illa﴾ with both hamzahs made clear (*tahqiq*). Abu ʿAmr and Ibn Shanbudh, on the authority of Qunbul, recited with the second hamzah made clear and the first omitted. Nazif, on the authority of Qunbul, narrated with the first hamzah made clear and the second changed into a *yaʾ*. Abu Jaʿfar, Warsh, and Ruways recited with the first hamzah made clear and the second softened to an intermediate sound (*bayna bayna*), like "al-suʾ ʿillā". Ibn Fulayh narrated with the second hamzah made clear and the first changed into a *waw*, which he then assimilated into the *waw* preceding it, so that it became a *waw* with a kasra and a shadda before the hamzah of *illā*.

His saying, Most High: ﴿Except what my Lord has mercy upon﴾. Ibn al-Anbari said: The linguists say this is a disjunctive exception (*istithnāʾ munqaṭiʿ*), and the meaning is: "But the mercy of my Lord is what is relied upon." Abu Salih narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas: the meaning is "except those whom my Lord protects." It was also said that *mā* here means *man* ("whoever"). Al-Mawardi said: whoever holds that this is the statement of the wife of the ʿAziz, the meaning is "except whom my Lord has mercy upon in restraining him from his desire, or in removing it from him." Whoever holds that it is the statement of the ʿAziz, the meaning is "except whom my Lord has mercy upon by sparing him evil suspicion, or by keeping him steady so that he does not hastily judge."

Ibn al-Anbari said: The view that this is the statement of Joseph is more correct, for two reasons:

One: because the scholars hold it.

Two: because the woman was a worshipper of idols, and what the verse contains is more fitting to be the statement of Joseph than of one who does not know God, Mighty and Majestic.

The exegetes said: When the king became convinced of Joseph's innocence and knew his trustworthiness, he said: ﴿Bring him to me; I will take him exclusively for myself﴾, that is, I will make him devoted to me, with no one sharing him with me.

If it is objected: You have narrated earlier that Joseph said in the king's assembly, ﴿That is so that he may know that I did not betray him in his absence﴾, so how could the king say, "Bring him to me," when he was present with him?

The answer: The proponents of this view say that the king ordered him to be brought so that he might appoint him over affairs outside the assembly in which he had been summoned to interpret the dream. Wahb said: When Joseph entered upon the king, and the king spoke in seventy languages, whenever the king addressed him in one language, Joseph answered him in that same language, and the king was amazed. Joseph was then thirty years old. The king said, "I love to hear my dream from you directly," and he related it to him. He said, "What do you think, O truthful one?" [p. 243] He said, "I think you should sow a great deal of crops during these fertile years and gather the grain, so that people will come to you to buy, and you will accumulate in your possession treasures such as no one has ever gathered." The king said, "Who will manage this for me?" Joseph said: ﴿Appoint me over the treasuries of the land﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: By his saying ﴿a trustworthy custodian﴾ he meant: "I have established you in my kingdom and entrusted you with it." Muqatil said: *al-Makin* means the honored one of high standing, and *al-Amin* means the guardian.

His saying, Most High: ﴿Appoint me over the treasuries of the land﴾, that is, the treasuries of your land.

Regarding what is meant by "treasuries," there are two opinions:

One: the treasuries of wealth. This was said by al-Dahhak and al-Zajjaj.

The second: the treasuries of food only. This was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib. Al-Zajjaj said: He asked for this only because prophets were sent with justice, so he knew that no one was more capable of this than he.

Regarding his saying, ﴿Indeed, I am a knowing guardian﴾, there are three opinions:

One: a guardian of what you have entrusted to me, knowing when famine will occur. This was said by Abu Salih from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: a guardian of what you have entrusted to me, knowing these years. This was said by al-Hasan.

The third: a guardian of the accounts, knowing the languages. This was said by al-Suddi, because people would come to the king from every region and speak in different languages.

They disagreed as to whether the king appointed him that day or not, giving three opinions:

One: that he appointed him after a year. Al-Dahhak narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), that he said: "May God have mercy on my brother Joseph. Had he not said, 'Appoint me over the treasuries of the land,' he would have employed him at once, but he delayed that for a year." Muqatil mentioned that the Prophet (ﷺ) [p. 244] said: "Had Joseph said, 'Indeed, I am a knowing guardian, if God wills,' he would have been made king at that very moment." Mujahid said: The king embraced Islam at the hand of Joseph. The biographers said: He remained in the king's house for a year. When it ended, the king summoned him, crowned him, girded him with his sword, ordered a throne of gold for him, and spread over it a canopy of brocade. He sat on the throne like the moon. Kings submitted to him. The king kept to his own house and entrusted his affairs to Joseph, removed Qitfir from what he had held, and put Joseph in his place. Then Qitfir died during those nights, and the king married Joseph to Qitfir's wife. When he entered upon her, he said: "Is this not better than what you were seeking?" She said: "O truthful one, do not blame me, for I was a beautiful woman in dominion and in worldly comfort, and my husband did not come to women, so my soul overcame me." When Joseph consummated the marriage with her, he found her to be a virgin. She bore him two sons, Ephraim and Manasseh, and his rule over Egypt was firmly established.

The second opinion: that he made him king after a year and a half. This was related by Muqatil from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The third: that he handed over the matter to him at once. This was said by Wahb and Ibn al-Sa'ib.

If it is objected: How did Joseph say, ﴿Indeed, I am a knowing guardian﴾ without saying, "if God wills"? There are three answers regarding this:

One: that leaving out the exception incurred a penalty, in that his appointment was delayed, as we have mentioned from the Prophet (ﷺ).

The second: that he implicitly intended the exception, just as they implicitly intended it in their saying: ﴿and we will bring provisions for our family﴾.

The third: that he meant that his guarding and knowledge exceed the guarding and knowledge of others, so this did not require an exception, since there was no doubt about it. Ibn al-Anbari mentioned these answers.

If it is objected: How did he praise himself with this statement, when it is the habit of prophets and the righteous to be humble?

[p. 245] The answer: Since his praise of himself was free from oppression and arrogance, and his purpose in it was to attain a truth he could establish, a justice he could revive, and an injustice he could nullify, this was beautiful and permissible. Our Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I am the most honored of the children of Adam before his Lord." ʿAli ibn Abi Talib (peace be upon him) said: "By God, there is no verse except that I know whether it was revealed at night or by day." Ibn Masʿud said: "If I knew of anyone more knowledgeable in the Book of God than I, whom camels could reach, I would go to him." These statements were made out of gratitude to God and to inform the one who benefits of what is with the one who gives benefit. Muhammad ibn al-Qasim mentioned this. The judge Abu Yaʿla said: The story of Joseph is evidence that it is permissible for a person to describe himself as virtuous before someone who does not know him, and that it is not among what is prohibited in His saying: ﴿So do not attribute purity to yourselves﴾ [al-Najm 53:32].

His saying, Most High: ﴿Thus did We establish Joseph in the land﴾. In the speech there is an omitted element; its implied sense is: "Appoint me over the treasuries of the land," and he said, "I have done so," and that was omitted because His saying ﴿Thus did We establish Joseph﴾ indicates it. The meaning is: In the same way as the favor We bestowed upon him in averting the harm from him, delivering him from prison, and bringing him close to the king's heart, We enabled him to do what he willed in the land of Egypt, ﴿to settle therein wherever he pleased﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: He would dwell wherever he wished. Ibn Kathir and al-Mufaddal recited ﴿wherever We please﴾ with *nūn*.

His saying, Most High: ﴿We bestow Our mercy upon whom We will﴾, that is, We single out with Our blessing of prophethood and deliverance whom We will, ﴿and We do not waste the reward of the good-doers﴾, meaning the believers. It is said that Joseph sold the people of Egypt food in exchange for their wealth, their jewelry, their livestock, their property, and their slaves; then for their children; then for their freedom. Then he said to the king: "How do you see the work of my Lord?" The king said: "We are only your followers." He said: [p. 246] "I call God and you to witness that I have freed the people of Egypt and returned their possessions to them." During those days Joseph would not eat his fill, and he would say: "I fear that I may forget the hungry."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 12, verse 57:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the reward of the Hereafter is better﴾. The meaning: what We give Yusuf in the Hereafter is better than what We gave him in this world, and likewise for others among the believers who have followed his path in patience.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 12, verse 58:

His saying, Most High: ﴿And the brothers of Joseph came﴾. Al-Dahhak narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: When the king entrusted Joseph with the affairs of Egypt, Joseph treated the people gently, and he continued calling them to Islam, so they believed in him and loved him. When the famine afflicted the people, it reached the land of Canaan, so Jacob sent his sons to obtain provisions (al-mirah). The matter of Joseph spread throughout the horizons, and his justice, mercy and compassion became widely known. Jacob said: "O my sons, it has reached me that in Egypt there is a righteous king. So go to him, convey my greetings to him, and introduce your lineage to him, perhaps he will recognize you." So they set out and entered upon him, and he recognized them while they did not recognize him. He said: "From where have you come?" They said: "From the land of Canaan, and we have an old man called Jacob, and he sends you his greetings." Then he wept, pressed his eyes, and said: "Perhaps you are spies who have come to look for the weakness of my land." They said: "No, by Allah, but we are from Canaan. Hardship has afflicted us, and our father ordered us to come to you, for good reports about you have reached him." He said: "How many are you?" They said: "Eleven brothers, and we were twelve, but the wolf devoured one of us." He said: "Who will know your truthfulness? Bring me your brother who is from your father."

Abu Salih narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas who said: When they entered upon him, they spoke to him in Hebrew (al-ʿIbraniyyah), so he commanded the interpreter (al-turjuman) to speak to them in order to confuse them. He said to the interpreter: "Tell them: You are spies, sent by your king to look at the people of Egypt so that you may report to him, and he will bring troops against us." They said: "No, (p-247) but we are a people who have an old father, and we were twelve. One of us perished among the sheep, and we have left behind with our father a brother from his mother." He said: "If you are truthful, then leave with me one of you as a pledge, and bring me your brother." So he detained Shamʿun with him.

They differed regarding how Joseph recognized them, on two views:

One: that he recognized them by their appearance, said by Ibn ʿAbbas. The second: that he did not recognize them until they made themselves known to him, said by al-Hasan.

His saying, Most High: ﴿while they did not recognize him﴾. Muqatil said: they did not know him.

Regarding the cause of their not recognizing him, there are two views:

One: that they came to him presuming that he was an unbelieving king, so they did not consider in him what would remove their doubt.

The second: that they observed in his dress and adornment what was the cause of their non-recognition. Abu Salih narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that he was wearing silk garments and had a golden collar around his neck.

If it is said: How could one be hidden who has been given half of beauty, and how could he be mistaken for another?

The answer: they had parted from him as a child and saw him as a grown man, and conditions change, and they did not imagine that he would attain this rank. Ibn Qutaybah said: The meaning of his being given half of beauty is that Allah set for beauty a limit and a measure and granted it to whomever He willed of His creation, whether to the angels or to the houris. So Joseph was given half of that beauty, as though he had a beauty close to those beautiful faces. It is not as people claim, that he was given this beauty and all people were given half of beauty.

"And when he had furnished them with their provisions," (﴿وَلَمّا جَهَّزَهم بِجَهازِهِمْ﴾). It is said: "jahhaztu al-qawm tajhizan" means: when I prepared for them what would set them right (their needs). Jihaz al-bayt means its goods/household equipment. The exegetes said: he gave each man of them a camel load. And he said: ﴿Do you not see that I give full measure, and I am the best of hosts?﴾ That is, I complete the measure and do not diminish it, and ﴿I am the best of those who host﴾ means: the best of hosts. That is because he treated them with excellent hospitality.

Then he threatened them for failing to bring their brother, saying: ﴿So if you do not bring him to me, there will be no measure for you with me.﴾ On this there are two views:

The first: he meant this for the future, and this is the view of the majority.

The second: he denied them measure at that time; this was said by Wahb ibn Munabbih.

"And when he had furnished them with their provisions," (﴿وَلَمّا جَهَّزَهم بِجَهازِهِمْ﴾). It is said: "jahhaztu al-qawm tajhizan" means: when I prepared for them what would set them right (their needs). Jihaz al-bayt means its goods/household equipment. The exegetes said: he gave each man of them a camel load. And he said: ﴿Do you not see that I give full measure, and I am the best of hosts?﴾ That is, I complete the measure and do not diminish it, and ﴿I am the best of those who host﴾ means: the best of hosts. That is because he treated them with excellent hospitality.

Then he threatened them for failing to bring their brother, saying: ﴿So if you do not bring him to me, there will be no measure for you with me.﴾ On this there are two views:

The first: he meant this for the future, and this is the view of the majority.

The second: he denied them measure at that time; this was said by Wahb ibn Munabbih.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They said, "We will seek to win him over from his father"﴾, meaning we will request him from him. *Al-murawadah* (persistent seeking to win over) means exerting oneself in the request.

Regarding His saying: ﴿And indeed we will surely do it﴾, there are three opinions:

The first: the meaning is, "We will indeed bring him to you, and we guarantee to you his coming with him." This is the view of al-Kalbi.

The second: that it is an emphasis (*tawkid*), as said by al-Zajjaj. On this basis, the act they pledged refers back to the seeking, so the sense of emphasis holds.

The third: "And we will persistently demand him from our father, and continually press counsel upon him in directing him to it." This is other than the seeking, and was mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari.

If it is said: How was it permissible for Yusuf to request his brother, when he knew what that entailed of bringing grief upon his father? On this there are five answers:

The first: it is possible that this was by a command from God, the Exalted, as an increase in Ya'qub's trial so that his reward would be greater. This is the most apparent.

(p-249) The second: he requested him not in order to detain him. Then, when he recognized him, he said, "I will not part from you, O Yusuf." He said, "I cannot keep you except by attributing to you a grave matter." He said, "Do what you see fit." This was said by Ka'b.

The third: that he intended by this to alert Ya'qub to Yusuf's condition.

The fourth: so that Ya'qub's joy at the return of his two sons would be doubled.

The fifth: to hasten his brother's joy at being reunited with him before the (other) brothers. All these answers are flawed except the first, for it is the correct one. What indicates this is what we have related from Wahb ibn Munabbih, who said: When God gathered Yusuf and Ya'qub, He said to him, "Between me and you is this near distance, and you did not write to inform me?!" He said, "Jibril commanded me not to inform you." He said to him, "Ask Jibril." He asked him, and he said, "God commanded me with that." He said, "Ask your Lord." He asked Him, and He said, "Say to Ya'qub: you feared the wolf for him, and you did not entrust Me?"

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 12, verse 62:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And he said to his servants﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, and Abu Bakr on the authority of 'Asim read: "li-fityatihi" (to his young men). Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs on the authority of 'Asim read: "li-fityanihi" (to his young men). Abu 'Ali said: al-fityah is the plural of fata in small number, and al-fityan is for large number. The meaning is: he said to his attendants: ﴿Put their merchandise﴾, which is what they paid for the food with, ﴿into their saddlebags﴾. Al-rahl is everything that is prepared for travel. ﴿So that they may recognize it﴾, i.e., that they may recognize it, ﴿when they return﴾, i.e., go back, ﴿to their family, so that they may come back﴾, i.e., in order that they may return.

Regarding his purpose in doing this, there are five opinions:

The first: he feared that his father would not have enough silver to send them back a second time, so he placed their dirhams in their saddlebags. This was said by Abu Salih on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: he meant that when they recognized it, they would not consider it lawful to keep it until they returned it. This was said by al-Dahhak.

The third: he found it reprehensible to take the price from his father and brothers while they were in need of it, so he returned it to them without their knowing the reason for its return, out of generosity and benevolence. This was mentioned by Ibn Jarir al-Tabari and Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi.

The fourth: so that they would know that his request for their return was not out of greed for their wealth. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi.

The fifth: that he showed them his generosity and kindness so that it would be more inviting for them to return.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 12, verse 63–64:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So when they returned to their father﴾. The exegetes said: When they went back to Ya'qub, they said: "O our father, we came before the best of men, who hosted us and honoured us with great honour. Had he been a man from the descendants of Ya'qub, he would not have honoured us as he did."

Regarding His saying: ﴿The measure has been withheld from us﴾, there are two opinions, which have already been mentioned in His saying: ﴿So there will be no measure for you with me﴾ [Yusuf: 61].

If we say that he did not give them a measure, then the wording "withheld" (muni'a) is clear.

If we say that he warned them of the withholding of the measure, then in meaning there are two opinions:

One: It was decreed against us that the measure be withheld after this time, just as you say to a man: "By God, you have entered the Fire because of what you did."

The second: The meaning is: "O our father, the measure will be withheld from us if you do not send him with us," so "muni'a" (was withheld) stands in place of "yumna'" (will be withheld), like His saying: ﴿He thinks that his wealth will make him immortal﴾ [al-Humazah: 3], meaning: will make him immortal, and His saying: ﴿And the companions of the Fire will call out﴾ [al-A'raf: 50], and ﴿And when God says: "O Jesus"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 116], meaning: "and when He says." Ibn al-Anbari mentioned these two.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So send with us our brother, and we will obtain a measure﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir read "nakhtal" (we will obtain) with the letter nun. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "yaktal" (he will obtain) with the letter ya'. The meaning: if you send him with us, we will obtain a measure; otherwise we have been denied the measure.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Shall I trust you with him?﴾ meaning: I will not trust you except as I trusted you with Yusuf, intending that this trust did not benefit him, since they betrayed him. ﴿But God is the best guardian﴾: Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read "hifzan" (as guardian). The meaning: the best in guarding than your guarding. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs from 'Asim read "khayrun hafizan" with an alif. Abu 'Ali said: its accusative is as a specification (tamyiz), not as a circumstantial state (hal).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 12, verse 63–64:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So when they returned to their father﴾. The exegetes said: When they went back to Ya'qub, they said: "O our father, we came before the best of men, who hosted us and honoured us with great honour. Had he been a man from the descendants of Ya'qub, he would not have honoured us as he did."

Regarding His saying: ﴿The measure has been withheld from us﴾, there are two opinions, which have already been mentioned in His saying: ﴿So there will be no measure for you with me﴾ [Yusuf: 61].

If we say that he did not give them a measure, then the wording "withheld" (muni'a) is clear.

If we say that he warned them of the withholding of the measure, then in meaning there are two opinions:

One: It was decreed against us that the measure be withheld after this time, just as you say to a man: "By God, you have entered the Fire because of what you did."

The second: The meaning is: "O our father, the measure will be withheld from us if you do not send him with us," so "muni'a" (was withheld) stands in place of "yumna'" (will be withheld), like His saying: ﴿He thinks that his wealth will make him immortal﴾ [al-Humazah: 3], meaning: will make him immortal, and His saying: ﴿And the companions of the Fire will call out﴾ [al-A'raf: 50], and ﴿And when God says: "O Jesus"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 116], meaning: "and when He says." Ibn al-Anbari mentioned these two.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So send with us our brother, and we will obtain a measure﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir read "nakhtal" (we will obtain) with the letter nun. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "yaktal" (he will obtain) with the letter ya'. The meaning: if you send him with us, we will obtain a measure; otherwise we have been denied the measure.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Shall I trust you with him?﴾ meaning: I will not trust you except as I trusted you with Yusuf, intending that this trust did not benefit him, since they betrayed him. ﴿But God is the best guardian﴾: Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read "hifzan" (as guardian). The meaning: the best in guarding than your guarding. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs from 'Asim read "khayrun hafizan" with an alif. Abu 'Ali said: its accusative is as a specification (tamyiz), not as a circumstantial state (hal).

**The verse: ﴿When they emptied their goods﴾**, meaning the containers of food, **﴿they found their merchandise﴾**, which they had brought as payment for the food, **returned to them** (*ruddat*). Al-Zajjaj said: The original form is *ruddidat*, so the first *dal* was assimilated into the second and the *ra'* remained with a *damma*. Whoever reads it with a *kasra* on the *ra'* has transferred the *kasra* from the *dal* onto it, as is done in *qīla* and *bī'a*, to show that the original vowel of the *dal* is a *kasra*.

**﴿What do we seek?﴾** There are two views concerning *mā* (in *mā nabghī*):

First: it is interrogative. The meaning is: what more do we want, since our merchandise has been returned to us?

Second: it is negative. The meaning is: we seek nothing, that is, we are not asking you for dirhams to take back there with us; this (what we have) is enough for us to return with. By this they intended to comfort his heart so that he would permit them to go back. Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Ya'mur, al-Jahdari and Abu Haywa read *mā tabghī* with the *ta'* (second person), addressing Ya'qub.

**﴿And we will bring provisions for our family﴾**, that is, we will bring food for them. Ibn Qutayba said: it is said *māra ahlahu yamīruhum mayran*, and he is *mā'ir* for his family when he brings them their provisions from another land.

**﴿And we will protect our brother﴾** has two views:

First: we will protect our brother Benjamin, whom you send with us. This is the view of most scholars.

Second: we will protect our brother Shim'un, whom he had taken as a hostage with him. This was reported by al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas.

**﴿And we will receive an additional camel-load﴾**, that is, a load (*wiqr*) of one camel. They meant by this their brother's share, because Yusuf would not give one person more than a camel's load.

**﴿That is an easy measure﴾** has three views:

First: that is a quick measure, with no delay. They meant: if he comes with us, the king will quickly measure out for us. This is the view of Muqatil.

Second: that is an easy measure for the one to whom we are going. This is the view of al-Zajjaj.

Third: that which we have brought you is a small measure that will not satisfy us. This is the view of al-Mawardi.

**﴿Until you give me a solemn pledge from God﴾**, that is, you give me a covenant I can rely on. The meaning is: until you swear to me by God **﴿that you will surely bring him to me﴾**, that is, that you will certainly return him to me. Ibn al-Anbari said: this *lam* is the answer to an implied clause, whose summary is: "and say: by God, you will surely bring him to me."

**﴿Unless you are surrounded﴾** has two views:

First: that all of you perish. This is the view of Mujahid.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 12, verse 69:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿When they entered upon Joseph﴾, meaning his brothers, ﴿he drew his brother to himself﴾, meaning Benjamin, who was his full brother, from the same father and mother. This was said by Qatadah. He embraced him and made him stay with him. Ibn Qutaybah said: It is said "āwaytu fulānan ilayya" with the alif lengthened (ā-wa-ytu) when you draw someone to yourself, and "awaytu ilā banī fulān" with the alif shortened (aw-ay-tu, i.e., awaytu) when you take refuge with them.

As for His saying, ﴿He said: Indeed I am your brother﴾, there are two views:

The first: when they entered upon him, he detained them at the door and brought in his brother. He said to him: "What is your name?" He said: "Benjamin." He said: "What is your mother's name?" He said: "Rahil, daughter of Lawi." Then he leapt up to him and embraced him and said: ﴿Indeed I am your brother﴾. This was said by Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas. Likewise Ibn Ishaq said: he informed him that he was Joseph.

The second: he did not disclose this to him; rather he said, "I am your brother" in place of your brother who has perished. This was said by Wahb ibn Munabbih. It is also said that he seated them two by two at a table, and Benjamin was left alone weeping and said: "If my brother were alive, he would have seated me with him." So Joseph drew him to himself and said: "I see this one alone," and he seated him with himself at his table. When night came, each two lay down to sleep together, and Benjamin was left alone, so Joseph said: "This one will sleep with me." When he was alone with him, (p-256) he said: "Do you have a brother from your mother?" He said: "I had a brother from my mother, and he perished." He said: "Would you like me to be your brother in place of your perished brother?" He said: "O King, who would find a brother like you? But Jacob and Rahil did not bear you." Then Joseph wept, rose to him, embraced him, and said: ﴿Indeed I am your brother, Joseph﴾ ﴿so do not be distressed﴾. Qatadah said: do not grieve and do not sorrow. Al-Zajjaj said: do not grieve and do not be dejected. Ibn al-Anbari said: "tabta'is" is of the form "tafta'il", from al-bu's, which is harm and hardship; that is, let no hardship befall you because of what they did.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿because of what they used to do﴾, there are three views:

The first: they used to reproach Joseph and his brother for their grandfather's (their mother's father's) worship of idols. So he said: do not be distressed by what they do of reproach toward us. This meaning was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas.

The second: do not grieve over what they will do after this time when they steal you, so "kanu" here means "yakunu" (will be). The poet said:

"I overtook those who were before me, and I left for those after me no monument of poems."

Another said:

"Sprinkle the sides of his grave with their blood, for he will surely be a brother of blood and sacrifices."

He meant: "fa-qad kana" (indeed he was). This is the view of Muqatil.

The third: do not grieve over what they did of envy toward us and their eagerness to turn our father's face away from us. Ibn Ishaq adopted this meaning.

(p-257) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So when he had furnished them with their provisions﴾. The exegetes said: He gave them full measure, and he loaded for Binyamin a camel in his name just as he had loaded for them, and he placed the drinking-vessel (al-siqaya) in his brother's saddlebag. It is the suwwa', and these are two names applying to one thing, like al-burr and al-hintah (wheat), and al-maa'ida and al-khuwan (the table). Some of them said: The real name is al-suwwa', and al-siqaya is a descriptive term, as one says kuwz (cup) and inaa' (vessel), while the specific name is al-kuwz. The exegetes said: Yusuf made that sa' a measure so that it would not be used to measure anything else. It was also said: He measured out to his brothers with it, as an honour to them. They said: When the brothers of Yusuf set off and got far away, he sent a pursuit after them, and they were overtaken and detained. ﴿Then a crier called out﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: a announcer announced; one says "adhantuhu bi-l-shay'", so he is "mu'dhan bihi", meaning I informed him; and "adhdhantu" means I greatly increased the informing about the thing, meaning that it was one announcement after another. ﴿O caravan!﴾ He means the people of the caravan, and used the feminine because he attributed it to the caravan. Al-Farra' said: "'ir" is only said of the owners of camels. Abu 'Ubayda said: al-'ir are the camels carrying loads, the ridden ones. Ibn Qutayba said: al-'ir are the people with the camels.

If it is asked: How was it permissible for Yusuf to accuse those who had not stolen? There are four answers concerning this:

The first: the meaning is, "Indeed you are thieves of Yusuf, when you cut him off from his father and cast him into the well." This was said by al-Zajjaj.

(p-258) The second: the crier called out while not knowing that Yusuf had ordered the drinking-vessel to be placed in his brother's saddlebag, so he was not lying in his statement. This was said by Ibn Jarir.

The third: the crier called out the accusation of theft against them without Yusuf's order.

The fourth: the meaning is, "Indeed you are thieves" according to what appears to one who does not know the reality of your affairs, like His saying: ﴿Taste it, indeed you are the mighty, the noble﴾ [al-Dukhan: 49], meaning in your own estimation, not in ours; and like the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Abraham lied three lies," meaning he said a statement that resembled a lie but was not one.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They said﴾, meaning the brothers of Yusuf, ﴿and they turned towards them﴾. In this there are two views:

One: towards the announcer and his companions. The second: the crier and those with him turned towards the brothers of Yusuf with the claim. ﴿What is it that you miss?﴾ What is it that has gone missing from you? ﴿They said: We miss the king's drinking-vessel (suwwa').﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: al-suwwa' is precisely the sa', and it is masculine and feminine, and likewise al-sa' is masculine and feminine. It has been read as "suyaa'" with a yaa', and read as "sawgh" with a dotted ghayn, and read as "sawa'" with an undotted 'ayn with the sad either fathah or dammah, and Abu Hurayra read "sa'a al-malik". All these are dialects returning to one meaning, except that al-sawgh with the dotted ghayn is a verbal noun of saghtu, and the vessel was described by it, because it was wrought (masuugh) of gold.

They differed about its material in five views:

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 12, verse 73–75:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They said, "By Allah!"﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: "Ta'allah" (تاللَّهِ) means "wallahi" (by Allah), except that the particle "ta" (التاء) is not used for oaths except with Allah, exalted and majestic is He. It is not permissible to say "Tarrahman la-af'alanna" (by the Merciful, I will certainly do it), nor "Tarabbi la-af'alanna" (by my Lord, I will certainly do it). The letter "ta" is substituted for the letter "waw," as they said in "wurath" (inheritance): "turath," and they said "yattazin" (he weighs), and its origin is "yawtazin," from "al-wazn" (weighing)." Ibn al-Anbari said: "The "ta" was substituted for the "waw," as it was substituted in "al-tukhama" (indigestion), "al-turath" (inheritance) and "al-tujah" (rank), and their origins are from "al-wakhama," "al-wurath," and "al-wijah," because they derive from "al-wikhama" (heaviness), "al-wiratha" (inheritance) and "al-wajh" (face)." The Arabs do not say "Tarrahman" as they said "Tallah," because the usage in swearing was frequent with Allah and was not with "al-Rahman," so the "ta" came as a substitute for the "waw" in the position where its usage is frequent.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed you know﴾, meaning Joseph, ﴿that we did not come to cause corruption in the land﴾, i.e., to wrong anyone or to steal.

If it is asked: How did they swear upon the knowledge of a people who did not know them?

The answer is in three aspects:

The first: They said that because they had returned the dirhams and had not made them lawful for themselves. The meaning is: "You certainly know that we returned to you your dirhams, which were more than the price of the sa', so how would we make your sa' lawful?" This was narrated by al-Dahhak from Ibn Abbas, and Muqatil said likewise.

The second: When they entered Egypt, they muzzled the mouths of their camels and donkeys so that they would not eat anything, and others did not do that. This was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas.

The third: The people of Egypt had known them to be people who do not wrong anyone.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then what is its penalty﴾. The meaning: the caller and his companions said: "Then what is its penalty?" Al-Akhfash said: If you wish, you may return the pronoun to the thief (al-sarigh), and if you wish, you may return it to the theft (al-sariq).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If you are liars﴾, i.e., in your statement, ﴿and we were not thieves﴾. ﴿They said﴾, meaning the brothers of Joseph: ﴿Its penalty is that the one in whose bag it is found, he himself is its penalty﴾, i.e., he shall be enslaved for that. Ibn Abbas said: This was the custom of the family of Jacob.

(p-261) The Qur'anic verse: ﴿So he began with their bags﴾. The exegetes said: The caller turned with them to Yusuf and said, "There is no way but to search your belongings." ﴿So he began﴾ Yusuf ﴿with their bags, before the bag of his brother﴾, to remove the accusation. When he reached his brother's bag, he said, "I do not think he has taken anything." They said, "By Allah, we will not leave until you search his baggage, for that is better for your own heart." When they opened his belongings, they found the drinking-vessel. This is His saying: ﴿Then he brought it out﴾.

There are three opinions regarding the pronoun of the particle ها (hā', the pronominal suffix in ﴿استخرجها﴾):

The first: it refers to the theft (al-sariqa). This was said by al-Farra'.
The second: it refers to the water-vessel (al-siqaya). This was said by al-Zajjaj.
The third: it refers to the cup (al-ṣuwā') according to the dialect of those who treat it as feminine. Ibn al-Anbari mentioned this.

The exegetes said: They turned to Binyamin and said, "What have you done? You have disgraced us and brought shame upon your father, the truthful one." He said, "The one who put this in my baggage is the one who put the silver coins in your baggage." Yusuf had told his brother what he intended to do with him.

His saying: ﴿Thus did We plan for Yusuf﴾. Regarding this there are four opinions:

The first: "Thus did We act for him." This was said by al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: "We devised for him," and kayd (plotting) means a stratagem. This was said by Ibn Qutayba.

The third: "We willed for Yusuf," which Ibn al-Qasim mentioned.

The fourth: "We arranged for him by inspiring him to do what he did to his brother, so that he could reach his detention." Ibn al-Anbari said: When Allah arranged for Yusuf what He arranged of raising his rank and perfecting his blessing, contrary to what his brothers supposed, this was likened to the scheming of created beings, because they conceal what they plot from the one they plot against.

His saying: ﴿He could not have taken his brother under the king's law﴾. Regarding the meaning of "law" (dīn) here there are two opinions:

The first: it means the authority (sultān), so the meaning is "within the king's authority." This was narrated by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: it means the judgment (qaḍā'), so the meaning is "within the king's judgment," because the king's judgment was that whoever steals is only beaten and made to pay a fine. This was said by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas. Its explanation: if he had subjected his brother to the king's ruling, he would not have been able to detain him, since the king's ruling was only fining and beating. So Allah caused his brothers to say that the penalty for the thief is enslavement. This was among the things by which Allah planned for Yusuf, out of kindness, until He granted him his aim by the will of Allah. That is the meaning of His saying: ﴿except that Allah wills﴾. It was also said: "except that Allah wills the manifestation of a cause by which he would be entitled to take his brother."

(p-262) His saying: ﴿We raise in degrees whom We will﴾. Ya'qub read ﴿yarfa'u darajāti man yashā'u﴾ with the letter yā' in both places. The people of Kufa read ﴿darajātin﴾ with tanwin (nunation). The meaning is: We raise degrees through various kinds of gifts, types of honour, doors of knowledge, the subduing of desire, and the granting of success in guidance, just as We raised Yusuf. ﴿And above every possessor of knowledge is one who knows﴾, meaning: above every possessor of knowledge whom Allah has raised through knowledge there is one who knows more than he does, until knowledge ends with Allah the Exalted, and perfection in knowledge is absent from anyone else.

Regarding the intended meaning of this statement there are three opinions:

The first: the meaning is "Yusuf knows more than his brothers, and above him is one who knows more than he does."

The second: it draws attention to the greatness of knowledge and shows that it is too vast to be encompassed.

The third: it is a lesson for the scholar to be humble, lest he become self-admiring.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 12, verses 77–79:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They said﴾ meaning: the brothers of Yusuf. ﴿If he steals﴾ they mean Binyamin. ﴿Then a brother of his stole before﴾ they mean Yusuf. The exegetes (al-mufassirun) said: Yusuf was made to bear three trials. He said to the cupbearer: ﴿Mention me to your lord﴾, so he remained in prison for several years. He said to the Aziz: ﴿That he may know that I did not betray him in his absence﴾. Jibril said to him: "Nor when you desired [her]?" He said: ﴿And I do not acquit myself﴾. And he said to his brothers: ﴿Indeed, you are thieves﴾. So they said: ﴿If he steals, then a brother of his stole before﴾.

Concerning what they meant by this theft, there are seven opinions:

The first: that he used to take food from his father's table during the years of famine and give it to the poor. This was narrated by Ata' from Ibn Abbas.

The second: that he stole a kohl-pot belonging to his maternal aunt. This was narrated by Abu Malik from Ibn Abbas.

The third: that he stole an idol belonging to his maternal grandfather, broke it and threw it on the road, and his brothers reproached him for this. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Wahb ibn Munabbih and Qatadah.

The fourth: that the aunt of Yusuf, who was the eldest child of Ishaq, used to nurse Yusuf and loved him intensely. When he grew up, Ya'qub asked for him, and she said: "I cannot bear that he be absent from me." He said: "By Allah, I will not leave him with you." So she took Ishaq's belt and tied it around Yusuf under his garments. Then she said: "I have lost Ishaq's belt; look for whoever took it." They found it with Yusuf. She informed Ya'qub of this and said: "By Allah, he is mine; I may do with him as I wish." He said: "You and that." Ya'qub could not act against her until she died. This is what his brothers reproached him with. This was narrated by Ibn Abi Najih from Mujahid.

The fifth: that a beggar came to him one day, and he stole something and gave it to the beggar, so they reproached him for that. Regarding that thing there are three opinions: the first, that it was an egg, said by Mujahid; the second, that it was a sheep, said by Ka'b; the third, that it was a hen, said by Sufyan ibn Uyaynah.

The sixth: that the sons of Ya'qub were at a meal, and Yusuf looked at a bone, and hid it, so they reproached him for that. This was said by Atiyyah al-Awfi and Idris al-Awdi. Ibn al-Anbari said: "None of these actions amounts to theft in itself, but they resemble theft, so his brothers reproached him for them in anger."

The seventh: that they lied about him in what they attributed to him. This was said by al-Hasan. Abu Razin and Ibn Abi Ablah recited: ﴿fa-qad saraqa﴾ with a damma on the sin and a kasra on the ra' and with shaddah.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So Yusuf kept it within himself﴾. Regarding the pronoun of reference in "ha' al-kinayah" (the pronoun) there are three opinions:

The first: that it refers to the statement mentioned after this, which is His saying: ﴿You are worse in position﴾. This meaning was narrated by al-Awfi from Ibn Abbas.

The second: that it refers to the statement they had made about him, which is their saying: ﴿a brother of his stole before﴾. This is the meaning of the saying of Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas. According to this, the meaning is: he concealed his answer to the statement, so he did not respond to them concerning it.

The third: that it refers to the argument, the meaning being: he concealed the argument against them in their accusation of theft against him. This was mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿You are worse in position﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions:

One: worse in conduct than Yusuf, because of your wronging of your brother and your disobedience to your father. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: worse in standing with Allah. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And Allah is most knowing of what you describe﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions:

One: what you say. This was said by Mujahid. The second: what you lie about. This was said by Qatadah. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: "And Allah knows best whether a brother of his stole or not."

Some of the exegetes mentioned that when he (Yusuf) brought out the drinking cup from the baggage of his brother, he struck the cup, then brought it near to his ear and said: "This cup of mine tells me that you were twelve men, and that you took away a brother of yours and sold him." Binyamin said: "O King, ask your cup about my brother: is he alive?" So he struck it and said: (p-265) "He is alive, and you will see him." He said: "Ask your cup: who put it in my baggage?" So he struck it and said: "This cup of mine is angry, and it says: 'How do you ask me about my companion when you have seen with whom I was?'" Then Rubil became angry, and when the sons of Ya'qub became angry, no one could withstand them; but when one of them touched another, his anger would subside. He said: "By Allah, O King, you must release us, or I will cry out a cry such that no pregnant woman in Egypt will remain who does not miscarry what is in her womb." Yusuf said to his son: "Stand beside Rubil and touch him." The boy did so, and his anger subsided. Rubil said: "What is this?! Is there in this land any of the offspring of Ya'qub?" Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 12, verses 77–79:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They said﴾ meaning: the brothers of Yusuf. ﴿If he steals﴾ they mean Binyamin. ﴿Then a brother of his stole before﴾ they mean Yusuf. The exegetes (al-mufassirun) said: Yusuf was made to bear three trials. He said to the cupbearer: ﴿Mention me to your lord﴾, so he remained in prison for several years. He said to the Aziz: ﴿That he may know that I did not betray him in his absence﴾. Jibril said to him: "Nor when you desired [her]?" He said: ﴿And I do not acquit myself﴾. And he said to his brothers: ﴿Indeed, you are thieves﴾. So they said: ﴿If he steals, then a brother of his stole before﴾.

Concerning what they meant by this theft, there are seven opinions:

The first: that he used to take food from his father's table during the years of famine and give it to the poor. This was narrated by Ata' from Ibn Abbas.

The second: that he stole a kohl-pot belonging to his maternal aunt. This was narrated by Abu Malik from Ibn Abbas.

The third: that he stole an idol belonging to his maternal grandfather, broke it and threw it on the road, and his brothers reproached him for this. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Wahb ibn Munabbih and Qatadah.

The fourth: that the aunt of Yusuf, who was the eldest child of Ishaq, used to nurse Yusuf and loved him intensely. When he grew up, Ya'qub asked for him, and she said: "I cannot bear that he be absent from me." He said: "By Allah, I will not leave him with you." So she took Ishaq's belt and tied it around Yusuf under his garments. Then she said: "I have lost Ishaq's belt; look for whoever took it." They found it with Yusuf. She informed Ya'qub of this and said: "By Allah, he is mine; I may do with him as I wish." He said: "You and that." Ya'qub could not act against her until she died. This is what his brothers reproached him with. This was narrated by Ibn Abi Najih from Mujahid.

The fifth: that a beggar came to him one day, and he stole something and gave it to the beggar, so they reproached him for that. Regarding that thing there are three opinions: the first, that it was an egg, said by Mujahid; the second, that it was a sheep, said by Ka'b; the third, that it was a hen, said by Sufyan ibn Uyaynah.

The sixth: that the sons of Ya'qub were at a meal, and Yusuf looked at a bone, and hid it, so they reproached him for that. This was said by Atiyyah al-Awfi and Idris al-Awdi. Ibn al-Anbari said: "None of these actions amounts to theft in itself, but they resemble theft, so his brothers reproached him for them in anger."

The seventh: that they lied about him in what they attributed to him. This was said by al-Hasan. Abu Razin and Ibn Abi Ablah recited: ﴿fa-qad saraqa﴾ with a damma on the sin and a kasra on the ra' and with shaddah.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So Yusuf kept it within himself﴾. Regarding the pronoun of reference in "ha' al-kinayah" (the pronoun) there are three opinions:

The first: that it refers to the statement mentioned after this, which is His saying: ﴿You are worse in position﴾. This meaning was narrated by al-Awfi from Ibn Abbas.

The second: that it refers to the statement they had made about him, which is their saying: ﴿a brother of his stole before﴾. This is the meaning of the saying of Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas. According to this, the meaning is: he concealed his answer to the statement, so he did not respond to them concerning it.

The third: that it refers to the argument, the meaning being: he concealed the argument against them in their accusation of theft against him. This was mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿You are worse in position﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions:

One: worse in conduct than Yusuf, because of your wronging of your brother and your disobedience to your father. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: worse in standing with Allah. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And Allah is most knowing of what you describe﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions:

One: what you say. This was said by Mujahid. The second: what you lie about. This was said by Qatadah. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: "And Allah knows best whether a brother of his stole or not."

Some of the exegetes mentioned that when he (Yusuf) brought out the drinking cup from the baggage of his brother, he struck the cup, then brought it near to his ear and said: "This cup of mine tells me that you were twelve men, and that you took away a brother of yours and sold him." Binyamin said: "O King, ask your cup about my brother: is he alive?" So he struck it and said: (p-265) "He is alive, and you will see him." He said: "Ask your cup: who put it in my baggage?" So he struck it and said: "This cup of mine is angry, and it says: 'How do you ask me about my companion when you have seen with whom I was?'" Then Rubil became angry, and when the sons of Ya'qub became angry, no one could withstand them; but when one of them touched another, his anger would subside. He said: "By Allah, O King, you must release us, or I will cry out a cry such that no pregnant woman in Egypt will remain who does not miscarry what is in her womb." Yusuf said: "And who is Ya'qub?" He said: "O King, do not mention Ya'qub, for he is Israel, the son of the Sacrificed One of Allah, the son of the Friend of Allah." When they found no way to free their brother, they asked him to take one of them in his place. Concerning this there are two opinions: one, regarding what has passed; the second, if you do it.

﴿He said: "I seek refuge in Allah"﴾. Its explanation has already preceded (Yusuf 33). The meaning is: "I seek refuge in Allah that we should take one innocent in place of one guilty."

There are two views regarding the pronoun in "minhu" (from him):

The first is that it refers to Joseph. The meaning is that they despaired of Joseph releasing their brother.

The second is that it refers to their brother. The meaning is that they despaired of their brother.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿they withdrew, conferring privately (najiyyan)﴾, meaning they withdrew from the people, with no one else among them, conferring together, consulting and deliberating. It is said: "qawmun najiyyun" (a people conferring privately), and its plural is "anjiyah." The poet said:

"When the people are conferring privately, and their necks are stirred like ropes of a well-bucket."

The reason "najiyyan" is in the singular is that it functions like a verbal noun (masdar), which is used for two persons, for a group, and for the feminine with one form.

Al-Zajjaj said: They went off privately, discussing what they would do on their way to their father, while their brother was not with them.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Their eldest said﴾. Concerning this there are two views:

The first is that he was the eldest in intellect. Regarding him there are two opinions: the first is that he was Yahudha (Judah), though he was not the eldest in age. The second is that he was the eldest in age, and he was Ruwbil. This was narrated by Qatadah and al-Suddi.

There had accompanied them a group of the Canaanites. Ibn al-Anbari said: It is also possible that the meaning is: "Ask the town and the caravan, for they will understand you, because you are a prophet, and prophets are addressed by stones and beasts." (p-269) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said, "Rather, your souls have made a matter seem fair to you."﴾ There is an abridgement in the speech, and the meaning is: they returned to their father and told him that, and he said to them this. We have explained this at the beginning of the surah [Yusuf 18].

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 12, verse 84:**

[p-270] Allah's words, ﴿And he turned away from them﴾, meaning he turned away from his sons, so that he would not prolong his speeches to them, and he was alone with his grief, and the remembrance of Joseph stirred up within him. ﴿And he said, "Alas, my grief over Joseph!"﴾ Ibn ʿAbbas said: "How long is my grief over Joseph!" Ibn Qutayba said: "al-Asaf is the most intense regret." Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: "This community has been given, at the time of calamity, what the prophets before them were not given: ﴿Indeed we belong to Allah, and indeed to Him we will return﴾ [al-Baqara 2:156]. Had the prophets been given it, Yaʿqub would have been given it, when he says: ﴿Alas, my grief over Joseph!﴾"

If it is said: "This is an expression of complaint, so where is the patience?"

The answer comes in two ways:

First: he complained to Allah, not to them. Second: he meant by it a supplication, so the meaning is: "O Lord, have mercy on my grief over Joseph."

Ibn al-Anbari reported from some of the linguists that he said: "Yaʿqub's calling out to al-Asaf (grief) in the wording is one of the figurative usages (al-majaz, a non-literal mode of expression) in which what is intended is other than what appears in the wording. Its summary is: 'O my God, have mercy on my grief,' or 'You see my grief, and this is my grief.' So he addressed the grief in the wording, while the one addressed in meaning is someone else, just as he said: ﴿O our regret!﴾, and the meaning is: 'O people, take notice of our regret.'" He said: "Sorrow and the soul's recoil from what is disliked and from affliction are not a fault or a sin, so long as the tongue does not utter a sinful word and one complains only to his Lord. Since his saying 'Alas!' was a complaint to his Lord, he was not blameworthy." It is narrated from al-Hasan that his brother died, and al-Hasan grieved intensely, and he was rebuked for that. He said: "I have not found that Allah blamed Yaʿqub for grief when he said: ﴿Alas, my grief over Joseph!﴾"

Allah's words, ﴿And his eyes turned white from grief﴾, meaning they changed to a state of whiteness. As for whether his sight went away or not, there are two opinions:

First: his sight went, said by Mujahid.

Second: his sight weakened because of a whiteness that covered it from much weeping, mentioned by al-Mawardi. Muqatil said: "He did not see with his eyes for six years."

[p-271] Ibn ʿAbbas said: Allah's words, ﴿from grief﴾, meaning "from weeping," intending that his eyes turned white because of his much weeping. Since grief was the cause of weeping, weeping was called grief. Thabit al-Bunani said: Jibril entered upon Joseph and said: "O king, noble before his Lord, do you have knowledge of Yaʿqub?" He said: "Yes." He said: "What has he done?" He said: "His eyes have turned white." He said: "How great is his grief?" He said: "The grief of seventy bereaved mothers." He said: "Does he have a reward for that?" He said: "The reward of a hundred martyrs." Al-Hasan al-Basri said: "Grief did not leave Yaʿqub for eighty years, and his eye never dried, and no one on that day was more honored by Allah than him when his sight went."

Allah's words, ﴿so he was kazim﴾. Al-kazim (suppressing one's grief) means the one who holds in his grief and does not show it, as Ibn Qutayba said. We have explained this at His words: ﴿and those who restrain their anger﴾ [Al ʿImran 3:134].

As for the nature of that merchandise, there are seven opinions:

The first: that it was dirhams. This was narrated by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas. The second: that it was worn-out goods, such as ropes and sacks; narrated by Ibn Abi Mulaykah from Ibn 'Abbas. The third: it was dried curd (aqit), said by al-Hasan. The fourth: it was sandals and hides; narrated by Juwaybir from al-Dahhak. The fifth: it was the flour of the doum palm (sawiq al-muql); also related from al-Dahhak. The sixth: it was habba al-khadra' and sanawbar (pine nuts), said by Abu Salih. The seventh: it was wool and a little ghee, said by 'Abd Allah ibn al-Harith.

As for "muzjah" (meager), there are five opinions:

That is why he said: ﴿And this is my brother﴾, though they knew him; he only intended: and this is the wronged one like my own wronging.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Allah has certainly favored us﴾. There are three opinions concerning it:

The first: with the good of this world and the Hereafter. The second: by reuniting us after separation. The third: by safety and then by honor.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, he who fears [Allah] and is patient﴾. Ibn Kathir in the narration of Qunbul read "man yattaqi wa yasbir" with a yā' in both pausal and continuous recitation; the rest read without yā' in both states.

Concerning the meaning of the statement there are four opinions:

The first: whoever refrains from fornication and endures afflictions. The second: whoever refrains from fornication and endures (p-282) celibacy. The third: whoever fears Allah and endures calamities; these opinions were narrated from Ibn 'Abbas. The fourth: he refrains from disobeying Allah and endures prison; said by Mujahid.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿then indeed Allah does not waste the reward of the doers of good﴾, i.e., the reward of one whose condition is this.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Allah has certainly preferred you over us﴾, i.e., chosen you and favored you.

In what did they mean that He favored him? There are four opinions:

The first: with kingship; said by al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas. The second: with patience; said by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas. The third: with forbearance and pardoning us; mentioned by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi. The fourth: with knowledge, intellect, beauty and all the other virtues He gave him.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And indeed, we were sinners﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: "Guilty, sinful, in regard to your affair." Ibn al-Anbari said: That is why "khati'in" was chosen over "mukhti'in," although "akhta'a" is more common on people's tongues than "khati'a yakhta'u," because the meaning of "khati'a yakhta'u," so he is "khati'," is sinful, while the meaning of "akhta'a yukhti'u," so he is "mukhti'," is that he left what is right without sinning. The poet said:

"Your servants err, and You are Lord, with the fates and the decrees in Your two hands."

He meant: they sin. He said: It is also possible that "khati'in" was chosen over "mukhti'in" for agreement with the ends of the verses, since "khati'in" is more fitting with what precedes it.

Al-Farra' mentioned two opinions regarding the meaning of "in" (and):

One: "and indeed we were sinners." The second: "and we were not but sinners."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿No blame upon you today﴾. Abu Salih narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: "I will not reproach you about this ever again." Ibn al-Anbari said: He only pointed to that day because it was the first time of pardon, and the way of one who pardons in such a case is not to revisit punishment. Tha'lab said: "Fulan reproached Fulan" when he enumerated his sins against him. Ibn Qutaybah said: "There is no reproach upon you after this day for what you did." The root of "tathrib" is corruption; one says "tharraba 'alayna" when he corrupted. In the hadith: "If the slave-girl of one of you commits fornication, let him lash her the prescribed punishment and not reproach her" — i.e., not shame her for fornication. Ibn 'Abbas said: He placed them in a state of pardon, and asked Allah to forgive them. al-Suddi said: When he made himself known to them, he asked them about his father; they said: "His eyes have gone white." So he gave them his shirt and said: ﴿Go with this shirt of mine and cast it over the face of my father; he will come back seeing﴾. This shirt had been in a silver tube hung around Yusuf's neck when he was thrown into the well, and it was from Paradise, and its mention has preceded [Yusuf: 18, 25, 26, 27, 28].

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿He will come back seeing﴾. Abu 'Ubaydah said: "He will return with sight."

If it is said: From where did he decide upon the unseen?

The answer: That was by revelation to him; said by Mujahid.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And bring me your entire family﴾. al-Kalbi said: His family numbered about seventy persons.

(p-277) His saying, the Exalted: ﴿When they entered upon him﴾ — there is an omission in the speech; its estimated meaning is: they set out for Egypt, and they entered upon Yusuf, and ﴿said: O Aziz﴾ — and they used to call their king by this title — ﴿Adversity has touched us and our family﴾, meaning poverty and need, ﴿and we have come with meager merchandise﴾.

As for the nature of that merchandise, there are seven opinions:

The first: that it was dirhams. This was narrated by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas. The second: that it was worn-out goods, such as ropes and sacks; narrated by Ibn Abi Mulaykah from Ibn 'Abbas. The third: it was dried curd (aqit), said by al-Hasan. The fourth: it was sandals and hides; narrated by Juwaybir from al-Dahhak. The fifth: it was the flour of the doum palm (sawiq al-muql); also related from al-Dahhak. The sixth: it was habba al-khadra' and sanawbar (pine nuts), said by Abu Salih. The seventh: it was wool and a little ghee, said by 'Abd Allah ibn al-Harith.

As for "muzjah" (meager), there are five opinions:

The first: that it means little. al-'Awfi narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Dirhams of no great value." Mujahid, Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Qutaybah also said this. al-Zajjaj said: The interpretation of it in the language is that "tazjiyah" is that by which one warding off; it is said: "So-and-so makes his livelihood pass" (yuzji al-'aysh), i.e., he gets by with little and is content with it. So the meaning is: we have come with merchandise by which we only ward off and sustain ourselves, and it is not something with which one lives in abundance. The poet said:

"The giver of a hundred purebred camels, and their slave-girl, a mother with her young, driving before her her young children."

i.e., she drives her children on (tudfa'u atfalaha).

The second: that it means inferior. Narrated by al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas. Abu 'Ubaydah said: It is only called "muzjah" for inferior goods because they are rejected, pushed away, not accepted by those who would spend them. He said: it is from "izja'," and "izja'" among the Arabs means driving and pushing. He recited:

"Let the guest, pushed away, weep for Milhan, and the widow who drives [her children] along with the night."

i.e., drives him.

The third: that it means unsalable (kasidah). Also narrated by al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas.

The fourth: that it means worn-out, i.e., shabby goods; narrated by Ibn Abi Mulaykah from Ibn 'Abbas.

The fifth: that it means deficient; narrated by Abu Husayn from 'Ikrimah.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So give us full measure﴾, i.e., complete it for us and do not diminish it because of the poorness of our merchandise.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and be charitable to us﴾. There are three opinions concerning it:

The first: be charitable to us by making up the difference between the price of good goods and inferior ones; said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Suddi. Ibn al-Anbari said: what they asked of him of leniency resembled charity, but it was not charity.

The second: by returning our brother; said by Ibn Jurayj, who said: that is because they were prophets, and charity is not lawful for prophets.

(p-279) The third: and be charitable to us by giving us more than our due; said by Ibn 'Uyaynah, who held that charity was lawful for prophets before our Prophet (ﷺ). This was related by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi, Abu al-Hasan al-Mawardi, and Abu Ya'la ibn al-Farra'.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah rewards the charitable﴾, i.e., with reward. al-Dahhak said: They did not say "Allah will reward you if you are charitable to us," because they did not know that he was a believer.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Do you know what you did to Yusuf and his brother﴾. Concerning the reason for his saying this to them, there are three opinions:

The first: that he brought out to them a copy of the document they had written against themselves concerning the sale of him to Malik ibn Du'r, and at the end of the document was: "and Yahudha wrote it." When they read the document they acknowledged its authenticity and said: "This is a document we wrote against ourselves when selling a slave who belonged to us." Yusuf then said: "You deserve punishment," and he ordered them to be killed. They said: "If you are going to do it, then take our goods to Ya'qub." Then Yahudha turned to some of his brothers and said: "Our father was constantly grieving over the loss of one of his sons; how will he be when he is told of our destruction, all of us?" At that, Yusuf was softened and revealed his matter to them, and said this to them. This was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: that when they said: "﴿Adversity has touched us and our family﴾," mercy overtook him, and he said this to them; said by Ibn Ishaq.

The third: that Ya'qub wrote to him a letter: "If you return my son, well; otherwise I will make a supplication against you that will reach your seventh generation." So he wept and said this to them.

Concerning "hal" (do you know) there are two opinions:

The first: that it is interrogative for the magnification of the story, not meaning the question itself. Ibn (p-280) al-Anbari said: The meaning is: how great is what you committed, and how ugly is what you preferred of severing ties of kinship and wasting the right. This is like the Arab saying: "Do you know whom you disobeyed? Do you know whom you antagonized?" He does not mean by this a question, but intends to make the matter appear appalling. The poet said:

"Do the sons of Marwan hope for my hearing and obedience?"

He did not intend a question; he meant that this is not hoped for from them. He said: It is also possible that the meaning is: Did you know the consequence of what you did to Yusuf and his brother, of Allah's letting them suffer hardship? This verse confirms His saying: "You will surely inform them of this matter of theirs."

The second: that "hal" here means "qad" (indeed); mentioned by some of the exegetes.

If it is said: What they did to Yusuf is known, so what did they do to his brother? They did not strive to imprison him nor intend it.

The answer has several aspects: The first: they separated him from Yusuf, thereby embittering his life. The second: they harmed him after the loss of Yusuf. The third: they reviled him when he was accused of stealing the drinking cup.

Concerning His saying: ﴿when you were ignorant﴾ there are four opinions:

The first: when you were children; said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second: sinners; said by Muqatil. The third: ignorant of the disobedience to a father, the severing of kinship, and following desire. The fourth: ignorant of what Yusuf's affair would come to; these two were mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Are you indeed Yusuf?﴾ Ibn Kathir, Abu Ja'far, and Ibn Muhaysin read "innaka" as a statement. Others read it with two clearly articulated hamzas, and some inserted an alif between them.

(p-281) The exegetes differed: did they recognize him, or did they take him for someone resembling him? There are two opinions:

The first: that they took him to resemble Yusuf; said by Ibn 'Abbas in one narration.

The second: that they recognized him; said by Ibn Ishaq. Concerning the cause of their recognition of him there are three opinions:

The first: that he smiled, and they likened his front teeth to Yusuf's front teeth; said by al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: that he had a mark like a mole on his forehead, and Ya'qub had one like it, and Ishaq had one like it, and Sarah had one like it; so when he removed the crown from his head they recognized him; narrated by 'Ata' from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: that he uncovered the veil and they recognized him; said by Ibn Ishaq.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And bring me your entire family﴾. al-Kalbi said: His family numbered about seventy persons.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 12, verse 94:**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When the caravan set out﴾, meaning it departed from Egypt heading for Canaan. The one who carried the shirt was Yahudha (Judah). Al-Suddi said: Yahudha said to Yusuf: "I am the one who brought the shirt to Ya'qub (Jacob) with false blood and grieved him, and now I will carry your shirt to delight him." So he carried it. Ibn 'Abbas said: He went out barefoot and bareheaded, running, with seven loaves of bread, of which he had not finished eating.

(p-٢٨٤) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Their father said﴾, meaning Ya'qub, to those of his family, relatives and grandchildren who were present: ﴿Indeed, I find the scent of Yusuf﴾. The meaning of "ajidu" (I find) is "ashummu" (I smell). The poet said:

"It is not the creaking of the bier that you hear,
but the joints of a people cracking.
And it is not the fresh musk that you smell,
but that is the praise that remains behind."

If it is asked: How did Ya'qub smell his scent while he was in Egypt? And why did he not smell it from the well, and after his exit from it, when the distance there was shorter?

There are two answers to this. The first: God, exalted is He, concealed the matter of Yusuf from Ya'qub at the beginning, so that the trial would occur through which the reward is completed. Then He caused him to smell the scent from a distant place when the trial ended and relief came.

The second: this shirt was in a silver tube hanging on Yusuf's neck, as was previously explained. When he unfolded it, the fragrances of Paradise spread in this world and reached Ya'qub, and he knew that the scent came from that shirt. Mujahid said: A wind blew and struck the shirt, so the fragrances of Paradise spread in this world and reached Ya'qub, and he found the scent of Paradise. He knew that there is no scent of Paradise in this world except what came from that shirt. Therefore he said: ﴿Indeed, I find the scent of Yusuf﴾. It was also said: The east wind asked its Lord for permission to bring Ya'qub the scent of Yusuf before the bearer of good news, and it was granted. For this reason every grieving person finds comfort in the east wind, and the distressed find relief in it. It is a gentle wind that comes from the direction of the east. Abu Sakhr al-Hudhali said:

"When I say, 'This is the time I forget,' it stirs me:
the breeze of the east wind from where the dawn rises."

Ibn 'Abbas said: He found the scent of Yusuf's shirt from a distance of eight nights, eighty farsakhs.

(p-٢٨٥) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Were it not that you would deem me senile﴾. Regarding this there are five opinions:

The first: "tujahhiluni", you would consider me ignorant. This was narrated by Ibn Abi Talha from Ibn 'Abbas, and Muqatil also said it.

The second: "tusafihuni", you would consider me foolish. This was narrated by 'Abd Allah ibn Abi al-Hudhayl from Ibn 'Abbas, and 'Ata', Qatada and Mujahid in one narration also said it. In another narration he said: "Lest you say: your mind has gone."

The third: "tukadhdhibuni", you would call me a liar. This was narrated by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Dahhak also said it.

The fourth: "tuharrimuni", you would deem me senile. This was said by al-Hasan, and Mujahid in one narration. Ibn Faris said: "al-fanad" is the denial of sound mind due to old age.

The fifth: "tu'ajjizuni", you would deem me feeble. This was said by Ibn Qutayba. Abu 'Ubayda said: "tusafihuni, wa tu'ajjizuni, wa talumuni", you would deem me foolish, feeble and blameworthy. He recited:

"O my two companions, leave off blaming me and deeming me senile,
for what has passed of a matter cannot be returned."

Ibn Jarir said: The root of "tafnid" is corruption, and the statements of the exegetes are close in meaning. I heard Shaykh Abu Muhammad Ibn al-Khashshab say: His saying, ﴿were it not that you would deem me senile﴾, contains an ellipsis (idmar), and its estimated meaning is: "I would have told you that he is alive."

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They said, "By Allah, you are surely in your old error."﴾ Ibn ʿAbbas said: "It was his grandsons (the sons of his sons) who addressed him with this, and likewise al-Suddi said: 'This is the statement of the sons of his sons, because his sons were in Egypt.'"

Regarding the meaning of this error (ḍalāl) there are three opinions:

(p-286) The first: that it means error (khaṭa'), said by Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Zayd. The second: that it means madness (junūn), said by Saʿid ibn Jubayr. The third: that it means misery and hardship (shaqa' wa-ʿanā'), said by Muqatil. He intends by this the misery of this world.

Ibn al-Jawzi, *Zad al-Masir*, on Surah Yusuf (12), verses 96–98:

Allah's words, ﴿When the bearer of good news came﴾, have two interpretations.

The first is that he was Yahudha (Judah). This was said by Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas, and Wahb ibn Munabbih, al-Suddi, and the majority of scholars held it. The second is that he was Shim'un (Simeon). This was said by al-Dahhak.

If it is asked: what is the difference between His words here, ﴿When he came﴾, and His words elsewhere, ﴿When there came to them﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:89)?

The answer is that both are dialects of the Quraysh, and Allah addressed them with both. The inclusion of "an" (أن) emphasises the completion of the verb in the past, and its omission relies on the past event being clear in itself. This was mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari.

Allah's words, ﴿he cast it over his face﴾, refer to the shirt, and ﴿over his face﴾ refers to Ya'qub (Jacob). ﴿And he regained his sight﴾: al-irtidad (ارتداد) means a thing returning to a state it was previously in. Ibn al-Anbari said: He said "irtadda" and not "uddda" (was returned), because this is one of the verbs attributed to the objects of action, like the saying: "The palm tree grew tall, and Allah made it tall," and "The tree moved, and Allah moved it." Al-Dahhak said: His sight returned to him after blindness, his strength after weakness, his youth after old age, and his joy after sorrow.

Yahya ibn Yaman related from Sufyan who said: When the bearer of good news came to Ya'qub, he said: "In what religion did you leave Yusuf?" He said: "In Islam." He said: "Now the favour is complete."

(p. 287) Allah's words, ﴿Did I not tell you that I know from Allah what you do not know?﴾: there are sayings concerning this which were mentioned shortly before.

Allah's words, ﴿O our father, ask forgiveness for us our sins﴾: they asked him to seek forgiveness for them for what they had done, because he was a prophet whose supplication is answered. ﴿He said: I shall ask forgiveness for you of my Lord﴾. Concerning the reason for his delaying this, there are three sayings.

The first is that he delayed it to wait for the time which is the likeliest for a response. Within this there are three sayings:
One: he delayed it until the night of Friday. Ibn Abbas related this from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Wahb said: He used to ask forgiveness for them every Friday night for twenty-odd years.
Two: until the time of the pre-dawn meal (sahar) on the night of Friday. Abu Salih related this from Ibn Abbas. Tawus said: This coincided with the night of Ashura.
Three: until the time of the pre-dawn meal. Ikrimah related this from Ibn Abbas, and Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Umar, Qatadah, al-Suddi and Muqatil also held this view. Al-Zajjaj said: He meant the time which is most fitting for the answering of supplication, not that he withheld seeking forgiveness for them. This is more in keeping with the character of the prophets, peace be upon them.

The second saying is that he deferred them from hastening the promise. Ata al-Khurasani said: Requests made to the young are easier than those made to the elders. Do you not see Yusuf's words: ﴿No reproach against you today﴾, and Ya'qub's words: ﴿I shall ask forgiveness for you of my Lord﴾?

The third is that he delayed them so that he could ask Yusuf, and if Yusuf pardoned them, he would seek forgiveness for them. This was said by al-Sha'bi. It is related from Anas ibn Malik that they said: "O our father, if Allah pardons us, well; otherwise there will be no comfort for us in this world." So Ya'qub supplicated and Yusuf said "Amin", but He did not answer concerning them for twenty years. Then Jibril came and said: "Allah has answered your supplication concerning your son, and has pardoned what they did to him, and has made firm their covenants from now on regarding prophethood."

The commentators said: Yusuf had sent with the bearer of good news to Ya'qub provisions and two hundred riding beasts, and asked him to bring his family and children to him. When Ya'qub set out and drew near to Egypt, Yusuf asked the king who was above him for permission to go out to meet Ya'qub, and he gave him permission and commanded the notables among his companions to ride with him. He went out with four thousand soldiers, and the people of Egypt went out with them.

It is also said that the king went out with them too. When Ya'qub and Yusuf met, they both wept. Yusuf said: "O father, you wept over me until your sight was lost; do you not know that the Resurrection will gather me and you together?" He said: "My son, I feared that your religion would be taken from you, and then we would not be gathered together."

It is also said that Ya'qub initiated the greeting, saying: "Peace be upon you, O remover of sorrows."
