Yahya ibn Yaman related from Sufyan who said: When the bearer of good news came to Ya'qub, he said: "In what religion did you leave Yusuf?" He said: "In Islam." He said: "Now the favour is complete."

(p. 287) Allah's words, ﴿Did I not tell you that I know from Allah what you do not know?﴾: there are sayings concerning this which were mentioned shortly before.

Allah's words, ﴿O our father, ask forgiveness for us our sins﴾: they asked him to seek forgiveness for them for what they had done, because he was a prophet whose supplication is answered. ﴿He said: I shall ask forgiveness for you of my Lord﴾. Concerning the reason for his delaying this, there are three sayings.

The first is that he delayed it to wait for the time which is the likeliest for a response. Within this there are three sayings:
One: he delayed it until the night of Friday. Ibn Abbas related this from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Wahb said: He used to ask forgiveness for them every Friday night for twenty-odd years.
Two: until the time of the pre-dawn meal (sahar) on the night of Friday. Abu Salih related this from Ibn Abbas. Tawus said: This coincided with the night of Ashura.
Three: until the time of the pre-dawn meal. Ikrimah related this from Ibn Abbas, and Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Umar, Qatadah, al-Suddi and Muqatil also held this view. Al-Zajjaj said: He meant the time which is most fitting for the answering of supplication, not that he withheld seeking forgiveness for them. This is more in keeping with the character of the prophets, peace be upon them.

The second saying is that he deferred them from hastening the promise. Ata al-Khurasani said: Requests made to the young are easier than those made to the elders. Do you not see Yusuf's words: ﴿No reproach against you today﴾, and Ya'qub's words: ﴿I shall ask forgiveness for you of my Lord﴾?

The third is that he delayed them so that he could ask Yusuf, and if Yusuf pardoned them, he would seek forgiveness for them. This was said by al-Sha'bi. It is related from Anas ibn Malik that they said: "O our father, if Allah pardons us, well; otherwise there will be no comfort for us in this world." So Ya'qub supplicated and Yusuf said "Amin", but He did not answer concerning them for twenty years. Then Jibril came and said: "Allah has answered your supplication concerning your son, and has pardoned what they did to him, and has made firm their covenants from now on regarding prophethood."

The commentators said: Yusuf had sent with the bearer of good news to Ya'qub provisions and two hundred riding beasts, and asked him to bring his family and children to him. When Ya'qub set out and drew near to Egypt, Yusuf asked the king who was above him for permission to go out to meet Ya'qub, and he gave him permission and commanded the notables among his companions to ride with him. He went out with four thousand soldiers, and the people of Egypt went out with them.

It is also said that the king went out with them too. When Ya'qub and Yusuf met, they both wept. Yusuf said: "O father, you wept over me until your sight was lost; do you not know that the Resurrection will gather me and you together?" He said: "My son, I feared that your religion would be taken from you, and then we would not be gathered together."

It is also said that Ya'qub initiated the greeting, saying: "Peace be upon you, O remover of sorrows."

Ibn al-Jawzi, *Zad al-Masir*, on Surah Yusuf (12), verses 96–98:

Allah's words, ﴿When the bearer of good news came﴾, have two interpretations.

The first is that he was Yahudha (Judah). This was said by Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas, and Wahb ibn Munabbih, al-Suddi, and the majority of scholars held it. The second is that he was Shim'un (Simeon). This was said by al-Dahhak.

Allah's words, ﴿he cast it over his face﴾, refer to the shirt, and ﴿over his face﴾ refers to Ya'qub (Jacob). ﴿And he regained his sight﴾: al-irtidad (ارتداد) means a thing returning to a state it was previously in. Ibn al-Anbari said: He said "irtadda" and not "uddda" (was returned), because this is one of the verbs attributed to the objects of action, like the saying: "The palm tree grew tall, and Allah made it tall," and "The tree moved, and Allah moved it." Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 12, verse 99:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So when they entered upon Yusuf﴾ — meaning Ya'qub and his children.

Regarding this entering there are two opinions:

One of them: it is the entering of the land of Egypt; then he said to them: ﴿Enter Egypt﴾, meaning the city.

The second: it is the entering of Egypt itself; then he said to them: ﴿Enter Egypt﴾, that is, settle in it.

Regarding His saying: ﴿He drew his parents close to him﴾ there are two opinions:

One of them: his father and his maternal aunt, because his mother had died. This is what Ibn 'Abbas and the majority said.

The second: his father and his mother. This is what al-Hasan and Ibn Ishaq said.

(p-289) Regarding His saying: ﴿If Allah wills, you will be secure﴾ there are four opinions:

The first: in the speech there is an inversion, so the meaning is: "I will ask my Lord to forgive you, if Allah wills; indeed He is the Forgiving, the Merciful." This is the saying of Ibn Jurayj.

The second: the exception returns to the security. Within this there are two opinions: one of them: he did not trust that the calamities had turned away from them. The second: that people in the past used to fear the kings of Egypt, so they would not enter except under their protection.

The third: it returns to the entering of Egypt, because he said this to them when he met them before their entering, as its explanation has already preceded.

The fourth: that "in" (in) has the meaning of "when" (idh), like His saying: ﴿if they desire chastity﴾ [al-Nur: 33]. Ibn 'Abbas said: they entered Egypt on that day, and they were a little over seventy, males and females. Ibn Mas'ud said: they entered while they were ninety-three, and they left with Musa while they were six hundred thousand and seventy thousand.

قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿وَرَفَعَ أبَوَيْهِ عَلَى العَرْشِ﴾ In "أبَوَيْهِ" (his two parents) there are two views, which were already mentioned in the verse before it. Here "al-'arsh" (the throne) means the seat of rule. He seated his parents upon it. ﴿وَخَرُّوا لَهُ﴾ meaning: his parents and his brothers "fell down before him."

Regarding the pronoun in "لَهُ" (before him), there are two views:

The first: it refers to Yusuf. This is the view of the majority. Abu Salih reported from Ibn Abbas: "Their prostration was like the posture of bowing, as the non-Arabs do." Al-Hasan said: "Allah commanded them to prostrate for the interpretation of the dream." Ibn al-Anbari said: "They prostrated to him as a form of greeting, not in the sense of worship. In that age, people greeted one another with prostration and bowing. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prohibited this." Anas ibn Malik narrated that he said: "A man said: 'O Messenger of Allah, when one of us meets his friend, should he bow to him?' He said: 'No.'"

The second: it refers to Allah. The meaning is: "They fell down in prostration to Allah." This was narrated by Ata and al-Dahhak from Ibn Abbas. The meaning then is that they prostrated in gratitude to Allah, because He had brought them together with Yusuf.

قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿هَذا تَأْوِيلُ رُؤْيايَ﴾ That is, the fulfilment of what I saw. He had seen them in his dream prostrating to him, so Allah showed him that in waking reality.

The scholars differed regarding the period between his dream and its interpretation, giving seven views:

The first: forty years. This was said by Salman al-Farisi, Abdullah ibn Shaddad ibn al-Had, and Muqatil.
The second: twenty-two years. This was said by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas.
The third: eighty years. This was said by al-Hasan and al-Fudayl ibn Iyad.
The fourth: thirty-six years. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ikrimah, and al-Suddi.
The fifth: thirty-five years. This was said by Qatadah.
The sixth: seventy years. This was said by Abdullah ibn Shawdhab.
The seventh: eighteen years. This was said by Ibn Ishaq.

قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿وَقَدْ أحْسَنَ بِي﴾ That is, "He was kind to me." Al-Badw means the open land. Ibn Abbas said: "Al-Badw means the desert (al-badiyah), and they were people of tents and livestock."

قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿مِن بَعْدِ أنْ نَزَغَ الشَّيْطانُ بَيْنِي وبَيْنَ إخْوَتِي﴾ That is, "Satan caused corruption between us." Abu Ubaydah said: "It is said: 'nazagha baynahum yanzaghu,' meaning he caused corruption and stirred up strife." Some read the zay in "yanzigh" with a kasra. ﴿إنَّ رَبِّي لَطِيفٌ لِما يَشاءُ﴾ That is, "Indeed my Lord is Subtle in what He wills," meaning He knows the fine details of affairs. We have already explained the meaning of "al-Latif" (the Subtle) in (al-An'am: 102).

If it is said: Yusuf received five blessings in succession, so why did he mention only the prison, and why did he not mention the well, which was more difficult?

The answer has several aspects:

The first: he left out mention of the well out of generosity, so that he would not remind his brothers of their deed. He had said: ﴿لا تَثْرِيبَ عَلَيْكُمُ اليَوْمَ﴾ "No blame upon you today."

The second: he went from the well to slavery, and from the prison to kingship, so this blessing was more complete.

The third: his long stay in the prison was a punishment for him, unlike the well, so he thanked Allah for His pardon.

The scholars of biographies (al-siyar) said: Ya'qub remained after his arrival in Egypt for twenty-four years. Some said: seventeen years, in the most pleasant of lives. When his death approached, he bequeathed to Yusuf (p-292) that he be carried to al-Sham so that he could bury him beside his father Ishaq. This was done, and his age was one hundred and forty-seven years. Then Yusuf longed for Paradise, and knowing that this world does not last, he wished for death. Ibn Abbas and Qatadah said: "No prophet before him had wished for death." So he said: ﴿رَبِّ قَدْ آتَيْتَنِي مِنَ المُلْكِ﴾ "My Lord, You have given me of sovereignty," meaning the kingship of Egypt, ﴿وَعَلَّمْتَنِي مِن تَأْوِيلِ الأحادِيثِ﴾ "and taught me of the interpretation of narrations." Its explanation has already preceded (Yusuf: 6).

Regarding the particle "مِن" (min) in "مِنَ الْمُلْكِ" (of sovereignty), there are two views:

The first: it is a redundant particle (silah), said by Muqatil.
The second: it is partitive (lil-tab'id), meaning "some of," because he was not given all sovereignty, nor all interpretation of narrations.

قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿فاطِرَ السَّماواتِ والأرْضِ﴾ "Originator of the heavens and the earth." We have explained this in (al-An'am: 6).

﴿أنْتَ ولِيِّي﴾ "You are my Guardian," that is, the One who takes charge of my affairs. ﴿تَوَفَّنِي مُسْلِمًا﴾ "Let me die as a Muslim." Ibn Abbas said: "He means: do not strip Islam from me until You cause me to die upon it." Ibn Aqil used to say: "Yusuf did not wish for death. Rather, he asked to die upon a certain attribute. The meaning is: take my soul when You take it, as a Muslim." The Shaykh said: "This is the correct view."

قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿وَألْحِقْنِي بِالصّالِحِينَ﴾ "and join me with the righteous." The meaning is: join me to their ranks. Regarding who they are, there are two views:

The first: they are the people of Paradise. This was said by Ikrimah.
The second: they are his forefathers Ibrahim, Ishaq, and Ya'qub. This was said by al-Dahhak. They said: When Yusuf was near death, he bequeathed to Yahudha (Judah), and then he died. People disputed over his burial, each one wishing to be buried in his own district, hoping for blessing. They agreed to bury him in the Nile so that the water would flow over him and reach everyone. So they buried him in a chest of marble, and it remained there until Musa carried it out when he left Egypt and buried it in the land of Kan'an (Canaan). Al-Hasan said: "Yusuf died when he was one hundred and twenty years old." Muqatil mentioned that he died two years after Ya'qub.

(p-293) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That is of the news of the unseen﴾, meaning: that which We have related to you of the matter of Yusuf and his brothers is among the reports that were hidden from you, so Allah sent it down to you as evidence of your prophethood. ﴿And you were not with them﴾, meaning: with the brothers of Yusuf ﴿when they resolved upon their plan﴾, meaning: when they determined to cast him into the well ﴿while they were scheming﴾ against Yusuf. In this there is an argument for the soundness of the prophethood of our Prophet (ﷺ), for he did not witness that story, nor did he read the Book, and yet he related it in this inimitable speech, which indicates that he was informed of it by revelation.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 12, verses 103–104:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And most of mankind will not believe, even if you should strive for it﴾. Ibn al-Anbari said: Quraysh and the Jews asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the story of Yusuf and his brothers, and he explained it in a thorough explanation, hoping that this would be a cause for their conversion to Islam. But they went against his expectation, so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) grieved, and Allah the Exalted consoled him with this verse. Al-Zajjaj said: Its meaning is: Most people will not be believers, even if you strive to guide them. ﴿And you do not ask them for any payment for it﴾, i.e., for the Qur'an, its recitation, and your guiding them. ﴿It is not but a reminder to the worlds﴾, i.e., it is only a reminder for them, containing what is good for them and their salvation.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 12, verses 103–104:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And most of mankind will not believe, even if you should strive for it﴾. Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 12, verse 105:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And how many a sign﴾, i.e., and how many (a sign) ﴿among the signs﴾, i.e., a sign and an indication guiding them (p-294) to the Oneness of Allah, from the affairs of the heavens and the earth, ﴿they pass by it﴾, i.e., they go past it, neither reflecting nor taking heed.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 12, verse 106:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And most of them do not believe in Allah except that they associate others with Him﴾. Regarding them there are three opinions.

The first: they are the polytheists (mushrikun). Then, concerning the meaning of this as it relates to them, there are two statements. One of them: they believe that Allah is their Creator and their Provider, yet they associate others with Him. This was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas, and Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, al-Sha'bi and Qatadah said the same.

The second: it was revealed concerning the talbiyah (the call of pilgrimage) of the polytheists of the Arabs. They used to say: "Here I am, O Allah, here I am; here I am, You have no partner, except a partner who is Yours, You possess him and what he possesses." This was narrated by al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second opinion: they are the Christians, who believe that He is their Creator and Provider, yet with that they associate others with Him. This was narrated by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: they are the hypocrites (munafiqun), who outwardly believe for the sake of being seen by people, while inwardly they are disbelievers. This was said by al-Hasan.

If it is asked: how can he describe the polytheist as a believer?

The answer: it is not meant as true faith. Rather the meaning is: most of them, while they display faith with their tongues, are polytheists.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Do they feel secure that there will not come upon them an overwhelming punishment from Allah?﴾ Ibn Qutaybah said: al-ghashiyah means that which covers them and envelops them. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is that there will come to them what overwhelms them of the punishment. Al-baghtah means a sudden onset, from a direction they do not expect.

(p-295) His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Say, "This is my way"﴾. The meaning: Say, O Muhammad, to the polytheists: "This is the call to which I invite, and the path upon which I stand, is my way" — that is, my sunnah (practice, tradition) and my manhaj (method, approach). The word sabil (way, path) may be treated as masculine or feminine, and we have mentioned this in (Al 'Imran: 195). ﴿I invite to Allah with insight﴾, that is, with certainty. Ibn al-Anbari said: Every Muslim does not fail to call to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, for when he recites the Qur'an, he has called to Allah by what it contains. It is also permissible for the sentence to be complete at His words "to Allah," and then begin: ﴿with insight, I and whoever follows me﴾.

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And glory be to Allah﴾. The meaning: And say: "Glory be to Allah," declaring Him far above what they associate with Him.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 12, verse 109:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We did not send before you except men﴾. This was revealed because of their saying: "Why did God not send an angel?" So the meaning is: how do they marvel at Our sending you, when all the (other) messengers were in the same condition as yours, ["to whom We revealed"] (yūḥā ilayhim). Ḥafṣ, from ʿĀṣim, read "nūḥī" with the nūn. By "the towns" (al-qurā) is meant cities (al-madāʾin). Al-Ḥasan said: God did not send a prophet from among the people of the desert (al-bādiya), nor from the jinn, nor from women. Qatada said: because the people of the towns are more knowledgeable and more forbearing than the people of the tents (ʿamūd, lit. "pillars", i.e., the nomadic tents).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Have they not travelled in the land﴾, meaning: the polytheists who deny your prophethood, ﴿and so they would look﴾ at the places of destruction of the nations that denied (their messengers), and so take warning from that. ﴿And the abode of the Hereafter﴾, meaning: Paradise, ﴿is better﴾ than the world ﴿for those who fear (God)﴾, that is, those who guard against polytheism (shirk). Al-Farrāʾ said: the abode (al-dār) is attributed to the Hereafter (al-ākhira), and it is the Hereafter itself, because the Arabs sometimes attribute a thing to itself when its wording differs, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, this is the true certainty (ḥaqq al-yaqīn)﴾ [al-Wāqiʿa: 95], where al-ḥaqq is the same as al-yaqīn; and as in their saying: "I came to you in the year of the first (ʿām al-awwal)" and "on the day of Thursday (yawm al-khamīs)."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Will you not then use your reason?﴾ The people of Medina, Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥafṣ, al-Mufaḍḍal and Yaʿqūb read "taʿqilūn" with the tā' (the second person), while the others read it with the yā' (the third person). The meaning: "Will they not then reason about this and believe?"

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 12, verse 110:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Until, when the Messengers despaired﴾. The meaning is connected to the previous verse, so its estimated sense is: "We did not send before you except men, and they called their peoples, and they denied them, and they were patient, and their calling and their people's denial went on for a long time, until, when the Messengers despaired." On this there are two views:

The first: they despaired of their peoples' believing, as said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: they despaired of Us punishing their people, as said by Mujahid. ﴿And they thought that they had been denied﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi, Abu ʿAmr and Ibn ʿAmir recited "kudhdhibu" (with the dhal shaddah and the kaf damma), and the meaning is: the Messengers were certain that their people had denied them, so here the word "zann" (thought) carries the sense of "yaqin" (certainty). This is the view of al-Hasan, ʿAta and Qatada. ʿAsim, Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited "kudhibu" (light, with the kaf kasra and the dhal sukun), and the meaning is: their people thought that the Messengers had been lied to concerning the victory they had been promised, because the Messengers would not think such a thing. Abu Razin, Mujahid and al-Dahhak recited "kadhabu" (with a fatha on the kaf and the dhal, light), and the meaning is: their people also thought that they (the Messengers) had lied, as said by al-Zajjaj.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿There came to them Our help﴾, meaning: the Messengers. ﴿So We saved whom We willed﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi, Abu ʿAmr, Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited "fanunji" with two nuns, the first damma and the second sukun, and the ya sukun. Ibn ʿAmir, Abu Bakr, Hafs (all from ʿAsim) and Yaʿqub recited "fa-nujjiya" with a shaddah on the jim, a fatha on the ya, and one nun, meaning: the believers, who were saved when the punishment descended.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 12, verse 111:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Certainly there was in their stories﴾, i.e., in the account of Yusuf and his brothers. ʿAbd al-Warith narrated the kasr of the qaf (qasasihim), which is the reading of Qatada and Abu al-Jawza'. "A lesson" (ʿibrah), i.e., an admonition, "for people of understanding" (ulu al-albab), i.e., for those with sound intellects. And that is for two reasons:

The first of them: what befell Yusuf of his being honoured and made a ruler after he had been enslaved. For the One who did that for him is able to honour Muhammad (ﷺ) and elevate his word.

The second: whoever reflects will know that Muhammad (ﷺ), despite being unlettered (ummi), did not bring this story in agreement with what is in the Torah from his own self. So he took this as evidence for the soundness of his prophethood.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿It was not a narration that could be invented﴾. Regarding what is referred to there are two opinions:

The first: that it is the Qur'an, said by Qatada.

The second: that it is the stories that preceded, said by Ibn Ishaq. According to the first opinion, the meaning of His saying ﴿but a confirmation of what was before it﴾ is: but it was a confirmation of what was before it of the books, and ﴿a detailed explanation of all things﴾ "which is needed" from the matters of the religion, ﴿and guidance﴾ (a clarification) (p-298) ﴿and mercy for a people who believe﴾, i.e., who affirm what Muhammad (ﷺ) brought. And according to the second opinion, it is a detailed explanation of all things from the account of Yusuf and his brothers.
